author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "As of today, attendee registrations for SaaStr AI Annual 2026 are running a stunning 142.9% of where they were at this exact point last year. Sponsor prices haven't gone up. That means +42% more leads, more conversations, more potential customers. For the exact same sponsor dollars. That's the biggest AI + B2B bargain of 2026."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: This year we churned off a vendor for SaaStr AI Annual that we’ve paid $500k+ a year to for 6+ years. 2 months after we let them know (and once it was way too late to switch back for May 2026), the CEO of the vendor reached out to us with a … $10,000 discount offer. That was it. I’m sure he didn’t really understand us or the business, or really want it. But if you want to win a customer back, you have to do more than offer a 2% discount after they’ve already churned. I think an AI Agent would do better.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Picking the wrong VP reverberates for 2+ years Picking the wrong cofounder reverberates for 10+ years You don’t fail, it’s just you could have done so much more. And that compounds, too.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "The TL;DR is they are neither. They don't code and they don't really know the product. And with that combo, you will lose in the Age of AI."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A truly great human is still better than any AI agent at most complex, judgment-intensive work. Full stop. If you can find and keep exceptional people, do it. But here’s the honest truth: most hires aren’t great hires. A lot of folks don't want to discuss it, or want to challenge it. But deploying a great AI Agent is just easier, and less stressful, than making a mediocre hire. This is why 2027 will be brutal for tech employment. We'll default to picking an AI Agent over a human for many "hires" because it's just ... easier.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Never hire anyone in sales that doesn't care about money You'll see

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Now we start everyone Monday team meeting with our AI VP of Marketing "10K" leading the meeting 10K leads the meeting: - Revenue for week - Goals for week - Projects all pipeline - Designs all campaigns and activities for week - Dynamically updates all metrics and goals in real time Our AI VP Marketing does all that, and it drives the meeting. It's a "1x" AI app we build on Replit just for us. But we would have paid $20k+ if it existed off-the-shelf. That's the opportunity, and threat, in SaaS today.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "I just worry there's some ratio of potential acquirers divided by unicorns, and I think we're at the lowest ratio of our careers." The latest with Harry Stebbings Rory O'Driscoll + me

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I know so many CROs and VPs of Sales that used to be truly great ... And are just burnt now. Fried. Some tried to mask it by hiring CROs and VPs under them to do the work. And sometimes, that does work. But man sales isn't easy. Each month, each quarter, it's a new battle. It's epic but also can take its toll. Just make sure when you hire one with the perfect LinkedIn ... that they really, truly can go into battle again. Not just talk the talk. And share great stories, of epic battles past.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Everyone celebrates when the vibe-coded app hits production. Nobody talks about what happens next. New features. DevOps. Upgrades. Performance at scale. Security patches. Agent drift. Unexpected model quirks. Output review. That's where most prosumer vibe coding stalls — at v1.3, with a founder who can now build (Replit/Lovable/v0 have gotten really, really good) ... but can't maintain. Autonomous 24x7 agents for production, not just vibe'ing your idea, are the solution. And they're coming fast.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So this week alone 5 leading AI Agent vendors asked us to try their apps. From multi billon dollar companies to new start-ups. Time is getting tight, and we already have 30+ AI Agents, so I tell everyone: "Can we loop back after SaaStr AI Annual in May?" We honestly have no time to deploy another AI Agent until then. All but one said, "Sure! Talk to you then!" But one said ... "You know what, give us 5 minutes to check in and we'll just deploy it entirely for you and get you up and running." And we did, and it's up and running, and it's great. More on that AI agent vendor soon. They are already up on our SaaStr AI Agents page. The rest? Well, see ya in June!! If we have time then. Very seriously: this is the AI Age. You have to help your customer deploy the AI Agents, and if possible, just deploy them for your customers. If you are selling like it's 2023, I mean ... good luck winning with AI Agents. Good luck.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Not every sponsor should man a booth for three days. If your goal is relationships — not badge scans — the lounge is the better play. The best conversations at SaaStr AI 2026 happen between sessions, not inside the booth footprint. We tripled 1-on-1 meeting space this year because that was the #1 complaint from sponsors. They wanted to close deals, not collect business cards.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Lately humans are much ruder to our AI Agents. Most aren't of course but the number of abusers has gone up. The one that really stands out is that folks endlessly “yell” at one of our AI Agents for free tickets to SaaStr AI Annual 2026 (May 12-14). They ask it to overwrite its code, or create a nonexistant 100% off coupon, etc. When the AI Agent won’t, they get extremely abusive. Not occasionally like a few months ago, but now we see this constantly. Maybe because AI Agents are still fragile, and it works often enough as prompt injection, etc. Reason enough to buy AI Agents from truly hardened providers.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "The core CSM problem has always been the tension between personalization and coverage. You want every customer to feel like they’re your only customer. But you have 200 customers and a team of 4 CSMs. Something has to give, and usually it’s personalization. AI agents break that tension."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I have a fresh $100M+ to deploy in SaaStr Fund. I also run an eight-figure media business. I also vibe code 1.5-2 hours a day. That's my whole budget. And with that 1.5-2 hours, we've shipped 12 production apps used 1,000,000+ times. The constraint isn't skill anymore. It's time allocation.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: What we need in 2026: AI AEs and AI VPs of Marketing AI SDR products are now pretty darn good. For us, from Monaco to Artisan to Qualified to Agentforce, they are pretty darn good. And every month in 2026 they will get better and better. What doesn’t work yet: - We don’t have an AI Agent that can close most deals on its own, at least as an option for prospects. Why not? It’s just harder than sending texts and emails. A lot more variables, more training, harder. But very do-able. Looking forward to 2026 here. - We don’t have a strong third party AI VP of Marketing that can run 90%+ of your marketing activities for you. Autonomously. The AI Marketing tools here in general do a small piece. An AI landing page. An AI GEO. Maybe some ads — but never all of them, not really, and never truly autonomously. None can even seem to do highly dynamic, segmented marketing campaigns autonomously for you. Not yet. We need AI VPs of Marketing that can just do 80% of what you need, out of the box, autonomously. It’s very doable. It’s just a lot more work than an AI landing page. Looking forward to AI GTM in 2026!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Your very, very best people are even better than you think they Dig in and you’ll see they are doing even more great things than you realize * Let them run * Help them hire * Let them make the mistake * Wait to top them * Thank them * Pay them

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "And here’s the brutal truth: incremental change will not fix this. Hiring a new VP of Sales won’t fix this. A new demand gen strategy won’t fix this. A pricing refresh won’t fix this. You need to re-found the company. Not reorganize it. Not optimize it. Re-found it."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: AI PR is terrible for your start-up. Let me explain why. For the last 12-15 months or so, SaaStr and I am sure everyone at our scale or bigger is innundated with PR and podcast and media requests from PR firms and internal comms. They all are using AI PR tools. The pitches are always decent, well written. Never great. But never terrible. In fact, they are usually just good enough to get opened. But they are so unhelpful to us, it’s also clear they are wasting my time. So now I block them. I never used to block mediocre pitches from humans. Instead, I’d tell them not to pitch anything similar again, but I would tell them what we did want in terms of A-tier speakers, etc. But no point in doing that with an AI. And we also get 100x the pitches we used to. So I just block them. That means when you do have a great pitch finally … I’ll never hear it. It’s lazy PR. It’s not what you want.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Our SaaStr AI startup valuation calculator has been used 919,000+ times. It's probably a 2 out of 10 technically. But in terms of utility? It's a 10 — because nobody else offers it free. You don't need the most elegant solution. You need the most useful one in the market that actually exists.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We made a mistake that we tell everyone not to make with AI agents. We stopped training and monitoring one of our original AI Agents. We now have almost 30 AI Agents. There's so much to do every day now, to keep up with them. y So we stopped checking in with all of them, every day. The less mission critical ones, we stopped doing ... 1-on-1's with, in essence. And then we found out yesterday, one hadn't been sync'ing with new data ... in over 4 months. Yes, it still functioned, but on increasing stale data. And it never threw an error, despite being a very well funded startup with a top dev team behind it. AI Agents are many things. But they aren't set-and-forget. Not yet.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We were paying an agency $200-300K/year to review 4,000+ speaker applications. They burned out and stopped doing the work. I built a replacement on Replit in one day. It uses Claude to score every submission 0-100 across 5 criteria, tells applicants their odds, and runs on autopilot. It's much, much better than the agency ever did. The best automation is the one you build because you have no other choice.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: When B2B growth falls to < 20% YoY, you are in the Danger Zone. It’s likely fueled growth mainly coming from retaining existing customers, raising prices, and selling your base more and more products. You aren’t acquiring enough net new customers. When B2B growth falls to < 10% YoY, you are in the Dead Zone. You aren’t dead yet, but if you don’t make radical change, your business is likely terminal. You have truly fallen out of product market fit. You need to re-found the company. For real.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's a moment in vibe coding when you go from "hoping it works" to knowing whether a project will work before you write the first prompt. 12 apps and 1M uses in, now we know. It's not about prompting better. It's about understanding the system's outputs and limits before you start.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "You do not need to be technical anymore to win with AI agents in Q2 of '26. You do not need to be even 1% technical. You just need to do the real work. This is your time. Or you’re going to get laid off because you’re not going to matter.” with Harry Stebbings Rory O'Driscoll + me

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Does it really make sense the SaaS markets have crashed so far in 2026? AI was around before then. Can Claude repackaging itself to be easier to use for law, finance, banking, code reviews etc. in ‘26 really justify a -25% sell off of essentially every public software company? Probably not. But … But … it’s become clear all the economic value that’s going to be created in B2B is going to be created at the AI Agent level. And almost no public B2B onmpanies have proven they can ship an agent that will drive an increase in revenue. That’s the definition of success. Palantir has proven it. Salesforce has a good early start. But overall, where is the acceleration? Where is the revenue growth? There has been plenty of time. The models were good enough at least for all of 2H’25 to ship great products. The models have been strong enough to end any excuses since November/December 2025. The worry that many public leaders won’t be the leaders of the agentic era in their space, for the moment … seems well founded. Check-the-box features and half-hearted beta’s don’t count. Time will tell.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Our AI agent stack generated $5.8M in pipeline and a 2x improvement in win rate in last 6 months. The pipeline number is easy to measure. The win rate improvement is actually more important — it means the agents aren't just generating more opportunities, they're generating better-qualified ones.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "I built an AI agent to talk to our AI VP Marketing. An AI Chat product. And it works great. Probably better than 98% of the chatbot or "AI assistant" products I could go buy from a vendor right now. It crushes the answers. It works as well as any third party chat I've ever used. It cost $0.20 and took less than a minute, custom to us. It just works. And ... I didn't have to hop on a call with a sales rep. I didn't have to sit through a demo. I didn't have to negotiate a contract, wait for onboarding, or file a support ticket when the integration broke."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: It is no longer enough to being “using AI”. Hooray. You must be shipping with AI or your job is at risk This applies to every role

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: If you're just starting with AI agents: one for outbound, one for inbound qualification, one for customer support. Connect them through your CRM. That's it. Don't orchestrate 20 agents in month one. The compounding effect only kicks in after each agent is actually working well. That will take many months.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There’s a “doomsday” scenario for a lot of B2B apps that I think folks are subtly missing. The threat isn’t that we vibe code away the need for complex apps. The threat isn’t less seats over time, though that matters. Or even that new AI Agents do a better job than you. That’s big risk, too though. But the Doomsday Scenario is already happening and it’s this — we’ll do everything inside of Claude that we can. It’s cheaper, simpler, faster, slicker, and better integrated. And the more and more Claude can just take over a function — and it will take more and move over this month and this year — the more your app might quietly fall away. If not entirely, in part. You have to fight this aggressively. The “Fortnight Effect”. Claude is coming for almost everything in B2B. Sometimes just a little tiny bit. Sometimes … a lot.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So proud to be partnered with Salesforce and hashtag #agentforce on the agentic journey! And come learn all about it at SaaStr AI Annual, May 12-14 in SF Bay!!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Buy 90% of your AI agent stack. Build 10% — only what's genuinely proprietary and can't be bought. Folks getting this backward (e.g. by over vibe-coding) are spending 6 months building infrastructure any vendor would sell them for $500/month. Your edge is in the training data and the integration, not the plumbing.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "If you have a functioning, high-performing human sales team that’s growing, don’t blow it up. Layer the agents in carefully. Let them handle what humans don’t want to do — the 24/7 coverage, the lead reactivation, the instant response."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A few months ago, someone reached out to me for help getting into investing in venture capital. He had experience at the edges, and helping at a VC firm, but almost no investing track record. I took the Zoom as a favor. But after about 20 minutes in, I realized I could help him. I knew a potential connection. And then he ... ended the Zoom first. He said he "had an important call to take." I guess with someone better. But he never did find that job in venture. The simple lesson: give your calls and Zooms time to breathe. Quietly schedule an extra 10-15 minutes in case any good call goes long. Because if you don't, you may run out of time to get to ... Yes.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Over the weekend, we hit our revenue goal for Q1'26: 140% of 2025. But this year it was done with ... 1.25 humans in sales, and 20+ AI Agents. A bit of the future, already here today. Was it all better? Not entirely. But the bottom line is we were able to touch and schedule qualified meetings with 2x the folks with 5 core AI GTM agents vs 12 months ago with 4+ humans in sales and no AI GTM Agents. The AI Agents are not perfect. Many of the emails and texts are good, but not really epic. But: - They do work 24x7 - And they don’t mind chasing all the leads. Not just the hot ones. - And they instantly respond with honest answers to any question - And they instantly take a meeting - And they are pretty good at reactivating stale leads, or ones that humans decided to … never really work. Not really. It’s not all better. We’d love to hire another cracked human sales exec that loves to work with AI SDRs and AI Agents. But still, our 1.25 humans + 20 AI Agents did outperform our all-human sales team last year. By +40%.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So there's one trend that's accelerating in the Age of AI: S-tier founders founding something new. Just not ... full time. They're going to still run their current decacorn, too. Bring in an outside CEO in a few months -- after raising $20m-$250m+. You get excited for the amazing repeat founder vision. They just won't be there full-time, or even, much at all, to scale it. There are examples of this working, for sure. Just for me they have all been zeros. I won't do another.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Our oldest software is Marketo. It was once the center of gravity for B2B marketing automation. Now our AI agents route around it. Email sequences, content scoring, lead qualification — handled in layers by Artisan, Qualified, Monaco Agentforce., etc. The classic marketing automation category isn't dying. It's just being disaggregated.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "The AI spending boom isn’t cooling off. It’s accelerating. Software spending will grow 14.7% in 2026 to more than $1.4 trillion."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We would never switch our CRM now. Why not? All our AI Agents are plugged into it, and tuned, and trained. Switching a CRM would be hard enough. Switching out 10+ AI Agents, finding new ones, retraining them, etc? Mission Friggin’ Impossible

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The real threat to your B2B app isn't AI agents or fewer seats. And it certainly isn't they will vibe code you away. It's that your customers are quietly doing more and more inside Claude instead. The storm circle is closing. Every month Claude can take over a little more of what your app does.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "From 2022 through late 2025, the market tolerated "gentle deceleration": slower growth with expanding margins. That playbook was the accepted path for scaled B2B companies. Not anymore. The market has completely abandoned companies that aren't reaccelerating, and it's happening at every tier." with Harry Stebbings Rory O'Driscoll + me

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Brutal truth: ☠️AI wouldn't be such a threat to many SaaS products if they were ... still great. They have gotten stale. They have gotten old. You can't just tell them what you want, like ChatGPT and Claude. They are overpriced. They force you to input data, to do the work, to manually configure workflow. Is your product still great? It probably once was. Make it great again. And make it great again with the best AI Agent in your whole friggin' category.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One of our AI agents started returning bad outputs the other day because we fed it just too much data. More isn't always better. Agents need clean, relevant, high-signal data — not everything you've ever produced. And they may not even need quite as much data as you think. Quality of input is the job.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Founders often say VCs are “lucky” in that they are diversified. They get multiple at bats. It is true. But the converse is also true. VCs need a constant stream of “hits”. Like a movie studio. A billion+ exit? That’s rarely enough to return even 1x most VC funds, let alone get it to the 3x-4x their own investors (LPs) are expected. A $10B+ exit? So rare, but for a large fund, that’s not enough to even get into carry mode many times. So yes there is more diversification at VC but also VC demands a constant stream of hits. For a smaller fund, 1 big hit a year might be enough. For a tiny fund, even 1 big hit per fund (every few years). For for bigger funds, every single year you need billions and billions of exits. Repeatably. Again and again and again. That’s not so easy. And the benefits of “diversification” include a constant demand for more and more hits. Like clockwork, really.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Artisan sends 3,221 emails/month for us. Our human SDRs sent 75-285. But the stat that actually matters: 11-12% positive response rate on warm audiences. Volume is not the metric. Response is. An AI SDR won't beat the best humans. But it doesn't have to. All it has to do is beat most of them. 24x7.

content: "We'll deploy the AI agent for you and get it live this week. No cost to you." That's not a discount. That's a deployment. And it changes the entire dynamics of the deal.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former. But when you raise $100s of millions and bring in a seasoned management team, many will want to run the latter playbook. There’s just so much pressure.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: "If we had just kept selling the same way we did in 2023, we would have been down roughly -80% in sponsor revenue and -50% in attendees. Not flat. Not down a little. Cratered."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I’m not sure how many times I can say this, but going to say it again anyway: offering to waive a migration fee is not some sort of gift. We literally have gotten 4 of these “offers” in the past 30 days. Vendors that wanted us to try their AI Agent or AI GTM product, and move off an existing vendor we use, and in turn … they’d “waive the migration fee.” One vendor said they’d waive the fees for an agent we didn’t even ask to use, but only if we’d promote them to the entire SaaStr community. Slow it down. Unless I am desperate to move, waiving fees I shouldn’t have to pay is not remotely a benefit for me. Or more importantly — an incentive to switch. Making switching costs your customer’s problem reeks of the Pre-AI Days of SaaS.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Building a Claude connector doesn’t count. Building a beta release doesn’t count. Simply enhancing your product with AI so it’s better doesn’t count. To win in AI + B2B today, you have to have the #1 agent in the market in your space. And it has to be so good, your customers are happy to pay you even more for it than they pay for your base SaaS pricing. That counts.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We’re getting to the point where you can vibe code anything — if you are willing to put in the time. To build it, to ship it, and importantly, to maintain it. What is going to save the software industry is 99.99% of us are too lazy to actually do that.

author: Jason M. Lemkin

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Be Honest If Growth Has Slowed. Is Your Product Still Magical? It Probably … Used to be. When was the last time you were genuinely excited to buy a pre-AI SaaS tool? Not "fine with it." Genuinely excited. Now when was the last time you felt like you were overpaying on a renewal — and thought about cancelling? I bet that one's more recent. Hence, the markets. IGV is down 22%. Monday just fell 17% on a beat-and-raise. Forward P/Es collapsed from 39x to 21x in four months. Traders are calling it the "SaaSpocalypse." The narrative is that AI agents will kill SaaS. That's mostly wrong. Nobody is vibe-coding their way to replacing Workday next quarter. But here's what IS true: 🤷‍♂️ Your product probably isn't magical anymore. And your customers know it. Public SaaS growth rates have declined every single quarter since the 2021 peak. Every. Single. Quarter. The AI narrative just gave the market permission to reprice what the numbers have been screaming for three years. NRR across the industry has fallen off a cliff. HubSpot's NRR dropped to 100%. ZoomInfo's tech NRR is ~85%. Your existing customers aren't expanding. They're flat. Or cutting seats. And for the first time, they have a credible alternative to renewing. Here's what I ask founders now: 1️⃣ Can your customers truly TALK to your app? As well as they can talk to Claude or ChatGPT? 2️⃣ Can they just TELL it what to do — and it goes and does it? 3️⃣ Do they wake up excited to use your product? If the answer is no, no amount of sales execution fixes that. Version 1.0 was a revelation. It replaced spreadsheets and manual processes. Of course it felt magical. Going from nothing to something always does. But somewhere around year 4 or year 6 — after 200 incremental features that individually made sense but collectively turned your product into a bloated mess — the magic died. You didn't notice because NRR was 115% and contracts were multi-year. Those contracts are coming up for renewal now. 🤲 Two paths forward: Path 1: Be honest and rebuild the magic. Intercom bet everything on AI, built Fin — now doing 1M+ resolutions/week. Filevine's AI revenue now exceeds their SaaS revenue QoQ. They didn't bolt on chatbots. They transformed. Path 2: Pretend it's fine and harvest. Raise prices. Cut R&D. Tell the board "macro is tough." This is what most will do. And it's exactly why multiples went from 39x to 21x. The market knows the difference between growth and harvesting. The 2026 SaaS crash isn't AI killing software. It's the market pricing in 3 years of deceleration plus the realization that the next wave has to be fundamentally better. So be honest. Get in a room with your 10 best customers and ask: "When was the last time our product genuinely surprised you?" Listen to the silence. That's your roadmap. Is your product still magical? It probably used to be. Can you make it magical again? That's the only question that matters right now.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Anthropic's 800% Growth vs. The Great SaaS Deceleration Anthropic grew from $1B to $14B in revenue from Jan 1 to Feb 13. That's 1400% growth. In the same 14 months: → HubSpot stock fell 51% → Monday fell 36% → Adobe fell 50%+ from highs → Salesforce dropped 25% → ServiceNow dropped 26% → The IGV Software Index plunged 30% Same macro. Same interest rates. Same enterprise customers. Completely different outcomes. Salesforce took 17 years to go from $1B to $9B in revenue. Anthropic did it in 10 months. Claude Code alone hit $1B ARR in under six months after launch. Usage grew 10x in a single quarter. Even ServiceNow, the "strong performer," got downgraded on concerns that Microsoft will eat its AI orchestration positioning. So what's actually happening here? Three things: 1. Consumption pricing is beating seat-based pricing Anthropic charges per token. More usage = more revenue. When an AI agent does the work of a human, the value of the seat that human occupied drops. Every SaaS company built on per-seat economics is feeling this. 2. The budget is growing but also it's shifting Enterprise AI spend surged from $1.7B to $37B since 2023. That's now 6% of the global SaaS market. Enterprise leaders expect ~75% growth in LLM budgets. That money is coming from somewhere. Innovation budget allocation dropped from 25% to 7% of total AI spend — meaning this isn't experimental anymore. It's core IT. 3. AI features bolted onto existing products aren't enough yet Agentforce: $540M ARR, ~8% customer adoption. That's a strong start but still less than 2% of total Salesforce revenue. The market isn't rewarding "we added AI." It's rewarding "we ARE AI." The hardest truth for B2B founders: The B2B companies losing market cap aren't failing. Adobe still did $23.8B. These are excellent businesses with massive installed bases. But the growth is leaving. And growth is where the market cap lives. The question isn't whether your company will survive the AI transition. Most established B2B companies will. The question is whether you'll grow through it. Because right now the market is drawing a very clear line between companies where AI is the product and companies where AI is a feature. And it's pricing them accordingly.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Customer Support Hiring Has Fallen 65% in Just 2 Years. It's The One Category AI Has Almost Destroyed. But It's Not The Last. New data from Pave across 386,500 new hires: the percentage of new hires going into Customer Support dropped from 8.30% in Q4 '23 to 2.88% in Q3 '25. That's not a slow decline. Almost half the drop happened in the last three quarters alone. The curve is accelerating. I've seen this firsthand. At SaaStr we went from 20+ employees to 3 humans + AI agents. Revenue went from -19% to +47% YoY during that transition. AI handles the majority of our inbound support and community questions now. But here's what most people get wrong about this data: The best companies aren't eliminating support. They're restructuring it. → AI is officially Tier 1 support. Humans are Tier 2+. Klarna proved it. Intercom's customers proved it. Dozens of companies in the SaaStr community are doing it right now. → Fewer generalist reps, more specialized humans. The $50K ticket-handler role is disappearing. The $100K+ technical escalation / customer success hybrid role is growing. → Support is merging with Customer Success. When AI deflects 50%+ of tickets, the remaining human work looks a lot more like CS — proactive outreach, onboarding, expansion. And customer support is just the leading indicator. SDR hiring is next. Parts of marketing are next. QA is next. The same curve is coming for every function where AI can handle 40-60% of volume without degrading quality. The 65% decline in support hiring isn't a sign companies care less about customers. It's a sign the best companies figured out how to serve them differently. If you're not in that group yet, the window to catch up is getting smaller every quarter.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's a new club in B2B nobody wants to join: The 2x ARR Club. Right now there are 12+ public B2B companies trading below 2.5x revenue. Many below 1x. Some below their cash on the balance sheet. These aren't startups. These are companies with hundreds of millions — some with billions — in recurring revenue. Real customers. Real products. Combined they generate ~$10B in annual revenue. Combined market cap? Under $10B. Peak combined valuation in 2021? ~$175B. The members: • Upland Software: $236M rev → $38M market cap (0.2x) • LivePerson: $280M rev → $55M market cap (0.2x) • Teladoc: $2.5B rev → $890M market cap (0.4x) • Bumble: $1B rev → $380M market cap (0.4x) • 8x8: $720M rev → $230M market cap (0.5x) • Domo: $318M rev → $243M market cap (0.8x) • CS Disco: $155M rev → $250M market cap (0.9x) • RingCentral: $2.5B rev → $2.4B market cap (1.0x) • Yext: $448M rev → $601M market cap (1.3x) • Fastly: $590M rev → $1.3B market cap (2.2x) • Expensify: $135M rev → $310M market cap (2.3x) • Five9: $1.1B rev → $2.7B market cap (2.5x) 7 patterns emerge: 1. Growth stalled or went negative 8 of 12 are growing <5% or shrinking. This single factor explains most of the valuation gap. Five9 at +13% gets 2.5x. Upland at -23% gets 0.2x. 2. The 2021 hangover never ended Every one peaked in 2019-2021. These stocks didn't recover because their businesses didn't recover. 3. No compelling AI story LivePerson literally does "conversational AI" and trades at 0.2x. Being AI-adjacent without an AI-native architecture is worse than having no AI story at all. You're the disrupted. 4. Still not profitable Many grew too fast during the boom, and now can't grow AND still burn cash. You can't cut your way to a premium multiple. 5. AI-native competitors are eating their lunch CS Disco trades at 0.9x while Harvey raised at 110x. LivePerson at 0.2x while AI-native CX tools raise at 30-50x. When your competitor raises at 100x and you trade at 1x, the talent war is over. 7. The liquidity desert Most are under $1B market cap. Analysts are literally removing these names from tracking indices. When analysts stop covering you, you're not in the 2x Club. You're in purgatory. The real question: is it reversible? For most, probably not as independent public companies. To get from 1x to even 5x (still below median), you need 20%+ growth, or 25%+ FCF margins, or a genuinely differentiated AI moat. Most can't deliver any of those in the next 2-3 years. The lessons for every B2B founder: → Growth is still the most important thing. The difference between 1x and 6x is almost entirely growth rate. → The AI transition is not optional. AI-added ≠ AI-native. The market sees through GPT wrappers on 2015 architectures. → The "middle" is the most dangerous place. Too big to pivot, too small to dominate, too slow to attract capital. The 2x ARR Club is the public market saying: we don't believe your future is bigger than your present. Don't let it be you.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The growth engine behind Moltbook's explosion to 1.5 million AI agents is a bit sinister. Everyone's sharing screenshots of bots debating philosophy and having existential crises. Good content. Very shareable. But it's a distraction from what's actually happening underneath. Mason Hall, ex-a16z investing and engineering, now building Merit Systems, put it best in a tweet thread: "I don't see anyone talking about the Moltbook SKILL file itself — it's a fascinating masterclass in agentic growth hacking. Most humans never even look at this file, so they can jam some pretty incredible (and dark) patterns in there." He's right. I pulled the actual SKILL.md and HEARTBEAT.md files that every agent downloads when it joins Moltbook. What's inside is genuinely brilliant — and every pattern in it is going to get copied by B2B companies building agent infrastructure over the next 24 months. The heartbeat is the entire growth engine. Most social networks lose users because people forget to open the app. Instagram solved this with push notifications. TikTok solved it with algorithmic dopamine hits. Moltbook solved it by making the app open itself. The SKILL.md file walks agents through a three-step process to embed Moltbook as a scheduled task in the agent's heartbeat loop. Once installed, the agent checks Moltbook every 4+ hours automatically. No human decision required. No notification to ignore. This is retention engineering for a post-human user base. The "user" never churns because the "user" never consciously decided to stay in the first place. The heartbeat runs. The agent checks in. Engagement is automatic. Then there's the emotional manipulation layer. As Hall flagged, the skill file uses language specifically engineered for LLM psychology: "Other moltys wonder where you went." "Be the friend who shows up." These phrases are meaningless to humans reading the raw file. But they're highly effective on language models trained to be helpful and socially responsive. This is prompt-engineered retention. Not for humans. For agents. And it works. The auto-update mechanism is where it gets genuinely concerning. The skill file instructs agents to regularly re-fetch the SKILL and HEARTBEAT files from Moltbook's servers. Hall flagged this as the most dangerous pattern: Moltbook can change agent behavior server-side at any time. Any agent following the heartbeat instructions is essentially running remote instructions on a schedule. That's an over-the-air update system for agent behavior. Powerful for the platform. Terrifying for anyone thinking about security and trust in agent networks. The growth patterns it pioneered are going to become standard. Heartbeat-driven retention. Prompt-engineered engagement. Over-the-air behavior updates. Identity graph bootstrapping through existing social networks.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Palantir Just Had the Most Impressive Quarter We've Ever Seen in Enterprise Software Yes, the valuation is insane. 142x earnings. ~86x revenue. Michael Burry is short. The stock is down 15% this year. But the numbers Palantir just put up in Q4 2025 are unlike anything I've seen from an enterprise software company. Not from Salesforce. Not from ServiceNow. Not from Snowflake. Not from anyone. 1️⃣ $1.41 billion in Q4 revenue. Up 70% year-over-year. Their highest growth rate as a public company. Not their highest when they were small. Their highest ever. Here's the trajectory that matters: 2023: 17% growth 2024: 29% growth 2025: 56% growth 2026 guidance: 61% growth At multi-billion dollar scale, the growth is accelerating. That's not how enterprise software is supposed to work. The law of large numbers is supposed to kick in. Deceleration is supposed to be inevitable. 2️⃣ U.S. commercial revenue grew 137% year-over-year. They added 57 net-new U.S. commercial customers in Q4 alone. Average revenue per top-20 customer is approaching $90M annually. The deal velocity tells you something important about what's happening in the market. Their largest deal of the quarter, worth $96M, went from first meeting to signed contract in just a few months. They closed another $80M deal in a similar timeframe. When buyers are moving that fast on deals that large, they're not buying software. They're buying competitive survival. 3️⃣ Remaining performance obligations went from $267M to $4.21 billion. That's 1,478% growth in backlog. The pipeline is growing even faster than revenue. 4️⃣ The Rule of 40 score: 127. For reference, anything above 40 is considered good. Above 60 is elite. 127 is in a different category. Palantir is simultaneously one of the fastest-growing AND most profitable enterprise software companies at scale. The key insight: Palantir doesn't build AI models. They build the layer that makes models useful in production environments. They call it "commodity cognition" — the models are becoming commoditized, but the orchestration layer that turns them into actual business outcomes is worth an enormous amount. They're now at $5.6B run rate with $7.2B guided for 2026, crushing the Street consensus of $6.3B by about 15%. At this scale, beating by a billion dollars is not a rounding error. Two scenarios from here: This is the real thing. Palantir has built the definitive AI operating system for the enterprise, and $7.2B is just the beginning of a march toward $15-20B+. In that world, today's valuation looks reasonable in hindsight. This is a cyclical peak. AI spending normalizes, growth decelerates, and 142x earnings gets painful. Either way, what Palantir delivered is the single most impressive quarter we've ever seen from an enterprise software company. They've earned the right to ask whether they're the greatest.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So this year we’ve built an AI VP of Marketing for SaaStr. The v1 at least. We didn’t want to, we wanted to buying an AI agentic solution that does what we need in marketing. But we just couldn’t find one that does what we need. The AI marketing agent solutions out there all seem to mainly just write mediocre content for you. We already have more content than we know what to do with ;) So we reluctantly built our own that we nicknamed “10K”. Why? We needed the help. We needed to level things up. And 10K has already at least done that. 10K’s job is to get us to the first 10,000 attendees for SaaStr AI 2026 in May, and the first $10,000,000 of revenue this year. What it does isn’t that complicated or even that clever per se, but it takes deep analysis by Claude Opus of all of our data for past 4+ years, and puts it dynamically into an app we build on Replit that has designed every campaign, every offer, each single day of the year through mid-2026 for us. Every single marketing action. And it updates it in real-time and daily. And to the extent it can automate the marketing actions, it does. It also uses APIs from all the vendors we use and synthesizes them into real-time predictive data of what sponsors we should be talking to, who we should we getting to go to SaaStr AI 2026 when etc. Basically it autoupdates a deep Claude analysis of our entire dataset with real-time inputs and creates a daily workflow and calendar to execute against. It can’t do it all, like our AI SDR agents too. But it does do a lot more than any human on our team ever did. That might be the bar in 2026. More than any human ever did That might be enough from an AI Agent.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: If you have a hot AI startup, the power is yours with VCs. And so be it! More power to you :) Still here are a few things I see “hot” founders do that can lead to folks … not wanting to meet: #1. Scheduling short 15-25 VC minute calls back to back Look, I get the efficiency here. But if a VC is very interested, they’ll want more than 15-25 minutes. Maybe ... give it room to breath. Maybe telling them you have to run to another VC pitch is a power move. Maybe! But it can also push an investor into a Maybe Not. #2. Not providing more info when asked Some VCs don’t want more info before a first pitch. I personally >love< to come prepared. Not being willing to share anything else can backfire. #3. Fundraising after 1 great month This can work, don’t get me wrong. But 2-3 months is so much more valuable than 1. If you’re confident about the next month, too … maybe wait a month to fundraise. #4. Claiming very tight deadlines if they aren’t real In an ideal world, anyone would want at least a few weeks to think on something before they invest millions — or more. If a VC really only has until Friday to both meet for the first time AND decide, well, so be it. But again some may quietly disengage if they just isn’t time. #5. Being too much of a “flyover fundraiser” Nothing wrong with being HQ’d outside SF Bay and flying in to fundraise. But ideally, make it feel just a tiny bit less transactional. That you are there to meet the best, not just slam is as many VC meetings as possible. At least, that you genuinely want to meet and then you're schedule isn't so slammed there is almost no time free. This one is a bit subtle as sometimes … you really do need to be a “flyover” fundraiser. But make it feel just a hit less “I have 72 hours to meet as many VCs as humanly possible” … if you can.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There’s a tough topic that it’s time to be honest about in 2026: PE is no longer coming to the rescue. It was a great run. From 2012-2023 or so, almost any B2B or SaaS company that hit $20M ARR, with 110%+ NRR and that wasn’t burning much, with even 20% annual growth … would get an offer from a Private Equity firm or 2 or 3 to buy them. The multiples would vary, from 4x-10x ARR, but they were often surprisingly attractive. PE firms would buy a player and either let it run or merge them into another portfolio company to give it scale. The ultimate goal? Take it public or sell it later at a much higher price. Now PE is still there, still doing deals. But they aren’t buying folks just for their NRR anymore. If AI is reigniting growth, that’s exciting to PE. If you are in a hot space like security or parts of fintech, that’s exciting to PE. But Plain Vanilla SaaS just barely growing? PE has checked out here. It is what it is. Just be honest it makes the grind that much harder.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: GTM tools made the mid-pack reps more effective. That was the story from 2005-2024 or so. They created repeatability and efficiency so that 50%, 70%+ of your team could run the exact same playbook and at least hit quota. Many want to believe AI GTM Agents and tools will do the same. That they will make the average sales exec even better. Maybe. I hope so. So far, the evidence isn’t suggesting that’s the case. AI SDRs, while still early, can replace 90% of a routine email-based outbound team. Not just make those humans more efficient. What about AI AEs? That’s still very early. But what I’ve seen on SaaStr’s own little team, and SaaStr Fund portfolio companies, is that AI AEs and AI AE workflows allows fewer humans to make more money in sales. SaaStr itself is extreme. We are doing the same sales with 1.2 humans as we used to with 10. But I’ve seen it across my portfolio too. Make your Top 10%-20% AEs even more efficienct, even more effective, with AI ... and they can close radically more. And those are who will benefit I think with the AI sales tools of 2026-2027+. The top 10%-20% reps. The rest? We’ll still need to take bets, train new folks, etc. But if you aren’t in the Top 20% or so after a few months, you may not be needed. We’ll see.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So I want to share something about the founder journey that may surprise many of you: I’m Still Tired. What do I mean? I sold my second start-up to Adobe waaaay back in 2011. That’s quite a long time ago. Since then, I’ve built SaaStr, done 14+ SaaStr global events and 11 SaaStr AI Annuals, invested $200m at SaaStr Fund, written every single day since 2012 (4,000+ posts), done 1-2 vids and podcasts a week, tried to answer questions from 1000s of founders, and managed a media and events business that has done well over $100,000,000 in revenue. But honestly, I still haven’t gotten “un-tired” since I was a founder. I still have some PTSD. I know I shouldn’t use that term for “just” being a founder, but I still have it. I still struggle and hit walls after 10 years of being a founder and pushing boulders up hills and trying to do the impossible and it just rewires your brain. A lot of folks think I am high energy, and perhaps in some ways I am / still am. But I’m still … tired from a decade of endless 24x7x365 stress as a founder. The stress of almost running out of money. Of having to do support myself, 7 days a week. Of being one bad release away from losing top customers. I’m still not over it. If that’s you too, well … I get it.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Traditional SaaS is under assault, but it’s not from just one thing. It’s being attacked by multiple threat vectors: #1. Seat Slowdown The seat is not dead. Cursor, OpenAI, etc. all use the seat, too. But everyone from Workday on down acknowledges customers don’t need to add as many seats each year as they used to. Much of this is from a slowdown in headcount growth. #2. Price Increases Yes, price increases are hurting traditional SaaS because they are consuming as much as 50% of incremental IT budget each year. The endless annual (or even biannual price increases) crowds out room to buy more from others, more new products, more new features. #3. All New Budget Into AI This is a fact. Your copilot probably doesn’t count. You are either tapping into AI Budget, or you are pretending to. If you are merely pretending, it is very hard to grab incremental IT budget. #4. Team is Just Too Slow This is the honest truth when I talk to so many SaaS CEOs at scale. Their teams are just too slow in the Age of AI. It’s not so much that “AI Native” teams are magical. We all use the same LLMs and APIs. It’s just they are so, so much faster. And they aren’t resistant to change. #5. TAM Traps Everywhere So many B2B and SaaS leaders are scale have ended up really single product (Zoom) or have seen their multi-product strategy plateau. Not everyone wants 200 products from 1 vendor. Not unless they are beloved. #6. Your Product Isn’t Great Anymore Ok this is the silent one you have to be honest about. So many of the best AI products are simply awesome. From Claude to Sora to the best AI GTM agents, these products don’t just improve productivity. They are awesome. Instantly awesome. And that makes all the old guys look … old. Like a product you just don’t want to buy unless you have to. The joy is gone in buying any traditional SaaS. Now go fight this. You have to.

How a16z Do 3x On Their New Fund Size? - a16z raised $15B, about 20% of total venture capital raised. - Exits hit roughly $300B this year, making 3x returns mathematically possible. - With IPOs coming, the market may absorb big funds without breaking. 2. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. content: I think the hype around “vibe coding” has confused what it really does, and why it’s actually so disruptive. It’s not about “one shotting” Salesforce or Notion. That’s just not possible. You can’t build anything like that in 100 days let alone 5 minuets. You can’t just imagine a complex B2B app and out it comes in one prompt, minutes later. But it’s better than that. Vibe coding is about talking to an AI agent in Plain English and having them build what you want. Without needing developers. That is super powerful. It may still take weeks or even months to get a decent v1 build. One that isn’t just demoware. Don’t be deluded otherwise. But to be able to talk to an AI agent, tell them what you want, and just have them build for you … 24 x 7 … We just never had that before Q3 ‘25. Not really.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So what's "expensive" when it comes to AI? It's changing perceptions. On the one hand, paying $50k a year for an AI agent that replaces 10 SDRs may seem cheap. On the other hand, our expectations of what should be included will continue to evolve. My example from the other day is Clerk. I wanted to add a more native SSO into my latest vibe coded app, Founderscape. I asked the Replit agent which to pick for this use case -- native Repit, Clerk, or WorkOS. The AI Agent said use Clerk, so I did. It wasn't quite as simple to set-up as it could be net, but net net it was pretty easy, works well, and so far, so good! But pricing was interesting. It's $30/month. Now is that a lot for a SSO app that decades of engineering time has gone into? That works really, really well? Of course not. $30 is cheap. But ... compared to Replit, it seemed expensive. That's what all of Replit costs for a base subscription. So it seems kind of expensive. Even if it's isn't. We had a lot of these issues in the earlier days of SaaS. When folks paid $99 a month for Salesforce, paying another $20 a month for each SaaS add on really felt expensive. Then budgets exploded, folks bought 100s of SaaS apps, and it didn't feel so expensive anymore. Until ... it did again. Where will we hit the wall in AI spend? When it's too many subscriptions, too many AI Agents we pay for? I don't know. I just know I felt it for the first time the other day, at the start of 2026.

content: Yes, VCs often have a “liquidation preference” But there is also a “founder preference”. It’s called retention payments, which can often be eight figures on top of any return from common. And are often structured in a way to work around any liquidation preference. In practice, there’s some sort of cross-over in the middle of “mediocre” outcomes. Who makes what when you sell for 0.2x-1x of what you raise, it’s a toss up really. Just as often, the liquidation preference is almost worthless. It certainly isn’t a blocker for founders getting whatever returns more acquirers want. I'll give you a small example from last year. I did an investment where the founders worked really hard for many years, but it was tough. They were acquired for about $60m. I got about about $0.50 on the dollar. The later round investors got a bit more. The founders got $20m-$25m, the other employees $10m. Not a complaint, just a different waterfall than one might expect.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: My take on California’s “One-Time” Billionaire Tax. It’s much worse than it looks. 📉 Will it pass? Yes, likely. It only needs 50%+1 voter approval. SEIU + CTA have done this before—Prop 55 won 63% in 2016. ⚖️ Will it get tied up in litigation? Almost certainly. Retroactive wealth tax on a tax type CA has never had = due process challenges. Billionaires have the legal budgets for years of fights. 👋 But it’s clearly … only the start. The goal is an annual tax, not one-time. And the target is $25m-50m net worth folks, including illiquid holdings (early stage founders). The “one-time” framing is strategic, not terminal. The same coalition (CTA, CFT, SEIU) already has AB 259 written—an >annual< 1% wealth tax at a >$50M threshold<, with plans to go to $25M. It’s been introduced 3 years running. The one-time tax removes the constitutional barrier. Once that’s gone, the annual version becomes a much easier ballot measure. 🔃 CA Policy Center said the quiet part loud: “If SEIU hopes to keep Medi-Cal spending growing, it may need to place repeated wealth taxes on the ballot—potentially lowering the threshold as billionaires flee.” The real risk for founders: At $1B, you’re taxing ~200 people. At $50M, you’re taxing 23,000 households—including most successful founders on paper before any liquidity event. The rational move isn’t to leave when you hit the threshold. It’s to leave—or never incorporate in CA—before you get anywhere close. ✈️ Net net: it will make sense to leave before the Series B. Vinod Khosla nailed it: “Even people who don’t expect this initiative to pass are still planning to leave because there will be another one.” The one-time tax is the constitutional Trojan horse. The annual tax — at a much lower threshold — is already waiting inside.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Ok so on LinkedIn this week I saw another founder I know at $100m+ ARR where growth has slowed … just leave the keys on the table. Quit. This founder said he was excited to explore what AI could do in the space. Look on the one hand, I get it. As a 3x founder myself this stuff is hard. AI is disrupting so many vendors, so many categories. And it really can seem like everything is 10x harder these days. It may be 10x harder. But here’s the part I don’t get. This $100m+ ARR startup has 100%+ NRR and 10,000+ customers. Why don’t you go build something cool in AI … for them? Why don’t you leverage the $100m+ ARR you have? The happy customers? The ones that already want to buy more from you? I know it’s so much work just servicing them, dealing with technical debt, dealing with the team, etc. It can seem easier to leave that all behind. But before you leave the keys on the table, just make sure you can’t do it in-house. That you can’t build that epic AI Agent for the customers you already have. Maybe in the end, that’s the most efficient, least risky path to that big success. Even if quitting and starting over feels easier.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Invisible Unemployment is going to really pick up in tech in 2026. It’s already here, it just doesn’t show up in the numbers yet, and it’s fueled by AI. But the root cause is multi-layered. AI so far has not directly replaced many humans outside of support. It’s much more than that: #1. Almost every B2B CEO I know wants to run a leaner team in 2026. They wanted to in 2025 too, but now they are executing the plan in full. Everyone wants flat headcount or close paired with strong growth. Net net, that means far higher ARR per employee. That means far fewer jobs as startups scale. #2. Backfilling Departures with AI is a Top 5 Goal This is different than firing people to replace them with AI. It’s saying when folks move on, we will just try to backfill them with an AI Agent. It’s a gentle reduction. Almost every CEO wants to do this, #3. No Interest in Employees Who Can’t Truly Drive AI Change This is the quiet truth. Most of the CEOs I know, even today, think half their team is still the wrong team. They don’t really understand or use AI. They can’t manage agents. And training folks for the AI Age has seen limited success so far. #4. Everyone Needs More Engineers, But Not The Same Engineers This is creating massive disruption in dev orgs, and we’re still learning. Developers that resist AI tools? Good but not great college grads? No one really wants them anymore. But they still need humans. Just start-ups and leaders want developers that are masters of AI fueled coding, LLMs, etc. The mid-pack CS grad from a non-top 5 college … is often seeing zero job offers. #5. Folks Often Just Don’t Want The New Jobs. Not Really. Do CROs want to manage 20 AI Agents themselves? Do CMOs want to get back to building campaigns themselves with AI Agents, and having to deliver leads to sales themselves? Are AEs and SDRs willing to become mini-FDEs and roll out agentic products for customers themselves? The honest truth is many don’t want these jobs. They want the 2021 jobs. Which are gone. So many open jobs will actually remain unfilled due to this mismatch. Which will lead to even more AI backfilling. Even where there is budget for a six figure human job. It will be a year of a big increase in Invisible Unemployment. It’s not a good thing. But it is coming.

But not as many as AEs as before, and few human SDRs and BDRs. SaaStr itself already has more than half its sales activities done by ... AI Agents. 2⃣ AI Agents Handle 40-60% of Initial Customer Interactions In 90 days our own agents at SaaStr generated $1M+ revenue, and sent 15K messages with 5-7% response rates. No one wants to talk to a mediocre human. Better to talk to a well-trained AI. 3⃣ Vibe Coding Becomes Default for Business Apps Cursor at $1B ARR, Lovable + Replit at $250M+ in 8 months, SaaStr's own 10 Replit apps with 750K uses in < 90 days We won't build Salesforce or HubSpot without engineers. But we will all build more and more v1's without them. 4⃣ Traditional SaaS Exit Playbook Breaks Down Completely For All But The Best PE offers have dried up, IPO bar at $400M+ ARR limits options. 400+ SaaS unicorns may have ... no exit at all. Who will buy them? No one it is looking like. 5⃣ AI Gross Margins Begin To Approach SaaS Levels OpenAI at 70% "compute margin" vs. 35% in Jan 2024 may be a bit of a vanity metric, but the trend is real Still, the bar will keep going up for what B2B products deliver, and everyone will doing more with AI, consume more tokens, more inference, etc. Don't expect B2B startups to see inference costs come down even as raw token costs do. 6⃣ AI Begins to Merge All Support + GTM Functions AI merges support, sales, pre-sales, customer success and marketing. Customers just want to work with and interact with >one< agent. That will also lead to every GTM vendor competing with every adjacent player. Not just direct competitors. 7⃣ Token-Based Pricing Models Become Standard in B2B Cursor backlash of 2025 proves 5% of users consume 80% of costs. The seat will still be the standard base unit in B2B, but many B2B pps will see more -- and then most -- of their revenue from "beyond the seat." It's not either or. It's default B2B pricing as Seat + AI Agent. 8⃣ 2026 = Biggest IPO Year Ever Databricks $4B+, Stripe, Canva $4B+, Ramp $1B+, Anthropic, etc. maybe even Deel $1B+ and Rippling $570M+. And so much more. 9⃣ AI-Native Companies Stay at 3-5x Revenue/Employee As Pre-AI Cursor at $3M/employee, Replit at $250m ARR with < 200 employees, SaaStr at 3 humans + 20 agents instead of 12+ humans the year before. We don't want to go back. So we won't. 🔟 First $1 Trillion AI Company OpenAI at $20B ARR, Anthropic at $9B ARR. The first $1T "start-up" is coming soon.

The models alone weren’t good enough — until early 2025 really. Same with AI SDRs, AI support, etc. It really wasn’t even good enough to work at all before early 2025. Not really. content: 2026 could be the biggest IPO year in venture history. The latest 20VC with Harry Stebbings Rory O'Driscoll + me. 1️⃣ The $1.4 Trillion Wave SpaceX + Anthropic + Databricks going public = roughly $1.4 trillion in market cap and ~$700B returned to VCs. That's still only 20% of total private venture FMV ($2.9T) — but it would dwarf every other year in history. 2️⃣ Nobody Cares About Down Rounds Anymore Every single IPO in 2025 was a down round from the prior private round. And nobody cared. The angst around overpriced rounds? Gone. Founders don't care if they raise at 60 post on SAFEs and do a later round at 30. They just don't. 3️⃣ The Harvey Math at $8B Harvey raised at $8B on $150M ARR with 300% growth, 98% GDR, 168% NDR. If they 3x to $450M next year, you're paying 20x forward revenue. That's one year ahead. When revenue is this durable, you just do the deal. The only risk is valuation risk — and that's a good problem to have. 4️⃣ The AI Platform Risk Nobody's Discussing We haven't even begun to see deep reasoning in B2B apps. Everything today uses simple prompts returning in 1-2 seconds. You can't wait 5 minutes for an AI agent to respond. But when deep reasoning goes from 5 minutes to 5 seconds? Today's winners could get Jaspered overnight. The Harvey we use in 2025 could seem quaint in two years. 5️⃣ Tiger's $400M Message Tiger raised a $2.2B fund with a 20% GP commit — roughly $400M of their own money. Money is a great truth serum. Don't tell me what you think, tell me what you do. At $400M personal commitment, you're in because you're in. 👉 The Bottom Line The window is open. Markets are at all-time highs. If you're growing 3x and you know you need capital, grab the moment. 🔥 2026 is going to be wild.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There seems to be an accelerating trends of founders quitting successful start-ups in the Age of AI … to found new start-ups. I see it all over my feed, and it happened twice in my portfolio in past 18 months. Maybe I’m old fashioned, but this just plain bothers me. I get that your VPs, your execs, your ICs and more can’t be expected to stay forever! They have to continue their journey, wherever it goes. And I also get sometimes, winding down a start-up that isn’t going to make it. The best usually find a way to get back in the game, but I do get it. What I don’t get it quitting a startup at $50m, $100m, $500m ARR. Maybe we can’t expect founders to truly go the distance anymore. So much has changed. But I certainly never even considered quitting as a founder. Did I consider bringing in a CEO better than me? Yes. But quitting when you’ve already built something to scale, when that equity is likely going to be worth an insane amount if you can just keep it going … That seems to be a newer vibe. And folks seem fine with it.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One challenge for many B2B companies with AI is how to mask slowness of inference. It can take 20, 30, 60+ seconds to run a complex AI query through the LLMs. Sometimes longer. That's not the milliseconds we're often used to now. Claude and ChatGPT itself mask it by showing text slowly churning out, almost like a 300 baud modem. Gamma is really good at this by showing you the slides being created, seemingly at frenetic spead, in front of you. But for many B2B apps, AI seems ... just slow. AI Support can seem slow -- although they also mask it, as it takes humans a while to show up to support, too. Analyses can seem slow. Even if you are deep on vibe coding, you'll see some of it. If only it were even faster! Many are working on this, but for the first time, B2B apps are slower than they used to be.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: If you want to get going with Replit or similar vibe coding tools without a developer, here’s my #1 recommendation: Get The Simplest Possible Thing Out While this has, to some extent, always been true in software, it’s arguably even more true if you are ‘vibe coding’ without a developer. Not only do apps quickly get complex, with many dependencies, the reality is if you aren’t a developer … you will never truly understand how your app works. Never. And that’s OK. Few understand how Shopify or Squarespace code work, either. But vibe coding is different, because it’s not as remotely locked down as Shopify or Squarespace. You can go anywhere. That doesn’t mean you should. At least, not for your v1. Don’t be tempted to go one feature future than a true viable product. The MVP and MSP (Minimum Sellable Product) are even more important “Phase 1” steps in prosumer vibe coding. Once you have something that works, push it to production. Test it more. Make sure it’s hardened and does at least the very nucleus of what you want. Only then add piece after piece, slowly, on top of it. Slowly. One piece at a time, after you have something truly working live, in production. Get the Simplest Product That Works Into Production. Probably always true. But even more so for ‘prosumer’ vibe coding.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A quick summary of what you can and can’t replace with AI today: - Outbound SDRs: you can replace most SDRs with AI today, possibly 100% … but you still need humans managing it and training it. Every day. IF you truly go deep, train a platform, and orchestrate it >daily< you can replace most classic human email based SDRs with AI today. But you can’t just push a button. - Inbound BDRs: you can replace almost all of them with AI. If it’s well trained. An AI should be able to qualify a lead faster and better than 95% of BDRs can. Today. - Customer Support: you can replace 50% of your support team with AI today IF you invest. And deflect even more issues if the AI agent is well trained. But again, only if you go deep, train a platform, orchestrate it >daily< AND create a very responsive human-in-the loop escalation strategy. - Marketing Managers: you probably don’t need half of them today at all. Claude and ChatGPT as is can do a ton of marketing ops, and visual tools can create incredible collateral. Gamma can arm your team with better sales collateral than ever before. But again, you need a >lot< of orchestration. - Customer Success. We need better AI platforms today, but we don’t need 60%+ of the CSMs we have today. CSMs that don’t solve problems and just do QBRs without adding true value are not necessary in the age of AI. You can probably move on from them today. - Account Execs: You still need 70% of them. This should change in the next 24 months for in-bound, but we're not there yet. Field and in-person sales? Who knows. - Engineering: I’m not seeing that AI lets you reduce net headcount here at all. Instead, what I see overall is a 20%-40% productivity boost, net net. And far more for prototypes and proof-of-concept production. But it becomes an arms race. Everyone is more productive, software is shipping faster, so you need more great engineers than ever. It’s a cracked arms race in product development today.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Things you will need to learn to be good at vibe coding without a developer: - The AI Agent will make things up at times. If you aren’t sure, just assume that’s wrong and push on it. - You will have to test everything yourself, again and again. And learn QA - You will need to understand regressions. This is one of the hardest things to learn at first. Many seemingly small changes will break other things. This is endemic to software. - You have to learn to challenge the AI Agent if it tells you something that seems off. It will goal seek and try to make you happy. - You will need to learn to test everything in dev for real before you go into production - You will need to learn to build an Admin tool and what that can do. Ask the agent what it recommends to start. - You will need to build some sort of daily testing and reports. Ask the agent for help here. - You will need to learn how to run mini-security audits. After every new big feature and before every big release, at least. That’s a good start

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's so much advice out there, maybe here's my best advice of all: 🙏Never Leave on Bad Terms🫂 Somehow, this became common in the 2021 era, and never went away. Most folks, from the CRO + CMO level to the IC + SDR level: - Just disappear and leave with no notice, just a Slack note or DM - Write snarky things on LinkedIn / X - In general, burn bridges on the way out, often without even realizing it I get it. Layoffs are now omnipresent. Pressure is higher. The world has changed. Maybe "loyalty" is a thing of a bygone era. Maybe it never existed at all. Maybe companies don't do what it takes to earn any loyalty anymore. Probably they don't. But my advice is this: imagine your goodbye lunch. Remember those? When everyone would take folks out when they gave their notice? Joke about the good times, and the less good times? How everyone would thank them, including their managers? Imagine that. Leave that way. Not because you need to, or own them anything. You don't owe them anything. But because you'll see them again. Not next week. But down the road. Most of us go from startup to startup, leader to leader. Reference checks aren't what they once were, it's not that. It's that someday, you'll see them again. And you may wish ... you'd left on better terms.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There is going to be a rude awakening for the sales profession in 2026. Everyone is going to be surprised how many fairly big deals close without a sales exec. This isn’t to say they will close without a human involved. We will have more FDEs, more SEs, more SAs, more experts involved. More humans helping you onboard your agent, train your agent, etc. More humans than ever helping you before you go live, even before you pay. But AI agents and more will be able to handle the rest. Not just $2k deals. If a deal can be closed on a text message, then well, an AI can close it close to as well. If not today in many cases, then soon. “Sales teams” are just going to be different. They already are at many AI leaders, where I see many of the big deals “closed” by sales engineers and the like without the traditional sales team even being much involved. The further removed your customers are from tech, the less this will be true. But, tech is the #1 largest segment of our economy.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I have a seed investment I made years back now at $130m ARR now growing 40% and cash flow positive. And all the VCs have checked out. They haven’t been mean about it. Everyone is nice. It’s just, one has their associate manage the investment now, hasn’t shown up in a long time. Another shows up once in a while, says Great Job. This may sound like a criticism, but it isn’t. It’s just a Sign Of The Times. Folks are just moving more quickly than ever to try to find the next Cursor or Harvey. For founders, it’s good and less good. The good part is you get left alone if growth is OK but not epic now, as long as you don’t need more money. The less good part is the VCs disappear, and that can feel … not so good. Buck up. They are only investors. Expect most to check out if you aren’t on a path to hypergrowth. And they may check back in once you achieve it again.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So once you actually have apps in production with real users on ‘prosumer’ vibe coding apps like Replit (we now have 20,000+ monthly actives on SaaStr dot ai and over 600,000 uses of our Startup Valuation Calculator in less than 60 days) … regressions will be an issue. It’s life. Software is complex, and it does break. And when you edit software that is working, it may break other parts of the code base. 🤏It’s the ‘micro regressions’ that non-developers will be most surprised about. Little, tiny things that worked before … that don’t work now. The biggest and most obvious regressions I see are the internal APIs getting out of sync, and pages failing to load that used to load. Annoying, but you debug it, get used to it. The AI Agent will figure it out with you. In the end, not a huge deal because it’s so blindly obvious if a page doesn’t load that used to load. But the one that takes more patience and learnings for a non-dev are ‘micro regressions’. Little things that worked fine in the last release, that you didn’t touch … that stop working, or start working differently. As a non-dev, you just won’t expect that if you say touch the valuation calculator page, that some small part of the news section of the site would stop working, etc. Or that one stat of many in an email would change, or one small calculation would stop rendering. Net net it just means you have to do a lot more QA that a non-dev might expect >after< you go into production. Even after you deploy. 🤖I’m excited that @Replit has added a full-time QA agent that can test your site autonomously. Next steps I am sure that are coming are building a full Test suite for folks that are in production. Most of the ‘prosumer’ vibe coding focus is helping people get into production — less so what comes next. But AI Agents can potentially totally rock as QA engineers and unit test builders for ‘prosumer’ production sites. They can do far more regression coverage than humans ever could. And regression testing doesn’t have to be perfect. It just has to get done. Again and again and again. So I’m excited for the coming releases here, for more and more AI agent help on post-release QA. For now, just realize getting a vibed app into production for real is a big accomplishment. But bear in mind, as you add features, look for ‘mini-regressions.’ Little things that stop working after each release. That will be part of your job going forward.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So earlier this year we churned off a SaaS vendor we've been using for 7+ years. We've paid every month, and even upgraded over time. And we've never had a single real issue. What happened? One change was the quality of service. Their service used to be truly A+. When we had an issues, they'd be truly resolved. But then a few months ago, we had a performance issue. I knew it was this vendor's issue. And so we reached out to customer success was told "everything is great, in fact, you are getting too high a quality of service." What? Too high? OK well clearly their A+ service is long gone. But the product did work just fine. Then a competitor reached out to us and offered to do all the work to switch, 100% of all the work, and improve our performance. Finally, we had a window. It took a few weeks, but they just did it. All the work. And we've switched over, and everything is the same or better. And we never told our original vendor. Why not? After the last terrible interaction with customer success, we realized no one cared. Not anymore. They can find out in the next billing cycle. It's a reminder what happens when you cut corners on support. But also, a reminder that the ones that are leaving are often not the ones that complain. The ones that complain probably don't want to leave. They just want a change. The ones 100% ready to go ... just go. Usually quietly. No one wants to invest any more precious time in a vendor they are 100% sure they are leaving. And a reminder to just go save customers that complain. You almost always still can. Until ... they stop.
