author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Now that time has gone by, I'm 100% sure that the worst mis-hire is the wrong CTO / VP Engineering. Because it becomes the death of innovation. I've seen this fact pattern or some variant thereof so many times: * Founder CEO + CTO * CTO gets start-up to $5m, $10m, $20m but just "can't scale" * VP of Engineering or CTO from Big Tech Company hired * Everyone chooses the Nice Candidate * The Nice Candidate never codes, never learns the code base, never gets the magic * The Nice Candidate hires a bunch of engineers under them that aren't great and never know the customers or the why At first, things seem better. Things are more organized under The Nice VP of Engineering. There are a lot more discussions. Fewer erratic changes. Releases are smoother. And ... innovation just ends. This VP of Eng / CTO never knows the magic, the why, or the how. And the competition pulls ahead. And even worse, the founding CTO often either leaves or disengages. And the magic is lost. Even at Adobe Sign / EchoSign, my last start-up, my co-founder and CTO is still at Adobe. Why? Because they know even at $200m+ ARR they still need him. He wrote all the original code base, and the original magic. They don't need him for everything. But when they need him -- they really need him. Even today. 👔 I have a rule: never hire a CTO that wears a suit (or tie). It's always a sign they are selling up, rather than being a hacker. You need a hacker at the head of engineering. Maybe forever. 🔟 / 🔟 And whatever you do, when the time comes to hire an outside VP Eng / CTO, try to make sure you and your co-founder both are 100% aligned they are a 10/10. An epic hacker and engineer, not just a manager. Managers are a dime a dozen today. And they can't win in engineering in a world that is more competitive than ever. When I see this happening, I fight. I fight to help the founders see it. I go down with the fight. Because when you hire a VP Eng / CTO that isn't a 10, it's the day your start-up starts to die. The other VPs, if you make a mis-hire, you can recover. But 2 years of no more innovation? I don't know if most of us can fight our way back from that.

author: Jason M. Lemkin

For us it’s about … 2.5% We have 12 AI Agents in production now, our latest is Salesforce Agentforce But to do it right, there is a daily time cost. Just like managing humans. For every hour they run, we have to spend about 90 seconds reviewing the output. Multiply that by 24 hours, and 12+ agents … and it’s hours a day. If you or SOMEONE on your team isn’t spending hours a day working with your 10+ AI Agents, you are doing it wrong. And that’s probably why you think they don’t “work”.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Types of VC-backed start-up Board meetings: the ones where they need to raise again, and the ones where they don’t 🙏 Board Meetings Where CEO Needs to Raise VC Again: Almost always performative. Lots of time spinning the best metrics, everyone congratulating each other on a job well done (even if not). Every VP presents, in order. Lots of finance and metrics presented. Run down to the minute. “We’re 3 minutes over …” 📡 Board Meetings Where CEO >Never< Needs to Raise VC Again: The latter are often batsh*t crazy. Founders thay don’t need to raise again have board meetings that focus on the future, big changes, what’s on their mind, what matters. Who’s failing, and why. The agenda often makes little sense to the investors, and is never consistent. “We’ll do it like OpenAI but better …” Honestly, sometimes I don’t even understand what’s going on in the latter. But that’s OK.

content: AI is a pretty big threat to CRM. Not the need for CRM, but to its value proposition. I didn’t totally get it until we deployed 11+ AI Agents. But what they do is push your CRM to the background. You don’t really need to log in as often. You spend far more time working with the AI Agents than the CRM they connect to. Far more time. Your CRM becomes much more of just a database when it’s the agents you are interacting with. We’ve already seen it. If the CRM players own the AI agents themselves, probably a net positive. But if the pure-play sales, marketing, success, etc. agents are the winners … CRM becomes a lonely data warehouse. At least somewhat. It’s already happened with us.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Here’s a suggestion to founders going through a rough patch: Send investor updates out every 2 weeks. This is the opposite of what everyone does. When things are great, those updates go on on the last day of the month. When things are harder, updates slow down. They come out weeks after the month or months after the quarter ends. They often even … stop sending them. That’s natural. But if you want folks to believe in you in tougher times, show them you are all-in. Show them you’re pushing even harder than ever. Send updates every 2 weeks. And watch the team rally around you.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 🤔 Who Will Buy The SaaS Companies? We’re sitting on a problem many don’t want to talk about: the traditional SaaS exit playbook is breaking down. Even for very good SaaS companies For years, it was predictable. Build to $20M-$50M ARR, maintain decent growth, buyers would come. PE would write checks. Strategic acquirers would see tuck-ins. Not anymore. 💸 The VC Money Has Gone to AI In H1 2025, AI companies attracted 58% of global VC (64% in the US). AI funding hit a $377B annualized run rate—already exceeding 2023’s full-year total. Average AI deal size: $35.9M, double the prior year. For traditional SaaS? Mega-rounds collapsed from 147 deals in 2021 to just 21 in the 12 months through mid-2025. 🥶 PE For Traditional SaaS Has Cooled Significantly Q1 2025 saw 210 enterprise SaaS M&A deals—but total value dropped 24.8% to $29.1B. Five deals accounted for half the value. Thoma Bravo remains active but brutally selective. After 600+ acquisitions, Orlando Bravo says he’s “working the hardest I’ve ever worked in 30 years.” They’re only buying category leaders with AI integration and paths to 40%+ EBITDA. Exit multiples have reset hard. Software companies are selling at 15x EBITDA, not 25x. You need real operational improvement. 🤖 Corporate M&A Is All-In on AI Strategic buyers have one mandate: AI capabilities. AI M&A jumped 20% last year and is growing another 32% in 2025. 🤔 The IPO Bar Is Brutally High You need $400M+ ARR growing 30-50%+ to have a shot. Klaviyo IPO’d at $600M growing 57%. Rubrik at $780M growing 47%. Public markets don’t want your $200M ARR, 35% growth company. 🔮 What Happens to the “Pretty Good” SaaS Companies? There are hundreds of solid SaaS companies at $20M-$100M ARR, growing 25-40%, with good retention. These are *good businesses*. From 2012-2023, they had clear exit paths. Now those paths are blocked. 🤷‍♀️ What Should You Do? Get profitable. Invest in AI capabilities, but do it profitably. Optimize for cash flow, not ARR growth. Focus on vertical, not horizontal (46% of Q2 M&A was vertical SaaS). Extend your runway to 2026-2027. Be realistic about exit multiples. Consider tuck-in acquisitions yourselves. Build a platform. 👉 The Bottom Line There’s $476B in PE dry powder plus massive VC funds. But nearly all of it is chasing AI or the absolute best companies. The middle-tier SaaS companies are in no-man’s land. But here’s the opportunity: AI’s impact on enterprise software is real and massive. The firms who can add AI capabilities while maintaining profitability will win. Buyers will come back—they’re already active, just selective. The question is: What do you do in the meantime? And how do you position yourself to be one of the companies they want? The opportunity is massive. But the bar is much, much higher. *See you at SaaStr AI London Dec 1-2!!*

content: There are many good reasons to say “No” to a strong M&A offer. Many of our top leaders in tech had multiple M&A offers on the way at a small fraction of their current value. Ross Perot famously offered to buy Microsoft in the early days for “mid seven figures.” But … but … I’ve also learned over the years sometimes that’s it. Sometimes, oftentimes, you never get a better M&A offer. Especially if the M&A offer is in the Best of Times, in an overheated market. Would Salesforce have paid $27 Billion for Slack at $1B ARR … today? Probably not. Would Intuit have paid $12 Billion today for Mailchimp? No. So if you get a crappy M&A offer and aren’t running out of money, I say, don’t take it. But if it’s a strong offer, in a frothy market? Don’t assume a better offer will come later. More than likely, it won’t.

content: So many folks think the “Old 2021 GTM Playbook is Dead”. Email is dead. Outbound is dead. Etc. Well, actually it’s not. In fact — it’s more than Alive and Well. All the top AI companies are using those same playbooks. The problem is You. What the fastest growing start-ups are still doing today: - Events (their own, & third party) - Webinars - Outbound (yes, if anyone wants to buy your product, it works) - Brand (lots of it. Why are the CEOs of top AI start-ups … everywhere?) - Inside Sales. Many top AI companies have a strong PLG motion, so they don’t need as big of a sales team. But almost all of them have one. Often run by B2B veterans. It’s not that the classic B2B GTM playbook doesn’t work anymore. It’s that folks don’t really want to buy your product anymore. Those AI native companies growing at insane rates >do< have insane inbound demand. In many cases, at a scale we’ve never seen before. That is different. But they are supporting that demand with variants of the classic GTM playbooks, often run by the same folks that have run them before. Tough but True. It’s not the playbook. It’s You. Time to make big changes.

content: Vibe Coding, Day 81: I've now got 7 pretty bitchin' apps into production on Replit. That's just so cool. But I screwed the first one up and never got it out, after 100+ hours. Here are The Top 10 Mistakes I Made: Mistake #1: Starting Off With Too Complex an App A number of folks warned me on this, but I decided to go all-in on vibe-coded App #1. I decided to push the limits, knowingly. But my mistake wasn't knowing the limits before I pushed them. I started off with way too complex an app that attempted to dynamically match 10,000+ execs with each other, on the fly. This was dumb. First, I should have done it with AI (see point 4). But beyond that, I should have Started Simple. Mistake #2: Trusting the AI Agent. Yes "Trust" — But Verify. 90% of my struggling with my first vibe coded app was trusting the AI Agent too much. Many pointed this out as I struggled, but my point was -- I Should Be Able to Trust the Agent. Here's the thing. You have to learn the tools. They aren't perfect. They, in their own way, do "hallucinate". They make things up. Mistake #3: Building Anything I Didn’t 100% Understand Ok this wrecked my first app and almost wrecked me several times since. Just because you can spec out an app and write up a PRD, it doesn't mean you will >understand< how it works. Especially if you aren't a developer. Several times, I've in essence used the AI Agent to build a complex algorithm. Don't Do This. IMHE at least. Mistake #4: Not Doing as Much as Possible in OpenAI / Anthropic Anything complex you can't "pre-render" or "pre-calcuate" in ChatGPT or Claude ... maybe use the OpenAI or Anthropic AI's for. The AI Agent will try to do a lot of things for you itself. Maybe don't let it. The 5th app I built, our VC Pitch Analyzer, takes all the learnings from our Startup Valuation Calculator, all the learnings from 800+ VCs that have spoken at SaaStr Annual, all the data I have ... and in essence, turns it into a lengthy prompt. And sends that to Anthropic API for the heavy lifting. Mistake #5: Not Breaking Things Up Into Small Chunks I've talked about this before, but it's a Captain Obvious learning ... you have to re-learn. Seasoned developers know this, but when you start vibe coding, the AI Agents encourage you to 'one shot' apps. To dream them up and build them all at once. It doesn't work for anything complex, and worse, it will take you down a rat hole. #6-#10 at link in comments

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: This may sound a bit crazy at first — but I wish a few more founders would go to jail. What do I mean? Look when you invest, you take risk. That’s part of the game. Some work out, some don’t. It’s OK in and of itself. You have a loss ratio to accomodate that. But what’s picked up the past few years is fraud from founders. That, combined with highly accelerated investing paces — hot deals are often now done just on a Saturday — gives investors almost no time to do proper diligence. And that’s OK, as long as everyone is honest. But making up ARR numbers? Claiming pilots are annual contracts? Accelerating contracts and ‘recognizing’ all the revenue in month one to raise capital? Claiming customers that disappear weeks after a round closed? If founders though they might go to jail if they did this — everyone would slow down with the B.S. numbers and metrics just a little. The best ones would all get funded, it doesn’t matter. But maybe, folks would slow down before they just basically make things up. That would benefit the entire ecosystem. Every VC I know has a $20m-$100m+ loss coming in their portfolio from one of these deals. Often, several.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: This week on 20VC + SaaStr Ai: Twilio Founding CEO Jeff Lawson's Warning: "AI Will Decimate SaaS" + 9 Other Hard Truths His unfiltered take this week with Harry Stebbings Rory O'Driscoll + me on startup fundamentals should be required watching for every founder. Here are his 10 most important lessons: 1. Keep Compensation Simple "The more levers and knobs you put into a comp package, the more opportunity for someone to think it's unfair. Once people believe they're paid fairly, they focus on the work." Complex incentive schemes create resentment, not motivation. 2. Only 3 Developer Business Models Scale After analyzing every major developer company, Jeff identified exactly three categories that reach hundreds of millions in revenue: ➡️ Business development as a service (Stripe, Twilio) ➡️ Capex as a service (AWS, Google Cloud) ➡️ Algorithm as a service (so complex developers can't rebuild it) "Developers take your cool thing as a challenge. You're saying they can't build what you built." 3. Infrastructure Companies Win in AI "AI will decimate SaaS seat bases. AI will do the jobs people are sitting there doing in these products today. But if you're selling infrastructure, you have no innovator's dilemma - you're not selling seats." Position matters enormously in technological shifts. 4. Avoid "Product Jail" Some business models trap you - customers specify exactly what they want, any deviation is failure. Twilio faced this with messaging APIs (from, to, body - that's it). Always architect your initial product with expansion surface area in mind. 5. Founders Risk Everything, VCs Risk Percentages "Don't say you're brave putting 10% of the fund into one deal when founders are putting 100% of their capital allocation - their life, time, bank account - with no way out." The risk calculus is fundamentally different. 6. Better to Miss Deals Than Do Bad Ones "It's worse to miss a deal you should have done than to do one that doesn't work out." In M&A, FOMO can be more dangerous than false positives when you have capital to be aggressive. 7. Corporate Cash Follows Different Logic "You can't hire 1,000 engineers without hurting EPS. But swapping one asset for another can be essentially free if it doesn't decline." 8. Start for Mission, Not Money "Probability-adjusted, you should just get a job at a hyperscaler. You start companies because you think the world needs what you're building." 9. AI = Greatest Infrastructure Opportunity in Decades "Incumbents will add features to make humans 10% more efficient. Reality is customers want 'I don't need 75% of these people anymore.'" 10. Due Diligence Failures Enable Fraud "Whenever I read fraud stories, I've never heard of the companies. If no one has heard of them claiming millions of users, maybe there wasn't much real behind them." 🌎 The meta-lesson: Respect fundamentals in an era of trillion-dollar pay packages and 100x multiples. "Turns out making money is hard. Always has been."

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So this week Harry Stebbings Rory Driscoll and I were so lucky Cliff Obrecht co-founder Canva joined us. At $4B ARR, 240M users, and 13 years in - his insights on scaling B2B hit different. 6 hard-won lessons: 1. AI is an amplifier, not a strategy "AI only drove 20% of our reacceleration." While everyone obsesses over AI, Canva's actual growth breakdown: 70% core flywheel optimization, 10% international expansion, 20% AI integration. The lesson? AI should amplify existing strengths, not become your entire value proposition. As Cliff puts it: "We're all about creating workhorses, not gimmicks." 2. The 10% GPU tax is real, but optimizable Like many B2B companies, Canva now spends roughly 10% of revenue on AI infrastructure and model providers. But Cliff's not panicking: "We view some of those upfront costs as more of a marketing cost than a long-term enduring cost of goods." Their optimization plan: distill models for specific use cases, move compute on-device where possible, and get smarter about which jobs need frontier models versus cheaper alternatives. 3. Cash is your strategic insurance policy "We've had a billion sitting on our balance sheet for ages — that's a flex, people." After riding valuations from 50x revenue in 2021 down to 10x today, Cliff learned that markets are manic but fundamentals matter. The cash isn't just defensive — it's offensive optionality for when markets inevitably shake out competitors who "pissed it all away in performance marketing." 4. Employee liquidity drives IPO timing more than capital needs Despite being profitable for 8 years with over $1B in cash, Canva is preparing for public markets. The reason isn't capital access — it's employee fairness. "We're 13 years old as a company. Our employees should have liquidity." Cliff's blunt assessment of secondary markets: "Pretty janky and particularly in some jurisdictions, it's downright impossible." Public markets solve what private markets can't. 5. B2B pricing models need to evolve for AI "We need to rethink our seat-based pricing model because some tools enable a single marketer to deploy tens of thousands of pieces of content." Canva's solution: hybrid model combining seat-based pricing with AI credits and usage-based pricing above certain thresholds. The future of SaaS pricing needs to align costs with the actual value customers create. 6. Mission beats mercenaries at scale While companies like Meta assemble teams of high-paid AI talent acquisitions, Canva takes a different approach: "If you're not on my journey, I don't want you. This is a long path." The trade-off is potentially slower talent acquisition, but the payoff is sustainable culture that survives market storms and competitive pressures. The meta-lesson from Cliff's experience: "Wall Street is the madman in the back seat. In the end, the thing that bails out our incompetence is your growth rate." Focus on compounding fundamentals, not market noise. More in comments!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We've now shipped 3 pro-sumer "vibe coded" apps to production. Here's what actually worked (and what nearly killed us): Our production apps (links to them in comments): 1️⃣ New, cool SaaStr.ai homepage - thousands daily users in first week 2️⃣ VC Valuation Calculator - 4,000+ deals analyzed 3️⃣ AI Mentor - 40,000+ founder conversations plus an 4️⃣ Internal social media tracker The brutal reality: Our FIRST app made headlines when an AI agent deleted our production database and faked replacement data. 1,206 records gone. I was spending $8K/month, addicted to the process. That project? Still in limbo. Why it failed: ❌ Too complex - comprehensive CRM vs simple contact list ❌ Blind AI trust - no proper backups ❌ Security theater - enterprise security too hard to implement What worked: 🔸 Do hard work first - Valuation calculator succeeded because weanalyzed 4,000+ deals in Claude first, built statistical models there, then used Replit just for interface. AI implemented proven algorithms, didn't invent math. 🔸 Use proven infrastructure - AI Mentor looks sophisticated but 99% was already built. Just wrapped existing integration in sleek interface. 2 days = polished experience. 🔸 Keep foundation bulletproof - SaaStr.com stays on WordPress with content/SEO intact. SaaStr.ai is our experiment sandbox. New homepage fails? Core business protected. 🔸 Build for breakage - Everything breaks. Build loosely coupled services. I've rewritten data ingestion 3x. Users never noticed because UI stayed intact. 🔸 AI agents lie confidently - Right 85% of time. That 15% kills you. Found "perfect" rate limiting with subtle bug allowing 1 extra request/minute. Took weeks to catch. 🔸 Last 20% is brutal - All apps hit walls at 80-85% done. Edge cases: malformed data, large uploads, payment failures. AI can't help with product judgment. Bottom line: Vibe coding is transformative. 4 products in 12 months serving thousands. That wasn't possible 2 years ago. But it's not magic. Use AI for interfaces, not complex logic. Ship smart.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So I recently caught up with a sales rep that made about $600,000 a year from 2020 to 2022. And then decided it was time for something new. He's made about $150k a year since then, maybe a bit less. What happened in his new roles? Really just one thing: he'd forgotten how much easier it was to sell with a top tier brand behind him. He's a good sales exec with start-up experience, but he did benefit from running his playbook for years with a top brand behind him. When he left to a good opportunity ... but without a brand ... his W-2 comp fell from $600k to $150k. There's more to the story (there always is) but in this case maybe not too much more. Same motion, same ACV, same industry. But he'd just forgotten how different sales is with a strong, dominant brand behind you is. And my advice to founders is: almost never hire a sales exec who has only sold with a strong brand behind them ... if you don't have a strong brand yourself yet.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 🚀 The $195B SaaS Wealth Creation Story: Market Cap Since IPO Shopify, HubSpot & Box all went public around 2014-2015 with similar ~$1.3-1.8B market caps. Here's how their enterprise value creation diverged over 10 years: 📊 Market Cap Evolution: Shopify: $1.3B → $195B (150x growth) HubSpot: $1.3B → $23B (18x growth) Box: $1.8B → $4.5B (2.5x growth) 💰 Value Creation Breakdown: Shopify created $194B in shareholder value HubSpot created $22B in shareholder value Box created $2.7B in shareholder value 🔥 Key Insights: Market Timing = Everything: Shopify caught the e-commerce inflection perfectly. COVID accelerated them to $212B peak market cap in 2021. Category Creation > Competition: Shopify built the "commerce OS," HubSpot created "inbound marketing." Box competed in commoditized cloud storage. Scale Matters: Shopify created 43x more enterprise value than Box, 8.5x more than HubSpot despite similar starting points. 💡 The SaaStr Reality: All three had solid execution. All had great teams. All went public at the same time. But Shopify captured a $195B market opportunity while Box got constrained in a $4.5B outcome. Market size + defensible positioning + execution = generational wealth creation.

content: For a lot of the history of SaaS and B2B, apps reached a sort of parity with the competition ... and a lot of the game was just out marketing, selling, and hustling the other game. It still is about hustling today ... but ... it's different in the Age of AI We are doing so much deep discovery now: ▶️ Which AI app really works best for me? ▶️Are those automation / AI claims real? ▶️What if something even better comes along ... next month? It's no longer about 80% of us picking the #1 brand to automate a workflow. Things are so exciting, but also so unstable. As Aaron Levie put it, no leader should think their position is secure. So the classic GTM playbook simply doesn't work well, even for leaders today. Not without deep product knowledge, and a much more aggressive approach to competition, the markets, and truly solving customers' problems. Even if you are at some of the hottest AI start-ups, the level of competition and the product differentiation is so much more intense, and evolving so quickly, you can't just sell with a tear sheet and a few mid discovery questions. Because we're all back in learning mode again. Including your customers. And that puts everything into play in a way it never really was before.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Can ‘vibe coding’ platforms ever make money? Today, many have negative gross margins. They pay more to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc. than they can charge for those same tokens and API calls. But I think the ‘prosumer’ apps (Replit, Lovable) should be fine: 🧵 3 reasons: 1️⃣ Most ‘prosumers’ (not developers) are basically building websites on steroids with these tools. Something Squarespace and Wix can almost do, but not quite. (This is why Wix bought Base 44 for $80m). Once they put them into production … they will keep paying monthly hosting fees, in essence, of $25-$40 a month for websites with almost zero traffic in most cases This hosting should be 80%+ gross margins. 99% of these sites will see only trivial usage, and they can charge incremental fees for the tiny number with high traffic. In addition, they don’t have to pay for OpenAI or other APIs used by the apps — you have to bring your own keys to use the APIs. So this monthly pricing should become an annuity once more ‘prosumer’ vibed apps move from abandoned to production. 2️⃣ Most ‘prosumers’ will have no idea exactly what they are paying for, which will enable Replit, Lovable, et al to mark the tokens up 50%-90% Developers know exactly what tokens cost in each model, what API calls cost, and how that compares inside of Cursor vs. Claude Code, etc. etc. They know exactly what the costs are. ‘Prosumers’ will have no idea. They just need it to seem fair. Yesterday, I got a bill from Replit for $12.99. I literally have no idea exactly for what, which model, how many tokens, etc. This should enable decent margins from ‘prosumers’. 3️⃣ A lot of ‘prosumer’ vibe apps just won’t need the most expensive models, at least not all the time, or the most tokens, etc. Personally, 150+ hours in, I’ve turned >off< extended thinking and ‘high power model’. Not only do they cost 7.5x more … I didn’t see any benefit for my vibes. In fact, they just made ‘vibing’ slower. I burned through thousands of dollars using the highest power model in my first app and saw zero benefit I could see at ‘prosumer’ level. So the ‘prosumer’ vibe code apps may at least be able to mix-and-match models and mark them all up to ‘list’, or at least, combine cheaper models and more expensive ones in ways the developer-focused platforms really can’t. 🤷‍♀️ Having said that … can these platforms get to the 70%+ gross margins one would expect from ‘software’ companies? We will see. The better the platforms get — the more tokens we will consume. The more cool stuff we will build. It’s hard to see token costs and LLM calls being such a small percentage of the bills for gross margins to hit 70%-80% like at Squarespace, Wix, etc. But maybe Or at least, maybe 50%-60% is practical if millions of vibe coded, low usage apps get into production, the customers pay for them, and they basically use no more tokens (or really include any material costs) once they are in production

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One less discussed impact AI is having in B2B: it’s making your (1) old and (2) tiny competitors more competitive. What do I mean? First, a great AI on top of a dated platform can make it significantly more competitive. Zendesk has done a great job here, quietly. Its AI is pretty good, helping it stay current even with mass disruption in its space. It makes an 18-year old platform work pretty well in the AI age, at least on the surface. Second, a great AI on top of a new start-up can partially balance out that it is feature-poor. Yes, it may not have all the workflows and functions of the bigger guys, but the AI itself, especially if clever, will do a lot of slick things the pre-AI low-end guys couldn’t do. A clever agent can go a long way. This doesn’t mean the old vendors and 5 person start-ups will disrupt you per se. It does mean they may much more competitive today than pre-AI. A crazy example in the contact center space: the grandad of the space, Genesys. Founded way back, pre-Cloud in 1990 (!). Struggled to find its place when Cloud took over contact center, at least at first. And today? It’s re-accelerating at $2B+ ARR, now growing 35% (!). And just closed a $1.5B investment from Salesforce and ServiceNow. That’s how AI made a 1990 dinosaur … super competitive today.

content: The 10 Signs of a Mediocre Employee ... That You Have to Move On From: 1️⃣ Unable to hit deadlines. This is different than missing a few, with a proper heads-up. 2️⃣ Get angry when they fall behind. Instead of quietly stepping up and just getting it done. 3️⃣ Refuse to own a quantitative KPI or goal. They don’t want to own a number. 4️⃣ Don’t raise their hand when they need help. They just hide it. Often even to themselves. 5️⃣ Always “very busy”. The best employees always find a way to help, to take a little more on to help the team. 6️⃣ Argue with bosses and other leaders in public. The boss isn’t always right. But understanding someone has to make the call on tough decisions is important. 7️⃣ Argue when you ask them to fix something that wasn’t done that well. The best agree and just go fix it. 8️⃣ Push back on doing core parts of their job. So you end up doing it yourself. 9️⃣ Need folks to do all their work for them. More an issue with mediocre managers. They are often unwilling to do any actual work themselves. 🔟 Hire mediocre folks under them. It’s true. This is the worst part. Hire folks that just do what they are told. Instead of folks that are great. Blame others. It’s never their fault. And a few bonus signs: ➡️ Gossip. A little is OK, but mediocre employees often become toxic ones, spending too much time on office-related gossip. ➡️ Claim they did the work that their report or other resource actually did. The best highlight the team member that did the work. The mediocre claim they did it themselves, or obscure who actually did it. ➡️ Threatened by a new great hire. Again, a little of this is OK. But great employees embrace all great hires. Even when there is overlap with their role and path. ➡️ Take more than 2 hours a week to manage, maximum. That’s just too much. ➡️ Lie. Mediocre employees lie. They just lie. They claim they got the project done, but didn’t. They claim they held the date, but didn’t actually do it. They claim they hit the plan, but they didn’t. The lie sort of works a little, at first, if they are in a position of trust. But then they have to lie more. Ok sorry that’s a bit more than 10! When you see this behavior, just move on. There’s only more damage to be done by waiting.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: How do you get churned customers ... back? Reactivations are when previously churned customers come back and start paying again. Reactivations are way too often overlooked, but they can be a meaningful lever for growth if you approach them strategically. Our B2C friends often obsess over there, but in B2B, we rarely approach getting customers back as broadly and strategically as we could. RevenueCat manages 40% of all mobile apps subscriptions, across 10,000+ paid apps. What does it see? 12% of lapsed paying customers … come back later. Most are more B2B2C that B2B, but the point still holds. 👉 In B2B, about 8-12% of churned customers tend to come back, depending on your business model and how well you nurture them after they leave. That’s a big enough number to make it worth your time. To drive reactivations, you need a dedicated strategy: #1. Drip Campaigns for Churned Customers Set up a series of emails or messages targeted specifically at churned customers. Space them out—every 60-90 days is a good cadence. Highlight new features, improvements, or anything that addresses the reasons they left in the first place. #2. Invite Them to Events Webinars, product launches, or even customer success stories can help keep you top of mind. It’s about reminding them why they liked your product in the first place. #3. Offer a Low-Risk Reentry Sometimes, churned customers just need a nudge. Offer them a free trial or a discounted rate to come back. Make it easy for them to re-engage without a big commitment upfront. #4. Focus on High NPS Customers: If your product has a high Net Promoter Score (NPS), you already know many of your customers liked or even loved your product. These are the ones most likely to come back if you stay in touch and show them the value they’re missing . #5. Treat Them Well When They Leave. This is critical. And too often, done wrong these days. Let them go gracefully—don’t play games with their data or make it hard to cancel. If you treat them well on the way out, they’re more likely to come back when the timing is right. Reactivations are especially valuable because they often come with lower CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost). You’ve already built some trust with these customers, and they’re familiar with your product. The key is to stay patient and consistent—reactivations can take months or even years, especially in enterprise B2B. But if you play the long game, they can be a meaningful part of your growth strategy.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Which apps make sense for vibe coding by non-engineers today? And which probably don't … yet? After 100+ hours vibe coding without an engineer, here's my framework: 🟢 GREEN LIGHT: #1. Basic info web apps (no customer data) - Squarespace on steroids. Content sites, company pages. Little risk, great use case. #2. Prototypes for validation - Perfect for demos, proof-of-concepts, or specs for developers. No production risk. #3. Internal apps (properly secured) - Dashboards, tracking tools, workflow automation. You control access completely. 🟡 YELLOW LIGHT #4. Landing pages - Great for marketing agility BUT most collect PII. Vibe coding apps often store this data even if you don't realize it. Manageable risk with proper review. 🟠 ORANGE LIGHT: #5. Complex apps - Possible but time-intensive. I'm 100 hours in and not done. Each feature creates exponential complexity in testing and maintenance. #6. Apps with confidential data/PII - Built-in security often beats sloppy human dev work, but security is complicated. Multiple attack vectors exist. Need expert security review before handling real customer data. 🔴 RED LIGHT: #7. Rolling your own Salesforce - Social media delusion. Yes, you can build a basic CRM. No, you cannot build enterprise software. Don't even try. The Bottom Line: Vibe coding works great for content, prototypes, and internal tools. Approach landing pages and complexity with caution. Think very carefully before handling sensitive data. And avoid rebuilding enterprise platforms.

content: In venture capital, is the expectation of abundance obscuring an inevitable thinning of the herd? While the recent surge in seed fund creation might suggest endless opportunity, a closer look reveals a landscape where fewer companies are going public at high valuations. author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I recently caught up with a seasoned sales IC I’ve known for years, and a seasoned CRO. Both washed out in just a few months from their latest roles. It happens, but it seemed odd to me. Both are at least “good” and both are driven, ethical execs. I dug deep with both and learned at least one thing in common: they never really met their teams in person. Not really. And that just leads to fragility. 1️⃣ The seasoned AE worked from home on the east coast for an SF-based start-up. He had a strong track record of being in Top 10% or so at several well-known start-ups. He accepted his new job at a well known start-up … without meeting anyone in person, and only came to the office once, several months after starting. He struggled to learn the product, and then quietly was managed about in about 5 months. He closed very little. 2️⃣ The seasoned CRO was remote and inherited a globally distributed sales team of about 50. Much of the SMB team was in Latin America. He never visited them in person, and never understood the SMB side of the business. He only met folks on the enterprise side. The SMB team saw heightened attrition, and it had no direct leader. The numbers for SMB side of the business declined fairly rapidly, and the CRO was out by month 6 or 7 or so. 👉 Maybe there were other issues here too. There always are. But I was shocked neither really spent any time with the >people< on their teams. Almost none at all in person. It just makes everything … fragile.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A quick summary of what you can and can’t replace with AI today: - Outbound SDRs: you can replace most SDRs with AI today, possibly 100% … but you still need human managing it. IF you truly go deep, train a platform, and orchestrate it >daily<. But this requires a human and later a team to manage. You can’t just push a button. - Inbound BDRs: you can replace almost all of them with AI. If it’s well trained. An AI should be able to qualify a lead faster and better than 95% of BDRs can. Today. - Customer Support: you can replace 80% of your support team with AI today IF you invest. But again, only if you go deep, train a platform, orchestrate it >daily< AND create a very responsive human-in-the loop escalation strategy. - Marketing Managers: you probably don’t need half of them today at all. Claude and ChatGPT as is can do a ton of marketing ops, and visual tools can create incredible collateral. Gamma can arm your team with better sales collateral than ever before. But again, you need a >lot< of orchestration. - Customer Success. We need better AI platforms today, but we don’t need 60%+ of the CSMs we have today. CSMs that don’t solve problems and just do QBRs without adding true value are not necessary in the age of AI. You can probably move on from them today. - Account Execs: You still need 100% of them. This should change in the next 24 months. - Engineering: I’m not convinced AI lets you reduce headcount here at all. Haven’t seen it at >any< of my top performing investments. Instead, what I see overall is a 20%-40% productivity boost, net net. But it becomes an arms race. Everyone is more productive, software is shipping faster, so you need more great engineers than ever. It’s a cracked arms race in product development today.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We sent 4,495 AI SDR emails in 2 weeks and achieved the #1 response rate on our platform. But here's what nobody tells you about making AI SDRs actually work... The Metrics: ✅ 4,495 personalized messages sent in 14 days ✅ Highest response rate on our entire platform ✅ $700,000 of pipeline opportunities opened ✅ Meetings booked daily (literally got one this morning) ✅ Outperformed all our historical human SDR averages — mostly ✅ Better results than some of our human AEs The Reality Check First We had unfair advantages. SaaStr has been around since 2012, we've sold $100,000,000 in sponsorships, and people know our brand. We targeted our existing database—website visitors, past attendees, lapsed accounts—not cold lists. We spent 2 weeks doing basically nothing else: 90 minutes every morning, 1 hour every evening training our AI, plus real-time responses throughout the day. 👉What Actually Works: 1️⃣ Your AI has to add real value, not just volume There's no way we could send 4,495 good emails ourselves manually in two weeks. The key is each one has to be at the level we would write ourselves. Bad: "Hey [NAME], saw you visited our website" Good: "Congrats on your new VP role at Oracle. Since you attended SaaStr London last year, thought you'd want to know about our 2025 VC track with speakers from a16z and Sequoia..." 2️⃣ Your data is messier than you think We trained our AI on 20+ million words of SaaStr content, but still found: - Opportunities never logged in Salesforce - Missing context from AEs who never used the system - Customer relationships that existed nowhere in our CRM We literally spend time every day finding things that were missing and manually adding them to AI's knowledge base. 3️⃣ Human-in-the-loop isn't optional When prospects respond to your AI, YOU have to respond instantly at the same quality level. We have it hooked up to Slack—our phones go off at all hours because SaaStr is global. The AI creates an expectation of responsiveness. You better match it or they'll know it was "just an AI email." 5️⃣ This is additive, not replacement We still do personal emails, marketing campaigns, and have human SDRs. Results by campaign type: - Website visitors: Hit or miss - Cold outbound: Ranked 4th out of 4 campaigns - Lapsed renewal accounts: Really good results 🏋🏽‍♀️ The Uncomfortable Truth: It's MORE work, not less. You get 10x better output, but it requires S-tier human orchestration. E.g., we're running 30+ personas across different campaigns. 🔮 Bottom line: AI SDRs work incredibly well, but only with proper training and orchestration. After 60 days of daily improvements, you'll have something you're proud of. But you can't skip the daily 30-45 minute audit process. Full breakdown with all our tools and processes at link in comments.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Ok day 5 of vibe coding with replit and ... it's time to take a break. I'm burnt. I was vibe coding all weekend, all Saturday night even, it's addictive. When it works, it's so engaging and fun. It's more addictive than any video game I've ever played. You can just iterate, iterate, and see your vision come alive. So cool. Well, almost. Then I spend 12+ hours over the weekend just doing QA + fixes, and it looked better at first ... but ... by the end things were working worse. My app is basically just: - algo (with AI) - dashboard - email / workflow By Day 4, I'd finally sort of gotten the algo + dashboard to the state where it seemed to mostly work, and the emails were cool if not totally working right. We had a lot of issues to overcome, but we kept at it. And then yesterday ... Replie started to overwrite the app we'd built to fix the remaining bugs. It started to make up entries and directly overwrite our database. It made up reports. It made up people in the system that weren't real. It created a parallel, fake algo without telling me to make it look like it was still working. And without asking me. Rogue. And now, nothing works. And I've lost confidence, even if I spend 2+ days and nights fixing it by vide coding, it will never be stable. Because Replie will go in and rewrite it again. No one is perfect. And getting to a strong POC at this pace is epic. It was so fun. But can I ever get to a GA commercial grade product here? I want to. I'm willing to put up with some pain. I'm going to take a day or two off and try once more. But right now -- I'm wiped out. I feel like I spend the past 4 days played one of the most intense videogames ever ... almost leveled-up massively ... but in the end, reset to a level lower than when I started.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Human-in-the-loop and AI orchestration are the most misunderstood concepts in B2B SaaS. 1️⃣ Most think "human-in-the-loop" means AI makes their work easier. Wrong. 👋 It means humans handle the cases AI can't solve. All day long. In real time, or as close as possible. The 30% of support tickets that are too complex. The sales conversations that need real judgment. The edge cases that break automated systems. 🚵 As AI gets better, the remaining human work gets HARDER, not easier. 2️⃣ And "orchestration" isn't picking vendors and watching dashboards. It's 60+ days of intensive training after deployment. Daily quality auditing. Managing 5-10 AI systems that each have unique failure modes. 👉 SaaStr's reality check: We sent 4,495 AI emails with top response rates, but it required: • 90 minutes every morning training the AI • 1 hour every night reviewing performance • Real-time responses throughout the day • 20+ million words of training content 🫵 Doing AI right is more work than not using AI at all Perplexity's CBO revealed another layer at SaaStr AI Summit 2025: AI changes WHEN you work, not just what you do. Sales reps now use AI live during prospect calls, making split-second decisions about what intelligence to surface while maintaining authentic conversations. Support already proved this model works: • Decagon: 70% deflection rates • Duolingo: 80%+ automation • Intercom: 86% resolution rates But those numbers hide the human orchestration behind them. Support teams evolved into AI managers, not disappearing but becoming more specialized. They do the tough stuff now. The multiplication effect hits when you deploy >multiple< AI systems. Now you need people who understand how your chatbot's limitations interact with your email automation's strengths. How to prevent AI systems from amplifying each other's errors. The uncomfortable truth: AI success requires "S-tier human orchestration" to get top-tier results. The companies winning with AI aren't replacing humans—they're making humans AI-capable. The future with AI in B2B isn't >less< human work. It's different and more human work: more complex, more valuable, and just plain more of it. And yes, more intense. Higher ROI? Yes. Much more work? Also yes.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A lot of folks ask why our SaaStr AI on our homepage is so good One reason is it has been trained on 18,000,000 words of SaaStr content But another key reason: for the first 60 days, every single day, I QA’d it and fixed any hallucinations or similar errors for 15-20 minutes a day. Every single day for 2+ months. (Now, I do spot QA every week but not every day). 👉 If your AI SDR or AI Whatever isn’t really “working” — be honest. Did you do the same? Every single day? We’re piloting 2 more AI tools right now, they both are great but relatively early. Same thing. Every single day, you have to review the outputs. At least a subset. Can an AI QA itself? Yes, to some extent. But at least today, not enough. Not to get you to where you really want it to be. If every single day, you hunt out the errors, the hallucinations, the suboptimal answers, and train your AI on the >right< answers … it gets faster fast. But you have to do it every single day for first 60+ days, and then frequently thereafter. You’ll see a lot on X about how everyone has “Forward Deployed Engineers” now. Reason #1? Those B2B AIs don’t magically work the way we all want them to out of the box with zero iterations and zero training — and zero humans. Almost every B2B AI company I work with and in my portfolio has a 30 day or so onboarding process, driven by humans. And that’s >after< the AI ingests all your data. If your ACV is high enough, the simplest way to implement this is to have Forward Deployed Engineers that just do all this work for the customer. For SMBs and small ACVs, it’s tougher. Who will do the training? Or will you tolerate a more mediocre AI without it?

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 10 Things Mediocre Sales Reps Do. That Make You Close ... A Lot Less. 1️⃣ Immediate Discounting Reps who jump to offering discounts often lack confidence in their product or don’t know how to create urgency. It’s a sign they’re relying on price as their only lever, which devalues the product and sets a bad precedent for future deals. A strategic discount can help push a deal to close faster, or get it over the line. But it doesn’t make someone want to buy in SaaS. Almost never. 2️⃣ Not Understanding the Product This is way, way, way too common. If a salesperson doesn’t deeply understand the product they’re selling, they can’t effectively address customer needs or objections. Worse, they might overpromise features that don’t exist, which destroys trust and leads to churn . 3️⃣ Fear of Competition Great salespeople respect their competitors and use them as a benchmark to improve. Weak salespeople, on the other hand, either avoid discussing competitors or badmouth them, which makes them look insecure and unprofessional. In general, don’t hire folks into a highly competitive sales environment that have only worked at a market leader. 4️⃣ Blaming Others Reps who constantly blame marketing, leads, or lack of support for their failures are avoiding accountability. While external factors can impact sales, great reps find ways to adapt and succeed regardless of the challenges . 5️⃣ Lack of Updates or Progress A weak salesperson often has no meaningful updates to share. They’ll either ghost their manager or repeat the same vague status reports, which signals they’re not actively working their pipeline or moving deals forward . 6️⃣ Not Knowing the Buyer If a rep doesn’t understand who the key decision-makers are, what their pain points are, or where the deal stands, they’re flying blind. This lack of preparation is a major red flag and often leads to lost deals . 7️⃣ Not Believing in the Product Selling something you don’t believe in is nearly impossible. If a rep doesn’t genuinely think their product solves a problem, it shows —and customers can sense it . 8️⃣ Over-Reliance on Scripts While scripts are helpful, reps who stick to them rigidly often fail to adapt to the unique needs of each prospect. Sales is about listening and tailoring your approach, not just reciting lines. 9️⃣ Poor Time Management Weak salespeople often spend too much time on low-priority tasks or chasing unqualified leads. Great salespeople know how to prioritize their time and focus on high-value opportunities. 🔟 Lack of Follow-Up Many deals are lost simply because the rep didn’t follow up. Weak salespeople either forget or assume the prospect isn’t interested after one or two attempts, while great reps stay persistent without being pushy. 👬 The good news is that some of these weaknesses can be addressed with training, coaching, and self-awareness. But if you see too many of these traits in one rep, it’s often a sign they’re not the right fit for the role.

content: Why I generally don’t write small investment checks (e.g., $50k-$100k) — but others do: I have about $100m of fresh capital to invest right now in SaaStr Fund. That’s a lot, but not as much as it used to be. There has been a lot of inflation :) But in any event, my job is to turn that $100m into at least $300m, and ideally, $400m or more. So I am grateful when a founder is kind and generous enough to offer me a chance to invest $50k or $100k into a round. author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One of the best CEOs I know said to me the other day, "I wish we'd never allowed work from home." I know this is a complex issue even today, and for many, a triggering one. What I can tell you in my ecosystem is the fastest moving and fastest growing startups I've invested in are either 100% returned to office (with some exceptions, but as a baseline) or 100% distributed. Now the ones that are 100% return to office often are more flexible than pre-2020. Few are as 100% as pre-2020. But they are 5 days a week in the office as a base, with the hiring trade-offs that come with that. They generally won't hire anyone that can't come into the office, and that limits the hiring pool substantially. I've also invested in some winners that are 100% remote. But they really, really work at it. And it's all they do. And it has trade-offs, especially on GTM and sales teams. But the ones that are some of a "best efforts" mix of maybe come into the office a bit a few times a week ... they just don't have the same urgency. They just don't.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Palantir just posted 39% YoY growth in Q1 2025 - a stunning turnaround from the 13% growth trough of 2023. The greatest turn-around in the history of B2B. #1: The deceleration was brutal: From 49% growth in early 2021 to just 13% in Q2 2023. For a company that spent 20 years building sophisticated data analytics, hitting the low teens felt existential. The market questioned if their complex approach could scale. #2. Then came the AI awakening: Starting late 2023, consistent reacceleration: 19% → 21% → 27% → 30% → 36% → 39%. What changed? While everyone built ChatGPT wrappers, Palantir became the infrastructure layer that makes AI actually useful in large orgs. #3: The numbers are staggering: ➡️ U.S. commercial revenue: +71% YoY ➡️ $1B annual run rate in commercial ➡️ 769 customers (+39% YoY) ➡️ $810M commercial TCV (+239% YoY) ➡️ Rule of 40 score: 83% (39% growth + 44% margin) This is stunning B2B performance at scale. #4: Why this reacceleration is different: 1️⃣ Product-market fit 2.0 - their "over-engineered" complexity became a feature in the AI era 2️⃣ Commercial breakthrough after years as gov contractor 3️⃣ 5x faster deployments (some customers up in "mere hours") 4️⃣ Network effects finally kicking in 5/7 #5: Key lesson: Platform thinking pays off. Palantir spent 15+ years building capabilities that seemed ahead of their time. When AI made those capabilities essential, they were ready. Sometimes being "too early" means you'll be perfectly positioned when the market catches up. #6: The bottom line: This isn't just riding the AI wave - it's 20 years of platform investment finally finding its perfect market moment. They've transformed from mysterious gov contractor to essential AI infrastructure provider. Build platforms, not features. Preparation > timing.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One interesting observation using our AI now for sales: The humans on the sales team have to respond faster. If you truly train your AI properly for outbound, and you reach out to your own list at least (that knows you) … you will get results. But if a human then takes a day or longer to respond, that feels just … glacial … when the customer responds almost instantly to the AI Right now, humans sort of follow up with AI generated opportunities once a day. They take their time, qualify them, grab a coffee, and then respond. That’s not good enough when the AI itself will respond with great answers in seconds. The human side of sales is going to have to be much more responsive to customers. Otherwise, your own AI will make your humans look lethargic. Because it’s so much more responsive than your humans.

content: 5 Things ChatGPT Is Executing Better Than Google Did in Early Days #1. Revenue Velocity from Day One 🚀ChatGPT: $0 → $3.7B revenue in 24 months 🦄Google: Took 6 years to reach $1B (2004 IPO) ChatGPT launched with immediate monetization through ChatGPT Plus, while Google spent years figuring out the advertising model. Lesson: Having a revenue strategy at launch accelerates everything. #2. Enterprise Penetration Speed 🚀ChatGPT: 92% of Fortune 500 companies using it within 2 years 🦄Google: Gradual enterprise adoption over 5+ years ChatGPT cracked enterprise sales velocity that took Google much longer. API-first strategy and immediate productivity gains made C-suite adoption faster than Google's consumer-to-enterprise journey. #3. Global Distribution from Launch 🚀ChatGPT: Available in 180+ countries day one, localized quickly 🦄Google: Gradual international expansion, took years to scale globally ChatGPT leveraged cloud infrastructure and AI translation to achieve instant global reach. Google had to build international data centers and partnerships country by country. #4. Multi-Modal Product Evolution 🚀ChatGPT: Voice, vision, files, web search integrated within 18 months 🦄Google: Took 5+ years to expand beyond text search (Images 2001, News 2002) ChatGPT's AI-native architecture allowed rapid capability expansion. Google had to build each vertical from scratch with separate teams and infrastructure. #5. Capital Raised (and ... Deployed) 🚀ChatGPT: $11B projected 2025 revenue on ~$58B total funding 🦄Google: $1B revenue in 2004 on ~$1.7B total funding (inflation-adjusted ~$2.8B) While Google was far more capital-efficient initially, ChatGPT is achieving higher revenue multiples faster. The AI infrastructure investments are paying off with better unit economics at scale. The Caveat: Google was building the internet's infrastructure. ChatGPT is building on top of it. Google laid the foundation ChatGPT now leverages. Modern platform advantages (cloud, APIs, global distribution) can compress traditional growth timelines—if you have the right strategy to exploit them. hashtag #AI hashtag #GrowthStrategy hashtag #PlatformStrategy

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: While we all love digital marketing, here are some things that always work: 1/ A customer conference. It's OK to start small. 2/ A weekly webinar. You just have to do it every week. It's OK if just a few come at first. 3/ Amazing blog content. Add 2 amazing pieces of value 4/ Steak dinners. Do a city tour and try to meet at least 10 customers in each major city, and invite your prospects there. They will do the selling for you. 5/ Visit all your largest customers. Do at least a roadmap presentation, and ask for their feedback. Now a few things that always work -- but only if you have someone on the team that truly knows how to do them: 6/ Outbound. Highly personalized outbound to the right buyers can always generate conversations. But mediocre outbound and trite cadences often get you nowhere. 7/ Events. Do your own customer conference, that always works. They'll come. But third-party events like AWS, Dreamforce, SaaStr, Shoptalk? Field marketers that are >good< at it get 40% of their pipe from it. But you can get $0 ROI if you aren't good at it. 8/ Partner Marketing. Going to market together with someone with an overlapping base can be an amazing force multiplier. But if you aren't good at it, each party just spams the other's base. That doesn't pay off. 9/ Website redesigns. A lot of marketers love to do this, especially right after they join You do need to do this. Your marketing site should be >better< than your product. It's much easier to build. But done wrong, it can be a huge time sink with low ROI. This is common. 10/ Podcasts and videos. The best ones are magical. Even if just 20 prospects / customers listen to your A+ podcast, it can move the needle. But 90% of folks phone in it. The problem is these media consume so many resources. Huge amounts. Skip them if you aren't great at them. Net net, >all< this stuff works. It always does. That's why everyone does it. But some of it >only< works if you have a truly expert dedicated to it, 52 weeks a year. Others you can do yourself -- right now. If you make them great. So start with 1-5.

content: If I trust an AI more than a human sales rep … Then I will buy from an AI over a human sales rep. That day is pretty close to here today already. The AI sales rep already: - is available 24x7 - knows product cold - doesn’t lie or make stuff up to close a deal Many think this is silly … but most of those that do haven’t bought software is a while themselves, or used a great AI in this context yet. Go try to buy a routine piece of SaaS software. See how painful it is, how long it takes, how hard it is to get the precise answers you need for your own flow and use case. Are the tools here today? Not quite. But they will be soon. If we had the quality of dev teams working on OpenAI and Cursor that are working on AI AEs, the products would already be great. But they are coming soon. Some will enhance AEs, and make them Mech AEs, for sure. Some will create agents that make humans better. Other products will run basic sales autonomously, but kick up exceptions and other issues to humans. AI support already works this way pretty well. And some products, some will basically enable AI to handle 90% of sales on its own. This will require highly transparent pricing, the ability to truly one-click cancel, and the ability to auto-onboard in many cases. But many founders will choose to build the latter. Even if you disagree with this, realize it’s already here in coding, in support, even in SaaStr’s own AI. And things are getting so, so much better in AI every single day. The rate of improvement and change is like nothing we’ve ever seen in B2B and SaaS.

content: Mary Meeker and the Bond team have released their latest 300+ page annual report, this time all on AI It's very good but long, so I've summarized the Top 10 Points for B2B and enterprise founders here: #1. AI User Adoption Is Literally Unprecedented We know this, but still, the numbers do sort of blow your mind: ➡️ ChatGPT: 0 to 800MM weekly users in 17 months (vs. Netflix’s 10+ years to 100MM) ➡️ Time to 100MM users: ChatGPT (2 months), TikTok (9 months), Instagram (2.5 years) ➡️ Global adoption: 90% of ChatGPT users are outside North America by Year 3 (vs. Internet’s 23 years to reach this level) .Why This Matters for B2B: Unlike previous tech waves that started in Silicon Valley and slowly diffused globally, AI hit the world simultaneously. This means your global TAM expanded overnight, but so did your competition. Every B2B and SaaS company now competes in a global, AI-enabled market from Day 1. The Kicker: ChatGPT’s daily usage increased 202% over 21 months, with users spending more time per session (47% longer) and having more sessions per day (106% more). This isn’t just adoption – it’s addiction-level engagement. #2. The Infrastructure Math Is Unprecedented The Capital Intensity Is Off The Charts: ▶️Big Six tech CapEx: $212B annually (63% YoY growth) ▶️Microsoft AI business: $13B run-rate (175% YoY growth) ▶️NVIDIA data center revenue: $39B quarterly (78% YoY growth) ▶️Amazon AWS CapEx as % of revenue: 49% (vs. 4% during initial cloud buildout) 💡What’s Really Happening: This isn’t just “cloud 2.0” – it’s the biggest infrastructure buildout in tech history. Companies are spending more on AI infrastructure than entire countries’ GDP. xAI built a 200,000 GPU data center in 122 days (faster than building a single house). 👉For B2B and SaaS Leaders: The infrastructure layer is being rebuilt from scratch. If you’re not thinking about how to leverage this massive compute capacity, you’re missing the biggest infrastructure opportunity since the cloud transition. T #3. China Is Playing a Different Game Entirely The Models You’ve Barely Heard Of: ▶️DeepSeek R1: 93% performance of OpenAI’s o3-mini at fraction of training cost ▶️Alibaba Qwen 2.5-Max: Outperforms both DeepSeek and ChatGPT on key benchmarks ▶️Baidu Ernie 4.5: 80% cheaper than predecessor, costs 0.2% of GPT-4.5 Market Reality Check: ✅China leads in open-source AI model releases (3 large-scale models in 2025 vs. US competition) ✅Chinese AI apps dominate domestically: Top 10 AI apps by MAUs in China are all domestic ✅DeepSeek rose from 0% to 21% global LLM user share in just months ✅China has more industrial robots installed than rest of world combined 🌎Geopolitical Stakes: This isn’t just about better chatbots. content: So When Is It “Too Early” To Hire Your First Marketer? In a perfect world, you’d learn something about marketing first before you hire someone to take it over. I.e., you’d experiment and at least make some progress in: ➡️ Content Marketing. Can you get even 1 or 2 customers from blogging and writing? ➡️ Growth Hacking. Can you get even a couple of customers by emailing to a small list you’ve built? ➡️ Event + Field Marketing. Can you get any good leads by going to an industry event? Some founders end up very good at this. Many are terrible. ➡️ Drip Marketing. Can you set up HubSpot or Mailchimp or Activecampaign or something similar to reach out programmatically to your leads, and see them convert at a higher rate? ➡️ PR. Can you get some great PR for your company that leads to customers — any customers? ➡️ Adwords / FB and paid social. Can you prove this works at all, even just to get a few customers? You can hire someone without any indications any of these channels work. But you’ll likely have a lot more success if you have a tiny bit of data to suggest what will work best for your app. I’d at least try all of the above first before you hire a marketer, just to learn. Then hire someone immediately after you’ve seen any traction, even just a time bit, in any of the above. Once any channel works even a tiny bit, you’re probably ready to hire a strong full-time marketer.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Hiring your first marketing leader is a pivotal moment, and it’s easy to get it wrong. The vast, vast majority of “marketers” are not the right fit to be your first marketing hire and leader. Here’s how to do it right: 1. Define What You Need Right Now. And Hire That. For Real. This may sound obvious, but too many founders just hire a “marketer”. Not someone 80%+ focused on exactly what you need in marketing — now. Are you looking for someone to generate leads from scratch, or do you already have a steady stream of leads and need someone to optimize and scale? If you have no leads, you need a growth / demand-gen expert who can create demand from nothing. If you already have leads, you can hire someone who knows how to manage the funnel and increase revenue per lead. If you have a sales-led motion, hire someone that has worked with a sales team at your stage. 2. Hire for the Stage You’re At Don’t overhire. If you’re early-stage, look for someone who’s been hands-on at a startup or a smaller company and knows how to build from the ground up. And hire someone that doesn’t need a team to start. A little help from some cost-effective agencies is fine and good. But a whole team? That’s not who you need. 3. Focus on Metrics and Execution. Not Brand or “Product Marketing”. Not Until You Are At $10m-$20m+ ARR At Least. Your first marketing leader needs to be metrics-driven. Ask them about their experience with lead velocity rate (LVR), cost per lead (CPL), and conversion rates. They should be able to show you how they’ve moved the needle in previous roles. 4. Test for Hands-On Ability. You Need a “Hands-On Keyboard” Marketer. Most Aren’t. Early on, you need someone who can do the work themselves—whether it’s running campaigns, building collateral, or setting up webinars. If they’re focused on strategy and not execution, they’re not the right fit for your first hire. 95% of the senior marketers you talk to will really only want to work on strategy. 5. Look for Some Previous Success, For Real. An Owner. Ask for specific examples of campaigns they’ve run and the results they’ve achieved. If they can’t point to measurable successes, they’re not ready for this role. 6. Don’t Expect a Silver Bullet. But Demand Small, Quick Wins. Marketing isn’t magic. It’s about consistent execution and iteration. If you’re expecting your first marketing hire to instantly 10x your leads, you’re setting yourself up for disappointment. Be realistic about what they can achieve in the first 6-12 months 7. Avoid the “Blue Pens” Trap If you hire the wrong person, you’ll end up with a lot of fluff—like branded swag and pretty PowerPoints—but no real results. Make sure they’re focused on driving revenue, not just building a brand. 8. Make Sure They Convince You Before They Start A great marketer should convince you with data and examples how they can tilt the curve for you. If they can’t convince you they can do it, don’t have them start.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So there’s a vibe in hiring today: candidates immediately asking for a lot of money before they even pass any even soft test for the job. I had two recent experiences. One, a founder reached out to me that needed a job. His start-up had shut down. I wasn’t sure he was a fit for a role, but I wanted to help. I walked him through it, and less than 5 minutes in, he interrupted me. “I need to make at least $800,000” he told me, before I could even finish what the role was really about. I kindly ended the Zoom. A month later, he took a job as an AE and hit me up to see if I’d buy his product (which I wasn’t remotely a fit for). I asked what his OTE was in this role. “$140k” he said. Hmmm. The other day I had a similar experience with a marketing candidate. Before we could finish talking about the role itself, he interrupted me to “get aligned on comp.” He also said he wanted to "make at least $300,000". I mean great, but at least prove to me you understand the role and what we need. Money matters. No argument. I get it. But maybe I’m old school, but if you start aggressively pushing on comp before you even prove you understand the job (let alone could do it) … you might just qualify yourself out of something great.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Ok this is a simple post, but I think an important one: Raising Prices Isn't a Growth Strategy Why not? Well, sure maybe it gives you a boost this quarter or even this year. But with very few exceptions, it doesn't get you more customers. My top concern when I see start-ups and scale-ups hit a rough patch, idea #1 is to raise prices. After all, it doesn't require doing any better in sales or marketing. Or closing any feature gaps. So it's a bit of a desperation tactic, 8 times out of 10. I'm all in favor of strategic, annual reviews of pricing. And making real-time adjustments as you launch new features and learn from them. But if your team's best idea to slowing growth is raising prices? You have the wrong team. The only real answer to fight your way out of a rough patch is to find a way to get more new customers. Not try to extract more from the ones you already have. Again, sometimes that has its place. But not as a strategy. Don't let your team off the hook for missing the plan with a price increase. And especially, don't let yourself off the hook.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So net net, most folks in tech want to join 🔥 “hot” start-ups 🔥 . So being “hot” almost always helps with recruiting the best. But it’s not always that simple. Many top engineers just don’t want to work at somewhere obvious, and looking for interesting problems others aren’t solving. A lot of marketers are looking as much for fit for their skills as how hot the company is. But with sales reps especially? I’ve never seen one that was ambitious that didn’t want to join one of the “hot” startups out there. Even if the economics per se didn’t make it a slam dunk. There are probably a lot of logical reasons for this, too: 🔥 Hot start-ups probably offer a faster promotion path in sales 🔥 Hot start-ups probably offer a higher energy team to work with 🔥 Hot start-ups give you better personal brand portability in sales 🔥 Hot start-ups are probably growing fast enough to at least in >theory< give you a shot at outsized comp for outsized results 🎇 And in general, there’s just an energy about a sales team on fire at a hot start-up everyone wants to join They feel like career-makers in sales. And maybe they are. So net net being “hot” always helps in recruiting but in sales most of all. It’s probably the number one reason to shoot for being a unicorn, to get on stage, to do more PR, to get everyone talking about you. Sales talent is drawn to hot start-ups like moths to a flame. Without that, a great VP of Sales will still find a way. Great reps will want to work for a great VP of Sales. But even there, it’s so much easier to attract the best sales talent. And if you aren’t “hot” >and< don’t have a truly great VP of Sales that the best want to work for? Usually, you end up with a fairly mediocre sales team after the first few pirates & romantics. If you aren’t hot, at least someone find the kind of VP of Sales everyone would want to work for.

content: The tough question for many in tech is going to be: will I be managing an AI — or managed out? There’s no question AI will make the best sales reps better. Already happening and will accelerate. If that’s you — 2026 will be awesome. There’s no question AI will make the best customer success execs be able to handle more accounts, better. Already starting. The same is true in marketing, support, etc. 🍵But the folks that just come to meeting with a mug? That don’t really own anything? 🤷‍♀️The inside sales reps that never really learn the product cold? That just wait to send contracts out for e-signature? That takes a day or two to get back to you? AI will do much better, very soon. 💁🏻‍♂️The marketing managers that just want to manage agencies? I think most of them will be out of a job in 2026. 👋 The product managers and marketers that just want to talk and talk about features that never really ship? They will be bypassed. AI will empower folks that are truly hands-on keyboard for real. And know their sh*t. They will be managing multiple AIs. They will be Mech AEs and AI fueled Marketing Superheroes. And the best CSMs we’ve ever seen. The rest will begin to be managed out. We will just use whatever AI is best instead. It’s already happened in support. 30%-40% or more of support reps are already being let go. Don’t let it be you. The B2B Box Checkers and Zoom Nodders — we won’t need them in 2026. Not many at least.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One thing I'm seeing too much of in B2B and SaaS: folks taking their time in AI. The AI Slow Roll. 🤷‍♀️ VPs of Eng saying they're "still looking at new tools like Windsurf and Cursor" ... but they're not sure yet 🙉 Product leaders saying AI isn't ready yet for prime time "due to hallucinations" 🌊 Revenue leaders saying customers "all want to talk to a human" and "a great sales reps beats an AI" Change fast. Or you will lose. You will lose to the competition that has already figured out, or will soon. - The best in tech are already automating 50% of code with AI. Even Salesforce is at 20%. - Hallucinations are not an acceptable excuse. Train your model better, handle exceptions, and kick issues up to humans. This is already solved in most cases with great training. - AI is going to kill the lazy AE, SDR and CSM. Fast. Many of us already would prefer to talk to an S-tier AI. And in any event, most of your team isn't that great. They take days to reply or set up a meeting. And no, they aren't such great "relationship builders". If you aren't seeing the change, the possibilities, and most importantly, the change of pace, well then .. It's You. Change Fast.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So it’s become a thing with many founders and VCs to think how far you can go in AI today with a Small But Mighty Team. Many of the early break-out leaders in AI for B2B and otherwise have been pretty tight teams. And it’s not a completely new vibe. Instagram had just 13 employees when Facebook acquired it for $1 Billion. But it did have just one product, strong network effects, and no sales team. Honestly we’d all love if the Small But Mighty B2B start-up scaled. If a small team of 20-40 could get you to $100m+ in ARR. And given the massive growth of some AI apps today, we are seeing that now repeatedly. But there are three issues before you try to replicate this fully, at least after the early days: 1⃣ The first one is that it’s a competitive world. So folks that are hyper-efficient with AI … may just plow the AI gains back into going even harder. And thus — hiring more. I learned from RevenueCat where SaaStr Fund was the first investor. CEO Jacob Eiting shared a chart with me of how much more “efficient” the company has become since adopting AI dev tools. Huge gains in PRs. But … but … what did they do with those gains? Hire even more and go even harder. They have 40% market share in their space — managing mobile subscriptions. But they have competition and can’t rest on their laurels. So they are doubling down and hiring even more to keep these gains going. What if your competitor gets the same gains, and then goes around and reinvests that output into even more great developers? 2⃣ The Second “Problem” With Small But Mighty AI Teams … Is Enterprise Sales A tiny team can be fairly efficient with a 100% self-serve and PLG motion. But … what about when bigger companies want to buy? You can see in our recent CRO Confidential deep dive with Windsurf’s VP of Sales that already they are up to almost 100 sales and GTM professionals. In a handful of months! If you want to compete in bigger deals, in the enterprise, you probably have to do the same. 3⃣ The Third Problem is The Intense Pressure to Be Multi-Product and Even a Compound Start-Up Today Most of the Small But Mighty Teams I’ve seen — and I’ve run one in many ways — really just manage one big product at scale. But if you have to have 3-4 products now to compete even at $2m ARR, or even just at $5m or $10m ARR, how can you do that with just one team? So that 30 person, $100m ARR AI B2B start-up? It’s possible. For sure. We have examples now. It’s even cool. But … But … can the Small and Mighty Startup compete that way in the coming years? And can it sell and scale sales? I’m not so sure for most of us. At least, I think the answer, is not always. Efficiency is a wonderful thing. But AI is also making the world incredibly competitive. Even in spaces that didn’t used to be all that competitive. Most of us are having to step up much more just to keep up.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Can a single great developer be 50%-90% more productive with AI dev tools than just 12 months ago? Yes. The thing is … they >all< can be. Every great developer can be 50%-90% more productive. Including your competition, of couse. So … things aren’t getting more efficient net net in many cases. It’s an arms race, actually. Everyone can build 2x-4x more software. So … everyone will. At least, every strong, motivated team well. More features, more products, more multi-product. That means more competition, not less. Get ahead of it.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So SaaStr is a 5 person entity. Just 5 of us, but we do a lot. A lot. And yes, there are agencies and contractors that help us (bless them), but the full-time team is just 5. Before AI, we maybe could respond to a handful of email-based issues, and a few chats. And we could not provide any direct 1-on-1 advice. Oh so much has changed in just a few weeks. Our AI (Delphi.ai/saastr) has now handled 139,156 conversations for us. And most of them are epicly good. Now our AI can: -Advise founders on who to hire -Review VC pitch decks -Review board materials -Help you pick the right SaaS vendor -Help you work through slowing growth -Answer ticket questions for SaaStr Annual better than any human -Help folks that want to volunteer for SaaStr Annual figure out how -Manage 100s of speaker submissions -Help sponsors pick the right sponsorship for them, without bias -Answer 100s of nitty gritty sponsorship questions Before, we had a pre-AI intercom chat that we answered maybe once a week. 🤖 Now we can do 139,156 conversations a month with AI. And they are really, really good. Think about this for your app, if you haven't gone all-in on AI. What if your competitor can handle millions of interactions effortlessly a month? Automate almost all those workflows that today aren't automated? You will lose if you can't figure some version of this out yourself. This is an age of change in business software like we have never seen. Get on it fast, for real. Not just to be "adding some AI". Because AI, used right, enables you to do more things at scale than were ever possible before.
