content: When most SaaS companies see growth slow, they move Customer Success into Sales. It usually seems to “work” at first as more energy and attention is put on account expansion. But then … it so often becomes An Excuse. As new logo count falls, new deals get harder, then sales leans even more and more into the base. Retention tactics become too aggressive as sales’ energy begins to focus more and more there. Sales even starts to threaten customers who plan to leave or downgrade. I see this time and time again. In the end, sales should be about new bookings. Otherwise, all the energy goes into farming when times get tougher. Your may make the plan for this quarter on upsells. But you can’t make the plan for the coming years without new logos and new, happy customers.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So a vendor we've been using since 2016 and sent multiple clients to over the years suddenly had a dramatic quality decline. Dramatic. After 8 great years together. What happened? Well, they got acquired. And that does lead to change. Still, I was surprised everything got so much worse. They lost our files. They missed deliverables. And this just never, ever happened before. So I talked to the CEO of the acquirer. He said he was super frustrated all 3 principals of the vendor be bought quit right after the deal. In his mind, they took the money and ran. I was at the point of not caring, given all the issues. But I do get it. M&A is tough. Acquiring assets is one thing. Acquiring people is ... hard. It's hard. Who wants to go work for someone now? Who wants to be on a different mission? Who wants to not set the pace or tone anymore? I get it. But also have been acquired twice, I have some ideas on how to do it better: 1️⃣ Ask the founders what they want to do after the deal closes. You may not like the answers, they may not be 100% honest, but ask. 2️⃣ It's better to have 50% of founders' engagement and time than have them leave and lose 100% of that knowledge. So get them help so they'll want to stay. 3️⃣ Take integration more seriously. No one does this right, not really. Bring in a great leader to manage the integration for real from Day 1. 4️⃣ Have a calm plan if the founders leave after you acquire them. No matter what the financial incentives, they may still leave. If you have a calm plan on Day 1, it will be much less disruptive. 5️⃣ Expect some deceleration after an acquisition. Folks just aren't going to work with the same intensity. If you demand that, you'll be disappointed.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There’s a lot of discussion about bootstrapping vs. raising VC but there’s one issue that is underdiscussed: What To Do With The Cash What do I mean? At first, for sure, bootstrapping arguably is harder. There’s no seed round, no big Series A, to fund things. Cash is even tighter. Everything takes longer. It’s harder, at least in some ways. But the thing is, to bootstrap, you have to be profitable. Or at least break-even. By definition. So you tend to get pretty good at it. Years go by, you grow to $5m, $10m, $20m ARR, and many times, the profits grow too. You might drop 20%-30% to the bottom line as you scale. And what do you do with those $2m, $4m, $20m of profits? It’s complicated: 💰First, you can just distribute them to yourself and the team. That’s great … and it’s something you can’t do as venture-backed. You can’t really pay yourself $2m of the profits as a VC-backed CEO. But it also means you aren’t investing as much or at all in growth. It’s too easy to underinvest here and distribute all the profits, or most of them. 🏦 Second, you can try to save it for a war chest. That’s great but you will have to pay taxes — a lot of them. This often comes as a shock to founders that haven’t seen this before. Why do I have to pay taxes if I’m saving the money to grow my business? But you do. ⚖️ You can try to load balance and do both. Take some profits out, invest the rest. This is what most do. The problem here is your venture-backed competitors are investing all of it, not just some. You’re almost by definition against under-investing. Being profitable is liberating and a wonderful place to be. But profitable AND bootstrapped has an interesting set of nuances. Do you invest in the future? Or take the profits now? It’s an extra choice the venture-backed generally don’t have (secondary stock sales aside).

content: It used to be if you were building a B2B app, it almost had to be in the Salesforce ecosystem or it was tough to get traction. Today, as huge as Salesforce is ($40B ARR), tech overall is so, so much bigger. So there’s no need to focus on Salesforce as a platform or GTM for most B2B apps. You don’t even hear it all that much as a core strategy. E-commerce B2B is the opposite. There literally is no point in building on anything but Shopify today. While nominally there are more stores outside of Shopify than on it (e.g., WooCommerce, Wix, etc) … and many huge merchants run on other platforms … at a practical level, for B2B, 90%+ of the addressable revenue is on Shopify. It’s Shopify or bust.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So who will benefit the most from AI in B2B? The hot new start-ups, rocketing to $100m ARR in record time? Or … the established leaders, who can add AI onto their apps and not just expose vastly more functionality, but leverage all that existing customer data, to create something brand new and fresh? We’re watching. AI has already completely rebooted many older leaders in the contact center, from Zendesk to Genesys to Intercom, which now are truly AI-first and thus in many ways radically different than they were just a few years ago. And ServiceNow seems to be on that journey. Salesforce is on it, too. And what about Workday? The grandad of HR SaaS, Workday? How is The of AI changing it? Well, it’s early. But Workday remains a force of nature: 👉Almost $9 Billion in ARR 👉Growing 15%, so adding well over $1B in new bookings a year! 👉Subscription backlog up 19.7%, to $25 Billion (!). So a huge amount of revenue booked but still to come. 👉27%+ Free Cash Flow margins, 26% non-GAAP profit margins, and $8 Billion in the bank, so generating massive cash 👉$57 Billion market cap, so trading at 6x+ ARR Workday is 20 years old this year. And in many ways, it’s just getting going. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. 98% GRR. No One Leaves Workday. No One. There’s enterprise software … and then there are folks like Workday and ServiceNow with 98%+ GRR. Where literally, on one leaves. Now when I was a VP at Adobe, I saw them deploy it and I get it. It tooks years to roll our Workday there, but when they finally did, it literally was embedded in every facet of how the company was run internally. Moving off would likely take half a decade. #2. Very Focused on AI Agents as The Future Workday is trying to leverage AI to remain the core system of record in HR and financials in the enterprise. And they want Workday to manage all your agents. #3. 11,000 Customers, So $820,000 ACV on Average Per Customer That’s pretty enterprise. Workday is a $1m+ a year and up solution for the Big Guys. #4. 30% of New Customers Are “Multi-Suite”, Buying Both CRM and Financials and More Yes, Workday is huge. But a reminder of how critical being multi-product is to scaling. #5. 30% of All Customer Expansions Involved AI Products. And It’s Already Leading to ACV Expansion. That’s AI in the enterprise today. Is it all magic today? Not always. But it’s where the incremental budget is in the enterprise.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: One tough question as a VC— tougher that you’d think — is how hard and honest to be with founders. You might think the answer is to be 100% honest and 100% transparent. And perhaps it’s that simple. But … on the one hand, when things get harder, many founders don’t quite face reality: - They think they’ll be able to raise another round … but the metrics aren’t there - They think growth is fine … when it’s not strong enough to get acquired, raise, IPO, etc. - They will run out of money not today but in < 9-12 months … and they don’t want to deal with it - They want to believe that VP is doing great … because hiring is hard … but they are clearly failing at almost all levels. 🤷‍♂️ If your board and investors don’t tell you the truth here, no one will. You need them to. Still, the fact is when the world seems a bit against you, when things are harder and tougher … founders often need to know their VCs and board have their back. If they don’t feel that or see that, there’s no safe haven. There’s no one they can share issues with, or plot a path back to success with in many cases. It’s tough to know how hard to push as an investor and how much just to be a cheerleader. What I do know is you can cheerlead someone right off a cliff. And also … you can also push them so hard, they start to check out.

content: It's totally OK to ask a VC at the end of a pitch meeting, "Based on what you know now, what are the odds you'd invest?" In fact, it can save a lot of time. Founders just mis-read the room (or the Zoom) way too often with VCs. Until you've pitched a ton of VCs, it's easy to. Too many founders get frustrated they were "ghosted". Or think just more data will help. Or think they are waiting to hear back, and that more time will help. Sometimes it does. But rarely. Just ask. Ask at the end of the first meeting. Any seasoned VC will tell you. And they won't mind at all.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So we’ve entered a new phase in SaaS B2B unlike anything in many, many years: things are just so much faster, and so much more competitive, due to AI. For a while, SaaS seemed like a well understood playbook. You struggle to hit product market fit, you hire a great management team, and you just get a little better every week, every month, every quarter. That has been upended the past 24 months: ↘️ Leaders in B2B and SaaS that are single product have seen growth slow to almost zero at scale 🔁 AI has completely upended several categories already, mainly contact center and programming / code creation 🤺 AI has fueled a vast legion of competitors overall, and especially in spaces that before had less competition: legal, sales automation, vertical SaaS used to be sleepy as examples. Now they have 100s of new AI players. The bottom line is across startups I work with I see everyone running the same playbook as a year or two ago slowing down. Often radically. 🙋‍♀️ So I ask you just one question, and be honest: Is Your Team Truly Better Than 24 Months Ago? ➡️ Does it push out more code? ➡️ Is it closing more deals? ➡️ Is your sales team working harder than it did? ➡️ Are you gaining market share, or losing it? ➡️ Are upsells and upgrades getting easier, or harder? ➡️ Are the VPs and C-level execs you’ve hired really better? Or placeholders? You have to be honest. The truth is, many start-ups have worked hard the past 12-24 months. But the teams aren’t better than they were 12 months ago. That doesn’t work in today’s AI-fueled world. If your team isn’t better, while it’s radical, one thing to think about is simply cutting everyone below the quality line. That can be brutal, but it often leaves you with a much higher quality core team. That inspires itself to go faster, and harder. Finally.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So there's an app we used a bit but over the years they'd begun to charge us over $1,000 a month and it was just too much. Other products could do the same for 1/5 the price today and it was just getting annoying to see the credit card charges each month. So we went to downgrade. They asked to do a live account review first. They said downgrading might not be possible at our usage level (which is nominal). I said we didn't have time, and if we couldn't downgrade, please just cancel the account, thank you. A few minutes later, it turned out there was a $149/month plan we could use! Thank you I said, and moved on. Until we got another email later in the day from "Account Management". They weren't going to honor the $149/month pricing. It was $1,200 a month or nothing. We cancelled. What obviously happened here is the retention team came into conflict with the revenue team. The logo retention team saved the account. But sales overrode them to get more revenue. And that led to a cancellation. I doubt sales cared. But the retention team lost. How do you make sure this doesn't happen? Or is it OK?

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The Strong Outbound, Crappy Follow Up What's that? It's going to be a more and more common playbook in the Age of AI. Take last week. I got an incredible well timed, well written email from an agency about helping on production side of our podcast. And we do need help. I told them to do a test project, and if it went well, we'd just use them. Then the shoe dropped. "How many podcasts do you do?" they asked. I mean, take 5 seconds and look. Go to Spotify, Apple or YouTube. You will see the answer. Deal lost. AI is probably going to accelerate this trend of Strong Outbound, Terrible Follow Up. Done right, AI will make our outbound better researched, more relevant, better targeted, higher value, and even more timely. But if overreliance on AI leads to terrible follow-up, performance in the end might be worse. We'll see

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Transitioning from founder-led sales is a critical milestone, and it’s one that founders often get wrong by either doing it too early or not doing it thoughtfully enough. Here’s how to do it right: 1️⃣ Don’t Transition Too Early Founder-led sales are essential in the early days. You need to be in the trenches, hearing objections, understanding what resonates, and refining your pitch. If you exit too early—especially in vertical SaaS—before hitting $10M ARR, you risk failure. You’ve got to suck it up and stay involved until you’ve built a repeatable sales motion. 2️⃣ Hire Your First AE Before a Head of Sales Before you bring in a VP of Sales, hire a few Account Executives (AEs). These AEs should be people you’d personally buy from—people you trust to represent your product well. They’ll help you scale the sales process while you’re still involved. This step is crucial because it allows you to test and refine your sales playbook before handing it off. 3️⃣ Find the Right Head of Sales at the Right Time The first Head of Sales is a pivotal hire, but they’re not the person who will take you to IPO. They’re the one who will build the foundation for scaling. Typically, this hire happens around $2M-$3M ARR for a sales-led motion. Look for someone who can be your wingman, someone you trust to lead and grow the team while you’re still involved in key deals. 4️⃣ Stay Involved in Key Deals Even after you hire a Head of Sales, you’ll need to stay involved in the biggest deals. Founders often have unique credibility and authority that no one else on the team can replicate. This doesn’t mean micromanaging—it means being strategic about where your presence adds the most value. 5️⃣ Empower Your Sales Leaders Once you’ve transitioned, trust your Head of Sales to build and manage the team. They’ll likely hire a more diverse group of sales reps than you would, and that’s okay. Great sales leaders know how to build teams with complementary strengths. Give them room to run, but hold them accountable for results. 6️⃣ Build the Supporting Infrastructure As you scale, you’ll need to invest in sales ops, demand generation, and customer success. These functions are critical for supporting a growing sales team and ensuring that customers are successful post-sale. Start layering these in as you approach $10M ARR. 7️⃣ Focus on Metrics and Repeatability The goal of transitioning from founder-led sales is to create a repeatable, scalable sales process. Track key metrics like win rates, deal velocity, and pipeline coverage to ensure the team is executing effectively. If something isn’t working, dig in and fix it before scaling further. ➡️ The bottom line: Don’t rush it. Founder-led sales are exhausting, but they’re also irreplaceable in the early days. Transition only when you’ve built a strong foundation, and then hire people you trust to scale it. And even then, stay close to the action—you’ll always be the best closer for your company’s biggest deals.

content: So outside of software development, few spaces have changed more already due to AI than support and service Freshworks is a great example. Today they are at $800m+ ARR, growing 22%, and ... reaccelerating! But so much has changed! 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Modest Re-acceleration Past Two Quarters Sometime in Q3’24 might have been the end of the “downturn” in many B2B categories, per HubSpot and many other B2B leaders, and also here per Freshworks. You can see Freshworks is growing materially faster now than last year — 22% vs. 20% #2. Customer Count Also Re-Accelerating Freshworks’ customer count was flat a year ago, but now is slowly growing again. Freshworks added 2,600 net customers last quarter, its largest net gain in four years. #3. NDR/NRR Hasn’t Bounced Back, However NRR is still flat / down. You really have to earn it in SaaS these days. I suspect this is due to increased churn and contraction in smaller accounts, as the larger customers by their nature should have higher NRR. #4. Biggest Growth in $50k+ Customers, Who Are 50% of Revenue The fact that NRR is flat even with $50k+ customers being the biggest driver of growth implies some contraction in smaller customers. In any event, like many from Zoom to Asana, the growth is mostly in bigger customers today. FBOW. 50% of revenue is now from $50k+ customers, and 90% from $5k+ customers. #5. 50% Attach Rates for AI In $30k+ Deals, But Much Lower for SMBs This is also what I’ve seen across the contact center. Deploying AI successfully does require work, and the demand is higher in the enterprise. Much more at link in comments!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So less than 30 days after launcheding our SaaStr AI we've had 35,000 conversations already. This has completely opened my eyes to what AI can truly do in the real world. My Top 10 Learnings: #1. Users Will Tell AI Things They Won’t Tell Humans We discovered people are asking our AI about topics they’d never bring up with me directly. Topics like “I’m thinking about quitting” or deeply personal founder struggles. #2. The AI Is Shockingly Good – It’s Not Perfect But It's Often Better Than Me (For Some Things) One of our fastest-growing portfolio companies had all board members and investors provide feedback on their investment memo – and the AI won. It beat me and the other investors in feedback. All the feedback was good, but the AI overall was the best. #3. Hallucinations Aren’t a Big Deal for Our AI – And Getting Rarer Everyone was skeptical about AI hallucinations initially, and many founders still mention this as a blocker. But the reality? In our experience, hallucinations are now: Correct ~80% of the time Mediocre/generic ~15% of the time Wrong only ~5% of the time #4. The Digital + Human Combo Creates a Superpower One of the most interesting paradigms we’ve discovered is when there are three of us in a conversation: two humans IRL plus digital Jason. This creates an IRL co-pilot that’s transformative. #5. Voice vs. Text: The Data May Surprise You Despite all the hype about voice being the future, our data shows a different story. In the first 5000 or so sessions: Web text: 2,000 sessions Voice: 500 sessions Embed (chat on our homepage): 500 sessions #6. Custom-Trained AI Vastly Outperforms Generic Models That Have Ingested The Exact Same Data One of the biggest surprises was how much better our specialized SaaStr AI is compared to ChatGPT or Claude with the same questions – despite those models having already ingested most of our content through web crawling. #7. It’s Already a B+ BDR Out of the Box I mean this is kinda cool. Without any specific sales training, our AI can already handle basic qualification questions like a B+ BDR. #8. People Genuinely LOVE Talking To Truly Good AI I was genuinely surprised by how much people love our AI – especially technical people who know how it works! When smart founders ask nuanced questions about their specific situations, the personalized responses create “magic moments” – something increasingly rare in traditional B2B SaaS. #9. The Price/Value Equation is Insane The economics of AI tools are mind-blowing. For $29-399/month, we’re getting 6,000+ additional interactions, surprise and delight, video conversations, and more. Compare that to $60/month social media tools that schedule three tweets. #10. The AI Itself Probably Isn’t Defensible. The Software Layer Around It Probably Is, However. As amazing as our AI is, someone smart could build a clone in a week. Still, when I tried a different but seemingly similar vendor, I couldn’t get it to really work well at all.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: What Can You Do To Increase Your Win Rates? Ok a lot of these may seem basic to many of you. But here's my checklist, and I still bet you aren't doing all 8: 1️⃣ Identify Your Top 3 Feature Gaps -- And Just Start Closing Them Start by figuring out why you’re losing deals. Are there specific features or capabilities your competitors have that you don’t? Closing just one or two of those gaps can make a big difference in win rates. Talk to your sales team and customers to pinpoint these gaps. Force them each week to force rank the gaps. If you don't, you'll get an endless stream of requests. But everyone together can force rank the Top 3 feature gaps they want closed. 2️⃣ If You Have To, Just Improve Sales Leadership A great VP of Sales can increase close rates by 50% or more. If your win rates are low, it might be time to evaluate whether your sales leadership is strong enough. A great leader will coach the team, refine the pitch, and focus on the deals you can win. It really works. If your close rates haven't improved at all under your head of sales, be honest about why. 3️⃣ Be Hands-On During Trials Are you losing deals during pilots or bake-offs? If your competitors are more hands-on during this phase—getting on calls, flying out to meet customers, or customizing solutions—you’ll lose. Make sure your team is fully engaged during trials and showing customers why you’re the best choice. 4️⃣ Align Reps with the Right Deal Sizes If your reps are chasing deals that are too big or too small for their experience level, your win rates will suffer. Match your reps to the deal sizes they’re best equipped to handle. This simple adjustment can have a big impact. 5️⃣ Train on FUD and Competitive Advantages Most sales teams aren’t great at handling Fear, Uncertainty, and Doubt (FUD) or articulating competitive advantages. Invest in training your team to address objections and position your product as the best solution. This is especially critical if you’re in a competitive market. 6️⃣ Focus Marketing on Winning Segments Look at where you’re already winning and double down. If you’re closing deals in a specific segment or vertical, focus your marketing and sales efforts there. It’s easier to win where you already have traction. 7️⃣ Set Incremental Goals Don’t try to go from a 7% win rate to 70% overnight. Focus on small, achievable improvements—like getting to 10% first. Even a small increase in win rates can have a massive impact on revenue. For example, going from 10% to 15% can drive 50% more growth. 8️⃣ Really Leverage Customer Success Stories Use case studies and testimonials from your happiest customers to build credibility and trust. Prospects want to see proof that you’ve solved similar problems for others. 8️⃣ Review Lost Deals Religiously Every lost deal is a learning opportunity. Conduct post-mortems to understand why you lost and what you could have done differently. Look for patterns and adjust your approach accordingly.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: For BigCos, the debate about full RTO is about … just getting folks to work. But for startups it's different. The debate about hybrid + RTO in 2025 is around Urgency. Can you create true urgency in a 100% distributed environment? For sure. But it’s real work. You have to go all-in, with different systems and processes. What about "hybrid"? Can you create true urgency when folks come in 2 days a week for 5-6 hours? Maybe. But hybrid environments might be the toughest of all to create true Urgency. My test with founders is if anyone is really in the office at 5pm in hybrid environments. Usually it’s not that many. The world is moving faster. So many hot start-ups are working 6+ days in the week together, often IRL. There are many ways to win. But what you probably do need to do today at a minimum is increase Urgency. Folks showing up 2 days a week to work 5-6 hours in the office probably doesn’t create that. And you will fall behind today.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So the 2021 GTM Playbook is Dead. Almost all of us agree about that. But what has replaced it? Or will replace it? It’s still murky. What doesn’t work so well today: - Endless outbound emails - Low energy digital “events” - Break-up emails - 2021 SEO strategies - 2021 mass scale content strategies - Spending all day on LinkedIn - Press and basic PR strategies What works a little but not enough to usually be worth it: - Lots of energy into social media - Lots of energy into your own pod What still works well today, but folks often lack the energy to run: - Highly targeted outbound, that adds real value - High energy IRL field events (connect with prospects and customers live) - Your own big events (see Stripe, Figma, etc) - Weekly webinars - Visiting prospects and customers in person - Aggressive brand awareness - Aggressively doing partnerships - Incredibly high quality video content about industry, not you AI tools are incredible here and evolving so quickly. But while we will all be using a suite of them soon if not already, they don’t solve for many fundamental challenges in 2025. The 2025 GTM Playbook in fact often requires you to get out of the home office more, to work harder, and to spend more human time per prospect, not less. Are we willing to do this?

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: AI is driving up churn all across the board in SaaS and B2B Why? In many cases, it's not that you did anything “wrong.” But it's because AI put the customer into play. CFO, CIOs, VPs, execs are all tasked to look into how AI is changing all elements of their stack, from support to sales to finance. And as part of that, they are reviewing every vendor. Even ones that are working just fine. And look at new ones that have a big AI pitch. And that means ... they just may switch now. Even if things are OK. Because AI mandates and AI curiosity finally got them ... to take a look. At other vendors. You have to be ahead of this. You have to make sure you have at least some sort of “AI Parity” with the next generation, if you aren’t the next generation. And also if you do lose a few key customers, Be Kind. Because I’m already seeing a number go back a year out or less to their original vendor. Burn them on the way out — and they won’t.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A few thoughts on 11x, I know nothing but what I’ve read: 1/ I like the 3 month out on a 12 month deal. I like it. I think everyone should do this in earlier days. It builds trust and is a great way to split the difference on having to invest in your customers to get them up to speed, but de-risk things. I did these all the time on way to $10m ARR. Not every deal but no problem when asked. You want an out after 90 days? You got it. If we didn’t earn your business by then, we didn’t deserve it. 2/ This space is going to be very dynamic and you have to commit to real ROI but understand current limitations I think it’s OK if a significant number of customers didn’t see fast ROI as long as some did. I’ve now been running our AI (http://Delphi.ai/saastr) and some of it is epic (it just solved an attendee problem for SaaStr Annual on its own before I woke up today), most of it is good, and some of it is wrong (< 5%). The amount of value varies. But we are much better already for it. 3/ Everything is getting better You have to pick a platform and if it works OK for you in AI I’d stick with it for a while, even if it doesn’t always hit goal. Every product in AI I use is constantly getting better so I’m sticking with anything that works reasonably well, with tolerance for issues. 4/ No one wants to do the work. So figure it out with AI. Have AI SDRs over promised? I think so. But that’s vs. a 2021 paradigm. As we head into 2026, there are fewer and fewer folks that really want to do the work. Fewer and fewer human SDRs that want to do 50 calls a day, and especially, that really want to research prospects. We have no choice but to start using AI for tech roles in which there are no humans of sufficient quality and quantity to do them. We have to use AI or nothing in many cases. Even if it’s not yet 100% there for what we want. 5/ It’s tough but maybe underpromise a bit in AI All the GTM leaders are making big promises. I get it, and it gets prospects’ attention. But maybe more reasonable goals would in the end lead to less churn and better outcomes. Again, you can beat a lazy human today with AI in most GTM categories. You can’t beat an S-tier AE or SDR or even an A-tier one but so what. Target the B and C-tiers. And one real criticism, which they acknowledged: 6/ Earn the logos It can be so tempting to use logos you haven’t earned. Logos from trials, pilots, etc. Logos from 2 users at a Fortune 500. Especially in deeply competitive spaces. The temptation is real. But what I’ve learned is you are better off with fewer, but real logos. With ones that will give you true testimonials, take a reference call, and importantly, that agreed in writing to be your logos and references. I’d take 3 strong logos that are superfans and agreed to be on the site over 30 that tried the product and never consented. We all are tempted to make this mistake, myself included. But I almost always see it eventually backfire. Often, deep into a large deal.

content: 2025 is year that AI takes over all of support and customer success … that isn’t sales. This is how the 2 related but different categories are segmenting out. 🤷 A lot of support is questions and problems from existing customers. Almost all of this is going to AI, as much as possible. And this trend is acceleration. 💰But, where support is really sales, humans will handle it still. We’re already seeing this bifurcation in e-commerce, because there the “support” chat is often used for sales questions. Which shoes, which size, does this run large, etc. AI for returns, humans to convince you to buy. Etc. The same is happening, just more slowly across customer success. Humans are still deployed in customer success for upsell. To get you to buy more stuff. Directly, or in “QBRs” and similar which now have become mainly about upsell. And the rest is being handed off to AI, support, etc. Or just being eliminated for now, to be replaced by AI soon. That’s where the world is going post-sales: 🧏🏻‍♂️ If you’ll buy more, you get a human 🤖 If not, you get an AI.

content: The start-ups, scale-ups and bigger tech cos I’m most worried about: the ones that aren’t truly AI Obsessed at the product level. All across the team. Everyone. What do I mean? I mean their teams aren’t constantly talking about what cool things they can do now, this week, to improve their product with AI. Constantly. There is too much AI lip service in B2B. Too much talk, not enough action among incumbents, especially in industries where AI isn’t incredibly disruptive at moment (e.g., much of vertical SaaS, fintech, etc) AI is not a feature, or an edition, or a box to check. It should be something your product and engineering teams just can’t stop talking about in B2B. Almost to the point where you can’t take it anymore. In some categories of SaaS — contact center, software development, etc. — AI has radically changed the entire industry already. In other categories, it’s still early days. That’s OK and maybe even good for incumbents. Many have time. But you have to be obsessed with AI, with everything amazing you truly can do today, I think to not fall behind over the coming months. Even if it’s not showing up in the numbers yet.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Could “Block” Be the Death of the AI SDR? I don’t claim to be an expert on email deliverability and spam. But I know a tiny bit. We send well over 1,000,000 emails a week in our SaaStr newsletters. And when I used to run Adobe Sign / EchoSign, I spent a huge amount of time worrying about deliverability. E-signatures, after all, are primarily an e-mail driven exchange. Even the tiniest issues in deliverability, we would hear about it — fast. And I wonder, and am worried, about the AI SDR. Because I don’t about you, but I am fine Blocking them. And even sometimes, Reporting to Spam. And I’d almost never do that to a human being. I don’t claim to be a social media expert, either. But again, we have over 1,000,000 social media followers. And one thing is clear — folks are reluctant to “Block” a human. It crosses lines. It creates ill-will, and folks lash out. And notice. Folks really notice when they are blocked. But the AI? It’s not even a person. They don’t care. Block away. And even more so, I've almost never actually asked for an AI SDR email I've received. Most of them seem to be me being dumped into a list I didn’t ask to join. So if I didn’t even ask for an AI SDR email? The easiest thing to do is Block. Today, I block multiple AI SDR emails a week. Before 2025? I don’t think I ever blocked a human-driven SDR. Even if it was a cadence, at least I could see it was from a human. I’d ignore it, but block seemed … aggro. Too much. But now, I block ’em all. We’ll see how this all gets resolved. At a minimum, there’s no way I would send AI SDR emails from my own domain.

content: In the debate around if outbound still works, how well, and what AI’s role will be, I think a huge point is missed: 👀 You’re wasting your shot. Email remains special. Literally every executive manages their >own< inbox. Every day I open 20-30 cold emails. So do the CEOs and CXOs of almost every public company, almost every buyer, etc. Almost everyone is thinking about email wrong. Are fewer, better emails better than spray and pray? Most of us now agree. But it’s more than that. Any emails that gets opened by a buyer is a gift. It’s your shot, your audience. I bet 95% of them, you are wasting: * Wasting on generic copy * Wasting on a lame pitch * Wasting on asking for a “quick call” * Wasting on not solving their problem No matter what, email still gets opened. That’s magic. Make sure that email solves their problem. If it doesn’t, it’s just sad if it got opened. Because that means … you had a chance. At least of something.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 🔥 Gong announced it’s just crossed $300 million in ARR 🔥 That’s impressive, but I think even more impressive than it sounds. Because while I don’t have the exact numbers, I do think Gong has reaccelerated the past 6-9 months. It’s clearly growing faster today, at $300m, than it did at $200m, when a wave of consolidation and cutbacks hit the overall space. CEO Amit Bendov was kind enough to join us at SaaStr Europa in June 2024 and talk about their approach to AI and more. And while they were doing well then, they weren’t growing as fast as they are today. AI isn’t the only answer, but it does seem clear that Gong has been able to in part ride the AI wave, rather than be overwhelmed by it: “The usage of Gong's AI capabilities has risen by nearly 50% in the last 12 months. Notably, Ask Anything, one of the most popular AI features, saw 400%+ year-over-year growth.” Which actually just makes sense. After all, Gong was perhaps the original ML player in the space — well before AI was cool :) Gong also noted that 25% of its customers now are multi-product. This is also a partial key to re-acceleration. Gong, Salesloft, Outreach, HubSpot as well as many of the newer guard have gone from partners to partial competitors. Many customers do want to consolidate on one platform. Gong in the early days of this wave was often hurt by consolidation at first during the Great App Purge of 2022, but today it seems to be benefitting as it itself has become a much broader platform and multi-product. 🙋 It begs the question: is the sales and revenue acceleration space “back”? Maybe. But it’s different: ➡️ ZoomInfo has seen churn stabilize, although it hasn’t yet returned to growth mode ➡️ New leaders like Clay are growing at jaw-dropping rates ➡️ Salesforce has invested deeply in AgentForce, with seemingly impressive early adoption — but so far it hasn’t boosted revenue ➡️ Pure play non-AI players don’t seem to be growing any faster or seeing any re-acceleration Gong crossing $300m ARR and re-accelerating is a great sign. It shows budget remains in the sales acceleration space — where and when it’s earned. But while it’s the best of times for many new, disruptive players in AI in B2B, it’s a bit early to see how big a boost it gives overall to the revenue management. But early signs are encouraging. Disrupt yourself with AI in SaaS and B2B. That’s where the budget is.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Customers don't "churn". They quit you. For something else. Something that meets their needs better. Ask where you stand. Do an NPS survey this week. Ask what you can do better. Ask how happy they are. “Churn" is a term we borrowed from our B2C friends. We probably never should have allowed it in B2B. It makes sense to use when you have 100,000+ small customers paying a few dollars a month. When you have tiny SMBs that naturally come and go. When the deal size is larger, and the customer count smaller though, replace "churn" with "customers we failed".

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Ready to hire your first VP of Sales? Here are 10+ good screening questions to see if you have a real VP, Sales candidate in hand — or not. These questions mostly don’t have right or wrong answers, but will help you determine the quality and fit of the candidates. 1️⃣ How big a team do you think we need right now, given what you know? (If they can’t answer — right or wrong — pass. They should at least be in the range.) 2️⃣ What deal sizes have you sold to, on average and range? (If it’s not a similar fit to you, probably pass. If he/she can’t answer fluidly, pass) 3️⃣ Tell me about the teams you’ve directly managed, and how you built them (If they can’t describe how they built and recruited at least a small team — pass. 50% of the job of VP of Sales is recruiting). 4️⃣ What sales tools have you used and what works for you? What hasn’t worked well? (If they don’t understand sales tools, they aren’t hands-on enough for your stage. If everything is dated and pre-AI, be a bit worried). 5️⃣ Who do you know right now that would join you on our sales team? If things progress, can I talk to them? (All good candidates should have a few in mind) 6️⃣ How should sales and customer success work together? (This will ferret out how well he/she understands the true customer lifecycle) 7️⃣ Tell me about deals you’ve lost to competitors. What’s going to be key in our space about winning vs. competitors? You’ll learn if they can sell in competitive environments for real or not. 8️⃣ How do you work with sales engineers and sales support? What role do they need to play at this stage when capital is finite? (So many folks can’t really run a demo or answer tougher or technical questions themselves) 9️⃣ What will my revenues look like 120 days after I hire you? (There’s no correct answer. But there are many wrong answers) 🔟 How should sales and marketing work together at our phase? (This will ferret out if they understand lead generation and how to work a lead funnel. Believe it or not, most candidates don’t understand this unless they were really a VP Sales before) If any of the answers aren’t good enough, trust me, just pass. If any don’t make sense, pass. And if you know more about any of these questions than the candidate does — pass. Your VP Sales needs to be smarter than you in sales, sales processes, and building and scaling a sales team.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Out there looking for a VP of Sales role, or just a senior AE role? Here's my #1 piece of advice to sales execs: 😴 Enough With The Phone It In Interview. What's that? It's something that I really only see sales execs do, that are confident in their sales skills. They go to interviews that they barely prepare for at all. I'm not just talking about not doing research before the interview -- do that too. You gotta do that to stand out. What I'm talking about is just showing up for a VPS, CRO, AE, SDR, etc. interview that isn't your #1 top choice. And doing nothing. Just showing up and talking a lot about your last role, to sound like a strong candidate. And then having your only question be, "Tell Me More About The Company." At larger companies perhaps the Phone It In Interview works. I don't know. It may be enough to get through an HR screen. But if you are directly interviewing with a CEO, founder, CRO, etc. -- don't phone it in. Do enough research so that you can truly act curious about the role. So you can truly ask good questions. Not just, "So Tell Me About The Company". Because anyone can smell the Phone It In Interview. And no one really wants to hire that person.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So there’s an uncomfortable truth that VCs don’t discuss outloud that often, but everyone has sort of accepted. Everyone resisted in 2022 and into 2023, but by 2024 they began to capitulate. The truth is that a lot of unicorns that hit $1B+ valuations in 2020-2021 … probably aren’t really unicorns anymore. How many? Per Carta, over 60% haven’t raised funding since 2021 and likely never achieved the scale to do so, or have seen growth slow. Per Carta, a𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗝𝗮𝗻 𝟭, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱: ➡️ 374 of the 616 unicorns have not raised a subsequent round ➡️ 83 have raised a flat or up round (13.5%) ➡️ 67 have raised a down round (10.9%, but nearly half of those that have raised anything) ➡️ 78 have exited through IPO or M&A (12.7%) ➡️ 14 have shut down This is what it is. In venture, we hope it all keeps going up. But the reality is, these are private companies. We often don’t talk about the ones that stop going up … unless they truly go under. Most of the time, if they don’t, we just stop talking. Some of these unicorns never made any sense. But some today are at $100m+ ARR, but have seen growth slow to less than 20%. A lot of them, in fact. That’s tough, but you still have scale and often, the burn rate is low or in many cases these centicorns are cash-flow positive. Just slow-growing now. Vs. hypergrowth a few years back. What if this is you? What if you raised at $1B+ or more in 2021, or even in 2025? And you don’t end up being worth that much? Look it’s not great but in the end, just keep growing as fast as practical and don’t run out of money. Private Equity won’t buy all of the almost 400 unicorns that didn’t raise another round. But they and others may buy a bunch. IF … if … they aren’t burning anything, still have some growth, and haven’t raised too much. Get to $100m+ ARR, with at least some growth, 100% NRR, and no burn, and you’ll have something or real value.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So I've fired almost no one in my career, and never done a layoff. In fact, the only folks I can remember firing are a few for inappropriate behavior (not OK), and just a couple who simply, literally refused to do their job at all. I had someone in customer support years ago who was supposed to do support in the U.K. But he wasn't willing to get to the office before 10am -- when offices were closed in London. So I did have to let him go. And a few like that. But that's it. I preferred to let folks move on, on their own, when the time came. It seemed simpler, calmer, and kinder. And I did it out of loyalty. I may have many faults, but a lack of loyalty isn't one of them. Now I see as time has gone by that was a mistake. For one simple reason: A lot of folks stay too long. It's not their fault, but a lot of folks will stay at a role 9-12 months longer than they should out of inertia. And their performance begins to deteriorate. That's not worth it for anyone. And I've also learned a "no layoffs" policy really doesn't get you any points or kudos. No one really values it. Not ... really. So now, I really don't want anyone great to leave -- ever. Never. Please stay forever. But when someone has stayed on too long, and they don't really want to be there anymore ... I'm just going to tell them. And help them find something new that energizes them once again.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: You are almost always better off the next week or so without a toxic employee. Even if they seemed mission-critical, the team adapts. And remember, it just ... is what it is. They may be much happier somewhere else. They may just be unhappy. It doesn't matter. Time never cures a toxic attitude. Giving them space never solves it. It doesn't matter "who's fault" it is. It's no one's fault. It just is. Thank them for their service. And move on. This week. But ... but ... don't turn someone struggling, someone just going through a tough patch ... into someone toxic. You can inadvertently push someone over the edge. If they are truly great, or were great, and it's only been a few months. Go talk to them. Tell them you love them. That they are great, or at least, they've been great. And you need them to be great again. That does work sometimes. Far less than 50% of the time. But often enough. And if they were great, you owe it to them to try.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So the other day a founder reached out to me about what to do with his #2 sales rep ... at least 12 months ago ... that was now his worst rep. #20 out of 20. We dug in a bit, and while every story is a bit different here, the root cause is usually the same: the business changed. Some of the best sales execs can roll with change. But others struggle. They nail a certain pitch, a certain motion, a certain moment in time. And then things change, and they struggle to evolve. In this case, the space became much more competitive due to AI. The set of competitors and questions was just radically different than just 12 months ago. And this sales exec went from #2 out of 20 to ... #20. It's tough and I wish I could tell you I've seen a lot of reps that fall from the top to the bottom find their way back. But honestly I almost never have. Maybe a great CRO or VP of Sales can get someone back to the top from the bottom, when there is a ton of change. I have seen that a few times. The best sales leaders know how to at least try to evolve top talent. But for founders -- just understand it happens. In the end, a sales rep that used to be great ... may need to find a new place. It's tough, but it happens. What have you seen here?

content: I'd say 30% of SaaS vendors now make it really, really hard to leave. Even if you pay month-to-month. 🗝️ This might help you manage the churn number for this month. 🫰 It might even help you end the year a percent or two higher in ARR. 🏃‍♂️‍➡️ But 0% chance I'll return when you do this. 0%. Literally, as I type this, I am battling with a vendor who has removed the ability to downgrade. Now you have to schedule a call with them, days later. This is for a self-serve product. The only way I could even get any attention at all was to type CANCEL in ALL CAPS repeatedly. Finally, they offered a downgrade. And now I'm just leaving. The easier you make it to leave ... the easier you make it to come back. So many have forgotten this the past 24+ months.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The honest truth: RTO is mostly about getting more performance out of your mediocre employees. 🚀 High performers will crush it — period. Home, away, office, remote, anywhere. 💥 Lowest performers get almost nothing done from home or in the office. 😬 It’s the middle where you are hoping to get more out of them. 100% remote can certainly work but it’s a huge investment for the middle category — and a very different way of working. 90% of CROs and VPs of Sales I’ve talked to want the team to be in the office today as much as possible. And probably 80% of CEOs. Ideally, 5 days. It’s not to help the high performers perform better. It’s to help get the middle to mid/low performers … working more. And working on work. Period. It’s not really about collaboration, or even training. You can collaborate in a Google Doc and you can train IRL and then go back remote after. It’s about trying to get the folks at 70%-80% attainment … up to 100%. And so on. And to get them to actually put in 30-40 hours of work. On work. Many don’t agree and I hear you. I’m not even directly taking a position. I’m just sharing the >real< reason behind RTO. The reason no one says aloud, at least not in public. But the real reason everyone talks about … in private.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 5 changes you can make today, to grow faster: 1️⃣ Visit all customers in person > $50k ACV They’ll churn less, buy more, and tell you how to close other customers like them. And you shore up the base. 2️⃣ Have a weekly 1-on-1 with VP you don't have one with now Yes, 1-on-1’s may be partially out of fashion now. And you don’t need to do them with all your reports. But pick one report that is doing OK but could be doing better. And invest the time. Do a weekly catch-up. 3️⃣ Hire a new recruiter + meet 30 new folks for #1 open role Look, recruiters aren’t magical. But we all exhaust our personal networks. You need help. Enough with the excuses. It’s time to get the #1 open role … filled. 4️⃣ Set a burn-rate budget for every month Just set a core burn-rate budget that you team needs to hit. Then let them suggest how best to hit it. But that it has to be hit. Period. 5️⃣ Cut out toxic folks Just move on from anyone bringing down the team. Especially, any negative B players. It’s hard for anyone to kill it and be their best when they see their peers are phoning it in. And even worse, being negative about the company. Let them find a role they are happier at … somewhere else.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Holy cr*p Shopify. At an $11.2 Billion run rate, it’s growing at a stunning 31%. And it’s accelerating. In fact, it’s growing the fastest it has in 3 years. It’s just stunning to see this sort of growth at this scale. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Offline Revenue Up +33%, B2B Growth up 140% While many think of Shopify as mainly an SMB online solution, its biggest growth now is in its largest customers (who run far more payments through Shopify), in its offline/ in-store business, and in B2B commerce. Relatively speaking, SMB online is softer. #2. Just 23% of Revenue From SaaS / Software, Down From 26% This isn’t new, but always helpful to see this over time. Shopify is effectively an ecommerce fintech that is powered by a SaaS solution. #3. Holding Almost All Expenses Just Above “Flat” Even as it accelerates, Shopify is getting more profitable. How? It’s only growing sales & marketing 10%, engineering and product 12%, and G&A 12% even as it grows 31%. So Shopify is hiring and spending, but at a rate about a third of how fast revenue is growing. #4. Effective NRR of Perhaps 105%-110% Shopify doesn’t break down its NRR but it does present Revenue by Cohort which is a good proxy. It’s well above 100%, even with its large SMB base. #5. Total Revenue Up 31%, But SaaS Revenue (Subscription Revenue) Only Up 9.1% Without payments and other merchant services, it would be a very different Shopify. One a quarter the size, and only growing 9.1%. What would that be worth? Maybe 1/20th of what Shopify is worth today. Maybe less. If there ever was an example of the power of adding payments and fintech to SaaS … it’s Shopify. More at link in comments!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So the first half of 2025 is when VCs, founders and other have to start dealing with the “Lost Generation” in SaaS and B2B What’s that? It’s folks at $10m-$300m ARR that just aren’t growing anymore. < 20% a year. There’s been so much shock to the system: - 2022: multiples crashed - 2023: buying and growth slowed - 2024: AI absorbed massive budget If growth slowed from 2023-2024, even 2022-2024, folks in some ways got a pass. No one was happy of course, but everyone sort of understood. But 2024 was your year to rebuild, and 2025 is the year to execute. 2025 has to be the year when growth re-accelerates, and realistically, that means it has to start in Q1 and pick up in Q2. If not, everyone will begin to check out. If you’re in the Lost Generation, you can still break out. But it’s probably gotta be right now.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: In most SMB SaaS, churn will eventually drag your growth down to 0%. Maybe at $5m ARR, maybe at $500m ARR, but it will come for most. A "steady state" for SaaS cos at scale is often 15%-20% growth plus expansion. So if NRR is 110%, then 25%-30% growth at scale. But SMBs often churn 20%+ by revenue, and have NRR < 100%. That can lead to 0% growth at scale if you aren't careful. You can ignore it in early days when growth is strong. But start putting a plan in place by $10m ARR: - Going multi-product - Going a bit more enterprise, even just a bit - Adding payments, agents, etc. - Being more viral - Being a true ERP / system of record for your customers - Driving NRR over 100%, whatever it takes Something

content: So you’re interviewing a new VP and … you’re not sure. Are they the right one, or not? Here’s a simple 5 point checklist to see if you’ve got someone great, or not: #1. The Best VPs Start Before They Start The best sales leaders start reaching out to a few great customers they already know. The best marketers are already building out a spreadsheet to increase pipeline — and show it to you for feedback. The best VPs of CS are already asking which customers they can fly out to and meet their first week, and already working on upgrading your CS systems. If you aren’t sure about a hire — see if they start .. starting. #2. The Best VPs Have Someone Ready to Join Them Junior hires often don’t. But the best VPs not only know a few great folks in the industry — they want to bring them over with them. Always. If they don’t have anyone to bring with them — they may still be good. But they aren’t a VP. #3. The Best VPs Have True Urgency They push the interview along. They take the first time slot open. They want to get going — now. Different folks express this differently. But if there’s no urgency at all during the interview — there won’t be any when they start, either. #4. The Best VPs Are At Least Somewhat Flexible They push you to be CRO, but you need a VP of Sales? They may push you on comp or timing or exact role. But in the end, they don’t make it all about the role, title, comp, etc. In the end, they know it’s a joint mission, and they are at least somewhat flexible. If it’s my way or the highway, it’s OK to get pushed at first. But there is zero flexibility — push on. #5. The Best VPs Are Truly Curious And because of this, they ask good questions during interviews. And push you sometimes in areas you weren’t expecting to go into. And expect more transparency on the company. To be a great leader at a start-up, you have to have a curious mind. Because you have to grow, and grow quickly. The best VPs keep asking more and more good questions the more you interview them. Not end the interview early — with no questions. Struggling on whether or not to hire that VP? Ask yourself honestly if they passed the above 5 part test .. or not. If they didn’t, move on. It’s better to struggle without, 9 times out of 10.

Moving From Global GTM Operations to Region-Specific Ones Generalist AEs and a matrix org led to too much of a U.S.-focus #5. Up to 9 Buyer Personas Per Deal This is one of many reasons I see B2B sales execs and marketers that are used to selling to a few specific personas struggle in vertical SaaS. content: When I look at the VP of Sales / CRO that didn’t work out the past 12-18 months across the SaaStr Fund portfolio and my ecosystem, one thing stands out. And it’s an old SaaStr theme: 👉 #1: You have to hire folks in sales where their last job was harder. There may exceptions at rocketships. When market pull is incredibly strong and your brand is #1, just hiring experienced folks may be enough. But 95 times out of 100, I see folks in sales fail when they join something early stage that is … harder: – When the product is more complicated – When the space is more competitive – When they get less deal help – When the product is more technical – When the buyer is radically different – When it takes 3-4 stakeholders to close a deal, not just 1 An old SaaStr theme, but one I think even more true today, when we hire even more on logos, with fewer reference calls, and when more veterans are available. It’s just hard to fly in sales selling something much harder to sell than your last role. But sell something even a smidge easier to sell than the last one? You often fly. Even if it’s still really had to sell. So long as it’s just a smidge easier to sell than the last one. 👉 Ok and the #2 reason seasoned sales execs (and others) fail: They Just Aren’t Curious Anymore I get it. How many times can you sell somewhat — sorry but — boring SaaS products? Payroll? Insurance? Voice APIs? Call center analytics? Security compliance? They can be interesting — but only if you truly curious. If you aren’t, you never learn anything new. And that’s makes selling anything remotely complicated just too hard. You’ll never be an expert. You’ll never know how to compete and win. And you’ll just run a basic playbook over and over. Sales execs especially that aren’t curious I see fail in any remotely competitive space. Especially at the VP level and above. There is no one to coach them, unless they can get SEs and others to do most of the heavy lifting. And they just start … making things up. Rather than truly learning. If they don’t ask good, curious questions during the interview process — I say pass for that reason alone

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So one of the weirdest calls you'll get as a founder is when a BigCo out of the blue wants to talk about acquiring you. Literally out of nowhere. Now, sometimes it's for real. Sometimes, it's the start of something. But if it's truly out of left field, it's often them doing diligence. Should they enter the market themselves? Or -- often, they are actually thinking of buying your competitor. It's a weird conversation when some BigCo randomly starts digging deep in your business, talking about "Build, Buy or Partner." That's the phrase you'll hear a lot. "Build, Buy or Partner." Now if you literally have zero relationship with this Big Tech Co, your spider sense may go up. This doesn't make sense. But there's always a logic. Here's my only advice: founders often hunker down when they get these calls. They don't want to share. They don't want to invest any time. Because their gut is, it's a weird fishing expedition going nowhere. And it may be. But my advice is always take the call. Spend the hour. And share more than you are inclined to. Why: 1️⃣ First, it's a great way to start building a relationship. 2️⃣ Second, even if they want to buy your competitor, that deal may fall through. They are often looking at a second choice, too. 3️⃣ Third, you can get some great intelligence. Corp Dev folks especially are often great at gossip. If you share, they'll often share. Your spider sense is often right. That weird call about "Build, Buy or Partner" may be off. But I think down the road you'll find putting in a hour and sharing a few data they could figure out anyway was worth it.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: AI is the Best Thing to Ever Happen to SaaS. Why? Because It’s Unlocked More Budget So there was a looming meta issue in SaaS many of us older timers worried about for years, until the 2020-2021 boom: 🤷 Will we run out of budget to buy SaaS? The dollars put into SaaS can’t just keep growing … forever. Or put differently, when will it no longer be “early innings” in the overall amount of global SaaS spend? Because forget about any individual SaaS or Cloud company, the overall SaaS markets kept growing at a breathtaking pact. Gartner not only has predicted SaaS spend will hit $300 Billion this year, but importantly, grow almost 20%. And that’s after years of similar growth. There was no way this could last ... forever. SaaS couldn’t consume 100% of all global IT budgets. It had to slow down at some point, and maybe soon. 👷‍♂️ And then all our jobs would just get a lot harder. Well, it’s not clear exactly how much of a permanent boost to overall software IT budgets AI is giving, but one thing is clear: the boost is real. Some budget is coming from headcount reallocated to agents and per resolution outcomes, e.g. in contact center. Some budget is coming from an expanded “we have to keep up” IT budget. Some is just experimentation budget. But it’s clearly expanding. I don’t think we’ll know clearly exactly how much AI is adding additional budget to overall business software spend. 🎁 But however much it is — is a gift to us all. It’s more budget to buy all our products. More than we would have anticipated just 12-24 months ago.

content: It’s a weird thing, but some of the worst fundraising advice comes from … your existing investors. Why? It’s usually not wrong, it’s just often, so, so biased: - Accelerators view VCs as fungible - Seed investors worry about dilution - Series A and B investors want to “control the ball” and decide who invests more - VCs with lots of money to deploy often want you to raise a lot more if you are doing well — even if you don’t need it - VCs with no more money to deploy often advise you not to raise more — even if it might help - Growth investors want to manage downside risk What terms are fair? author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So Asana went through a "tech downturn", with its strong reliance on tech customers. That hit it hard as we'll see below, while adjacent players like Monday saw growth stay much stronger -- without seeing any real downturn at all. Today Asana is at: 1⃣ $750M ARR 2⃣ $4.75B market cap 3⃣ Growing 10% 4⃣ 4% non-GAAP loss; But ... 5⃣ AI is giving it a boost 6⃣ Its stock is up a stunning 41% past 6 months! 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. NRR Fallen to 98% Overall, 99% For $100k+ Customers — From 115% at $600m ARR This is half the reason growth has slowed at Asana. At $600m ARR, NRR has 115%. Today, it’s 98%-99%. While the root causes are multiple, from seat contractions in tech to budget scrutiny, at a higher level it’s a visceral reminder of the importance of keeping NRR at 110%+. If Asana had the same NRR today it had even at $600m ARR, it would be growing twice as fast. And probably be worth 50% more. #2. 150,000 Total Customers. 100k+ Customers Are The Fastest Growing This isn’t unqiue to Asana, it’s true of many SaaS leaders at scale, from Zoom to Shopify. The enterprise customers are growing the fastest. Just remember not to leave the smaller ones behind! #3. Getting More Efficient, But Not Profitable Yet Asana has a PLG-SLG mix, but it’s a reminder PLG isn’t magically more efficient than SLG. Asana has gotten much more efficient, But it may not be non-GAAP “profitable” until $1B ARR. #4. 40% of Revenue from Outside U.S. Just our regular reminder to Go Global as early as you can, if you can. #5. Pushing Into Non-Tech Verticals Asana’s traditional strength has been in tech, but it has pushed outside of it to recapture growth. Non-tech verticals are growing 15% -- so far faster than tech. And that's where Monday's strength is, for example. And a few other interesting learnings: #6. Charging a Base Platform Fee for AI Studio, Then Variable Charge for Power Users I think we’re all still figuring this out, but Asana will charge a platform fee for its AI studio and include a base amount of credits. And then charge users that go beyond 100s or 1000s of workflows per month. Will this stick? Is it too complicated, or is it what the market now expects? Let’s see! #7. NRR Trending Slightly Back Up There’s a general consensus that the B2B segments that saw a downturn the past 2 years saw that downturn end in Q3’24. That’s consistent with what Asana is seeing — a modest rebound in NRR.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So a big theme of 2023 and 2024 was “work-life balance”. Moderation in growth, in spend, and in time spent on work and the journey. 😄 That a start-up maybe growing 40% but that is profitable might be better than a start-up growing 400% but addicted to venture capital. 🤽‍♀️ That maybe hitting 80% of quota but working 20 hours a week is better than killing yourself to hit 120% of quota and getting that big bonus check. 🏠 That everyone would be just as productive working 20-30 hours a week from home than 40+ in the office plus commute time. Well look, 2025 is the year to be honest here. The ones that work twice as hard, that grow twice as fast, that even … work in the office … are often thriving. And the ones that grew slowly, and in their minds, more sanely for 2 years are now being eclipsed by a new generation, often AI-fueled. It is tough to have balance when the competition is working 6 days a week, 10 hours a day, often half of that in the office. In fact, across the SaaStr Fund portfolio, I see the top-performing start-ups working harder than ever. Harder than in my entire career. 2025 is the year to be honest: for most of us in tech, if you want to do great things, there is no balance. There is nothing wrong for looking for an easy job, a 20-hour-a-week role, a fractional life. Just be honest with yourself where it may lead. Likely not to a big success. The world is more competitive than ever. And AI has fueled 10,000 new hyper-competitive start-ups. The lifestyle job and start-up in many cases has become the terminal start-up and career.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So a newer issue that is discussed a lot at start-up board meetings and investor meetings is AI Engineer comp. In general, I find most start-ups want to keep engineering comp fairly flat. Back in the day, my CTO just wanted 3 tiers: entry level, top IC, manager. That was it. 3 pay bands, and they were very tight. Equity varied a lot more, but I know it was important to my CTO that everyone on his team felt like equal stakeholders, relative to experience. I do think this is true at most start-ups, today too. They want fairly consistent comp across engineering, and fear if nothing else, lots of issue if favorites are played, the new “guy” gets a better deal, etc. But AI is challenging this. No start-up can compete with OpenAI”s massive comp and annual tender offers to provide partial liquidity. But it has created a two-tiered comp system for engineers. The “AI Team” often makes a lot more. I don’t have any answers here but I found the above Business Insider article with a leaked Microsoft memo helpful: 👉They pay AI engineers 48% more. 💰They have special spot retention bonuses for AI engineers to keep them This is roughly what I see, too. The “AI Team” at many SaaS startups makes 30%-40% more. It creates issues and drama. But probably not paying their premium will create just as many issues and drama as well. What I often see is many SaaS companies aren’t truly AI-native and often just have 1 or 2 true AI magicians on the team. The ones that really make the AI magic happen. And you often can’t afford to lose them. Are they worth 48% more? Fairness aside — of course they are.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So it’s 2025 and time to just be honest about some things. Like: what’s objectively wrong with a side hustle? The side hustle was always a thing but became memorialized as almost essential to sales reps in particular the past few years. That everyone needed multiple revenue streams. I’m not here to convince anyone on the issue. But I think the data on a lot of things is now in, from hybrid offices (don’t really work) to ‘lazy’ outbound (not working anymore) etc. 👉And here’s the problem with a side hustle: it takes up that last 20%. And that’s where you get great at sales. What do I mean? The best reps are still there on Dec 31. They are still closing deals when others have given up. They aren’t moving on when they need to pitch 3-4 stakeholders, not just 1. But that takes a >ton< of energy. To not just pass on pitching to 4 stakeholders. Only the obsessed in sales have that energy, from the SDR level to the CRO level. And what I’ve now seen clearly over the past 24 months, from SDR to CRO, is that it’s the obsessed that really win in sales (and everything, really). That doesn’t mean working 100 hours a week. It might really just mean truly doing 40 a week. But it means being so obsessed about winning, that you always push harder. You can’t get any bigger at the gym if you don’t push harder. And I’m not convinced you can be a very good seller, either. Almost every sales exec I know spending a ton of time in real estate, selling courses, etc. is struggling now. Not every one. But almost all of them. Nothing wrong with working nights and weekends on a passion project, or for a sense of security. But if it holds you back from going the extra yard at work … and I think it so often does … it’s just hard to excel. The data is now in. The world is more competitive than ever, and AI is making is 10x more so. There are 100s of new entrants in every space the past 12 months. If you’re distracted with your side hustle, you are going to lose to someone that isn’t. It’s not 2021 anymore.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So we’ve talked a ton on SaaStr over the years on the risks and benefits of hiring your various VPs and C-level execs. We’ve spent the most time on hiring a great first VP of Sales, but all the VPs are super important. Now that time has gone by though, I’m 100% sure that the worst mis-hire is CTO / VP Engineer. Because it becomes the death of innovation. I’ve seen this fact pattern or some variant thereof so many times: 1️⃣ Start with Great Founder CEO + CTO 2️⃣ CTO gets start-up to $5m, $10m, $20m but just “can’t scale” 3️⃣ VP of Engineering or CTO from Big Tech Company hired 4️⃣ Everyone chooses the Nice Candidate 5️⃣ The Nice Candidate never codes, never learns the code base, never gets the magic 6️⃣ The Nice Candidate hires a bunch of engineers under them that aren’t that great 🫠 At first, things seem better with Mr. Nice Guy CTO / VP of Engineering. Things are more organized under Mr Nice Guy VP of Engineering. There are a lot more discussions, which everyone feels great about. Fewer erratic changes. Releases are smoother. Everything is calmer. And … innovation just ends. This VP of Eng / CTO never knows the magic, the why, or the how. And the competition pulls ahead. And even worse, the founding CTO often either leaves or disengages. And the magic is lost. Even at Adobe Sign / EchoSign, my last start-up, my co-founder and CTO is still at Adobe as one of the most senior scientists. Why? Because they know even at $250m+ ARR they still need him. He wrote all the original code base, and the original magic. They don’t need him for all that much on a weekly basis. But when they need him — they really need him. Even today. 🫂 Whatever you do, when the time comes to hire an outside VP Eng / CTO, try to make sure you and your co-founder both are 100% aligned they are a 10/10. An epic hacker and engineer, not just a manager. Managers are a dime a dozen today. And they can’t win in engineering in a world that is more competitive than ever. When I see this happening, I fight. I fight to help the founders see it. I go down with the fight. Because when you hire a VP Eng / CTO that isn’t a 10, it’s the day your start-up starts to die. The other VPs, if you make a mis-hire, you can recover. But 2 years of no more innovation? I don’t know if most of us can fight our way back from that.

content: New!! CRO Confidential with Sam Blond + Checkr, Inc. COO Lindsey Scrase: "Usage-Based Revenue Models: Successes and Pitfalls" When Lindsey joined ... 1️⃣ Bookings to revenue conversion rates were significantly below target With only 4% conversion by month two versus a 10% goal. At first, Lindsey thought customers weren’t ramping as expected. But as she dug in, the real answer was too many sales reps were overbooking deals because of the pressure to hit their bookings quota. Under Lindsey’s direction, the conversion has now tripled to 12%. 2️⃣ The team lacked visibility into key metrics like average revenue per customer At Checkr, it’s not a license-based model, and yet the team had no visibility in the usage-based equivalent metric of average revenue per user, which is average revenue per report that the customer is running. Lindsey found a way to track this data, then brought it into every meeting. From weekly business reviews, to team meetings, to individual meetings – every call focused on bookings to revenue conversion. 3️⃣ Better RevOps uncovered excessive discounting The broader sales team had oversized incentives for upfront commitments, leading to excessive discounting for larger customers. Lindsey took that specific incentive out and started spiffing compensation on revenue realization, which is better for the customer. Much more at links in comments!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So what gets you more leads -- smaller, more "intimate" industry events? Or massive ones like Dreamforce, Inbound, SaaStr Annual, Shoptalk, Money 20/20 etc? It's a question especially a lot of marketers with slashed or limited budgets discuss a lot on LinkedIn and elsewhere. 🙅 But -- it's the wrong question. 👉 Here's the right one: where are your customers? And your top prospects? Wherever they are, both digital and IRL -- go there. Be there. Ideally, in force. There is no question the ideal event in theory is just you and you alone ... and 50-100 of the very top prospects in the world. Just the 50-100 of you. No one else. The problem is zero small events are like this -- unless you create them yourself. And you should create them yourself. Do your own steak dinners and a mini-roadshow, do 6-8 of these a year. And invite all your top customers and prospects. This is great and always works. But doing steak dinners and roadshows, while very valuable, has an inherent limitation. The only folks that show up are those in your own network. And only a subset even there. Ones that aren't in your network just aren't going to come to your steak dinner. 🛩️ But your top prospects out of your own network >do< go to the top events in their industry. Often just 1-2 a year. If they are smaller events, even better. Go there. But in general, they go to the biggest ones. They go to Reinvent and Dreamforce. And yes, Shoptalk for e-commerce and SaaStr for SaaS, Money 20/20 for fintech, etc. Not everyone goes. But a critical mass goes to the biggest in the industry. Our data shows it. We do small, smaller, medium and large events. The medium ones are probably the most fun. SaaStr APAC was great at 1,200 attendees, and SaaStr Europa at 3,000 really is more fun than SaaStr Annual at 10,000 attendees. But the best leads, the best prospects, the most buyers ... go to the flagship. Our sponsors at our flagship event just plain get the most revenue, the most contacts, the highest quality and highest volume of leads. Field marketing and events are a pain. They are a lot of work, a lot of travel, a lot of energy for leads that often take months or even years to close. But the playbook does work. There's a reason 40% of marketing budgets go to field and events. Because your buyers and customers go there. And before you say Smaller is Better, or even Bigger is Better, think instead: where are my prospects and customers? And just be there. That should be your field marketing strategy.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There are a lot of posts about how VCs make a ton of money with liquidation preferences when founders ... make zero. I find that’s rarely true. There are cases — 100% for sure. But when a tech acquirer goes to buy a company, they almost always want the founders to stay and go big. Departed founders, that’s different. But they almost always want as much consideration as possible to go to the founders and top execs still there — and NOT the VCs. In fact, in my worst investments so far in 11 years of investing, the founders made $10m+ and the VCs lost money. The opposite of this narrative. I literally had one the other day where the investors made $0.50 on the dollar and the founders $15m. Liquidation preferences or not. Raising venture capital can all seem like a game. It isn't. It's super expensive capital. And once you raise a lot, high stakes capital. And if you don't return at least 3x of what you raise, usually no one wins. Build a great company. Don't raise vastly more capital than you need. And create value for everyone. Do that, and there won't be any VC horror stories.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Come Back Happy in 2025 So over the past few weeks I’m doing a lot of end-of-the-year catch-ups and I’ve heard this one story again and again: “I replaced my entire management team this year” Or "I'm not sure I want to do this anymore." Or "I want to fire my top client" Etc. I push founders and the reason in the end is basically always the same. The existing team just wasn’t happy or motivated in the environment of 2023-2024. I’ve got a meta takeaway from this for everyone out there that’s a bit unsettled, unhappy, wistful about their tech role: 👉 If you’re respected, well paid, and have a good job — see if you can come in fresh in 2025 with a better attitude. Seriously. Even I get grouchy and feel sorry for myself at times. When a founder isn’t appreciative. When a co-investor does things they shouldn’t. When I see disloyalty. Sometimes even I quietly think, “hey, they’ll see how it is without me.” But if you can — stop. All the changes in the world from March 2020-mid 2024 are behind us now. In fact, Q4'24 was pretty good in SaaS and Cloud. Not 2021 good, but pretty good. IPOs are back, many (not all) SaaS stocks are back, AI is on fire. It’s time to put it all in a box. Easier times, bigger teams, and easier quotas are all behind us. Come back in 2025 happy. Even if you have to fake it at first. Come back appreciative. Even if you feel you’re owed more. Everyone wants to work for folks that are positive, on the mission, and great to be around. Whatever happened, in 2025, be one of those folks.

Its stock is up a cool +64% this year! 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Highly Durable Revenue Growth, Still Growing +23% a Year Even Well Past $10 Billion in ARR (!) And RPO is Up +33% (!) This is about as good as it gets at scale. Importantly, RPO (bookings) is accelerating, up 33% year-over-year. That’s a great sign not just for today, but for future growth and the years to come. #2. 2,000 $1M+ Customers. And 2 $100m+ ACV Customers (!) Very, very enterprise. #3. 98% GRR. Year after Year after Year The best of enterprise retention. No one leaves ServiceNow. And customers sign 3+ year contracts. #4. Super Efficient — Rule of 50 (!) It’s easy to be efficient at scale — if you aren’t growing much. But to also grow 25% or so year after year? That’s magical. 5. 26,000 Employees, So About $430,000 in Revenue Per Employee This is the level of efficiency it takes to be a top-tier SaaS company at scale.
