author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So I’m back full time-ish to the SF Bay Area. As, often quietly, are so many leaders and execs I’ve known for years. I spent about 60% of my time since lockdown in SoCal, 30% in Palo Alto, and the rest in Misc. It wasn’t to work at the beach, it was for family reasons. But still, I like many of us went from someone who never felt they could leave the SF Bay, to someone who well, did. The SF Bay Area is back. It’s clearly the center of the AI Boom, even if many are based outside of it, in Paris and elsewhere. YCombinator is having a renaissance, with 4 batches of 100s of top tier startups being hatched in Dogpatch in SF. Most will stay. Even top European accelerators like EF have come to SF. Many VCs that for whatever reason left, have returned. New York is great, SoCal and Miami are great places to live and OK for tech, and certainly there are segments of SaaS and B2B where SF isn’t as compelling. Vertical SaaS and parts of eCommerce may well be so focused on other geos, for example, it’s not worth it to be in SF Bay. But we’ll all kind of back. At least most of us. It is different though. That’s the subtle thing: •The SF Bay may no longer make sense for anyone that isn’t truly ambitious. Better to find a remote job and live in a cheaper, and calmer geo. •It will take years for parts of SF to be nice again. Some parts are great though. But SOMA and much of the financial district are still awful. Palo Alto and the Peninsula are as pretty, sunny, and expensive as ever. •The density isn’t quite there. But it’s still #1. Before March 2020, you could reach out your window and see a dozen leading SaaS execs. The hour after the Stay at Home order went out, I bumped into the President of Atlassian on the street. That doesn’t really happen anymore, at least for now. •All VCs will invest anywhere now. But it’s much easier if you are in SF Bay. It makes getting to know each other so, so much easier. •Most founders are OK hiring VPs anywhere now — but really, strongly prefer to work together in the office. It just gives you a leg up as a VP, especially a first-time VP, to be in SF Bay. •It’s by far the easier place to meet up with other CEOs and founders. You can do it anywhere. But it’s so much easier in SF Bay. My somewhat obvious learnings. I’m back. I miss the beach. I like it here, but I don’t love it. It lacks the density of pre-March 2020, that’s underappreciated. But if you are really going for it, I think most B2B founders will really benefit from being here. And probably most ambitious VPs and VPs-to-be, as well. It’s time. I’m back. It might be time for you to come back, too.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There are 3 types of hires you may be tempted to make now, but you just can't: The Jaded, The Broken, The Done They've always existed, it's just there are so many more folks with great LinkedIns and experiences in these categories in SaaS. We're 20+ years into SaaS, and especially the past 4 years have taken their toll on many of us. Maybe almost all of us. The Jaded You can hear it, see it, almost even smell it from the first Zoom. They blame the last CEO. They blame the VCs. Worse, one way or another, they blame The System. It's all rigged against employees and in favor of others. There's some truth in all of this. Just don't hire them. They will be even more jaded when they join you. The Broken This one is tough. They just can't sell themselves anymore. They can't get back on the road. They can't run campaigns anymore. They've been in the game a while, and it's taken its toll. You can see the signs in their body language. You can see the reluctance to work from the office. You can see a general approach that ... is just a bit too slow. Hints of it. You can't hire them. Everything slows down when you do. The Done These ones are often nice. They're often "fractional". They're always focused on strategy and coaching. They've done it, at least in part. They get it. They're just done. A few hours of them are great. Just don't hire them. Top tells: they've been consulting for years. They spend a ton of time on LinkedIn. They speak everywhere. They are focused on "process". They think sales is all about being a "people person". Because that's so much easier. I really didn't meet too many of the Jaded, the Broken, and the Done when I started in SaaS. But that was a long time ago. Most of us can't go forever in this. So I get it, and have empathy. You just can't hire these folks. Have your spider sense out, and don't lower the bar here when you get a bit tired, even a bit desperate, in hiring.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So Toast is one of the most iconic B2B leaders out there. We've all used Toast 10s or 100s of times by now. But while the brand and market penetration is strong, the business model is challenging. It still loses money on the hardware, and the payments side is fairly low margin (28% or less). The software license is high margin, but it's only 20% of the total revenue. So Toast has had to not just get efficient like everyone else these days, but >extra< efficient. So what did it do? * It forced reps to close 13% more locations per sales rep. In essence, increasing quotas +13%. * And it shrunk territories -27%. A double whammy from an AE's perspective. That makes their job 40%+ harder. And what happened? Well -- it worked. And fast. At least for now. Sales continues to grow at an epic 29% at $1.5 Billion, hitting records. And reps had to work that much harder. Will this work for you? What's the line here? And won't reps complain to the high heavens when you shrink territories? And quit if you increase quotas? Maybe. But Toast had no choice. It did what it had to with its sales team. It forced them to hit the numbers it took to go profitable. And ... it worked.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Dear SaaStr: Growth Has Slowed and My VP of Sales is Pushing Me To Hire More Reps. Is That The Right Way to Go? No. Not 9+ times out of 10. In fact, the #1 sign your VP of Sales is really struggling is when their best answer to slow sales is to hire more AEs. Of course you need enough reps to hit the plan, and enough capacity to hit the plan. But when grow slows, when you miss the plan, more bodies does not solve the problem. In fact, fewer sales reps often in the short term solves the problem. You focus leads and opportunities on the best reps, and then rebuild the sales team from there. Once a VP of Sales that is struggling starts pushing for a lot more sales headcount ... it's time to realize it's not working. It's a hail mary than on paper might work, but in reality, doesn't.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So if you've been around startups for a while, and especially sat on any boards, you'll see a VP of Sales answer a slow Q1 and even Q2 with this: "We'll make up for it in Q4." Or some variation thereof. In fact, in so many sales plans, you often see Q4 bookings at 2x or more Q1! Even when growth overall is slow. It may look possible on a spreadsheet, but I've almost never seen a sales team magically make up for a weak Q1 or 1H with an insane Q4. It just doesn't work that way. The other day in fact we looked at a decade of SaaStr Annual ticket selling data. We've literally been selling tickets to SaaStr Annual for 500+ weeks, almost every week, for a decade. Phew. And that gives us a massive dataset across $30,000,000+ of ticket sales and much more. And one thing is clear, and many counter-intuitive: we -- and you-- can't make for a missed campaign, for a missed week, for a missed quarter. It's just too late. You would think in our case at least, hey, you forget to send an email campaign 6 months before SaaStr Annual. Surely they'll still buy a ticket the next month? In the next campaign? In theory, sure. In practice, No. We've had a few marketers come and go that stubbornly tore up our playbook and didn't send campaigns for several slots. And we never made up for that lost revenue. At least, not entirely. Never. Ok is this a perfect analogue for SaaS sales? Not exactly, but maybe. One thing I can tell you for sure, having been in SaaS since 2005, is if your VP of Sales claims they'll make up all the lost ground at the start of the year with a massive Q4 ... they won't. And unfortunately, you're gonna need a new VP of Sales.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: What one thing or characteristic do customers appreciate the most in a salesperson? That I matter. This is actually a rare skill, and hard to hone: That I’m not just a transaction. That my concerns matter. That I won’t be abandoned the second the deal closes. That all my questions will be answered, even if it takes longer than it should. That One More Demo is OK to ask for, without pressure. That I don’t have to “get on a call” about everything if I don’t want to. That the follow-ups I get from you will all be about helping, not pressure. That the pricing will be fair, and the same others pay for the same usage. So I don’t have to stress about negotiating. That if I need to do a trial, or a pilot, it’s fine. Totally fine. That if I need 2 months to make a decision, not 2 days, you’ll still be there. That I matter. It means treating each customer like you’d like to be treated yourself. Like their money really matters. It means putting more time in than might seem to make sense. It means treating tiny customers as well as, or even better than, large customers. Do it right though, and you close more. And if times are tougher these days? Listen to their calls. Listen to your team's calls. Do your reps all treat your prospects this way? Or is too transactional? Or too many games? Or all about price and next steps? Listen. Listen. And then go make some changes. If you truly care about your customer's problems, you'll close more. A lot more. I remember the first magical moment I had like this. I went to buy Salesforce for the first time. We only needed 2 seats, and I felt guilty about using up a sales rep’s time. But he made me feel like he had all the time in the world. He showed me I really only needed a lower end edition to use the API. He showed me how Salesforce really worked, for real, for a small startup. And he helped me figure out how to get into their partner ecosystem. I bought that day, and have ever year since. Since 2006.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A few “rules” in raising venture capital that founders somehow … seem to constantly miss. Or get wrong: 1️⃣ If your existing investors have a strong brand and aren’t positive on you, it can much harder to raise. At a minimum keep them in the loop. Don’t just ignore them after they write a check. The converse is also true. Your existing investors are often your best source of leads for the next round of funding. 2️⃣ It has to be the CEO that pitches the VCs. It just has to be. Don’t send your co-founder or your “COO” or your CFO or whatever. For most investors, that’s almost an immediate No. 3️⃣ The initial VC decision is made within 20 minutes of the first conversation. Make it exciting, speak with data, and get to the point. The initial Yes, Maybe or No decision is made within 20 minutes. So save slides 20–200 for questions and back-up. 4️⃣ Making stuff up is death, or close to it. If you don’t know the answer, just say that, it’s fine. But make something up that the VC knows the answer is otherwise … that’s almost always a No right there. 5️⃣ You have to know your competition cold. Every great salesperson and CEO does. Learn more here if you don’t. 6️⃣ Cold outreach works. It just has to be very, very good. Everyone reads email. But if you are going via cold outreach instead of a warm intro, make the email amazing. Simple, but metrics-filled and to the point. Hide nothing. Don’t ask for coffee. Get to the point. This is your one shot. At least, there is a decent chance it will be read if the headline is exciting and of interest. 7️⃣ Slow growth is death in fundraising. Just wait to raise then. If you just aren’t growing quickly enough to support a venture investment, it can be better to wait and go out in a few months. At least, you need to have 3–4 good months strung together in a row to show a pattern (and hope). 8️⃣ Your existing investors often save some money for a second check. Treat them that way. Most institutional investors can give you at least a little more money if you are doing OK and need it. So again, keep them in the loop. Otherwise, they won’t reserve this money. 9️⃣ Be yourself. A top “sin” in fundraising is acting like someone else. Yes, being a CEO involves a little bit of acting. A bit. But overall, be yourself. Be true. 50% of fundraising is the VCs getting to know the CEO. It’s OK to overindex on the topic you are most passionate about (product, sales, marketing, etc.). It’s OK if the presentation doesn’t look exactly like some deck you saw on Business Insider. Make it all great. Rehearse. Take it seriously. But don’t not be yourself. Don’t act like someone you think you should be to fundraise. Good luck!

author: Palmer Houchins
content: ☀ Coming up for air after a very, full and busy three days in San Mateo for SaaStr Ai Annual 2024. 🗒 A few of the highlights for me this year: 1️⃣ Meeting with so many G2 customers, partners, and (dare I say?) prospects in person. Great chatting with the teams from Factors.ai, Nooks, Rockbot, Enghouse Systems, Pavilion, DemandOS, Knotch, and Zencoder, among many more. Love hearing how G2 is helping them turn reviews into revenue. 2️⃣ Content is still king. As popular as the sponsor hall and braindate tracks are, nothing beats the presentations, panels and Q&As at SaaStr Ai. From Jason M. Lemkin's state of SaaS and Sydney Sloan's presentation on what G2's Buyer Behavior Report is telling you about your GTM to Nicole Baer, Gail Moody-Byrd, and Denise Persson's CMO panel on next year's growth strategies, SaaStr Ai just consistently delivers in this area. Speaking of marketing and content: I have to mention SaaStr's on-site CMO Summit. Shoutout to Carilu Dietrich for pulling together a great group of marketing leaders with outstanding presentations and panels on metrics, board presentations, pipeline growth, plus a great conversation about AI's impact on marketing. 3️⃣ Not everything happens on-site. Some of my best conversations were offsite over drinks at the countless happy hours and parties that pop up around SaaStr. I particularly enjoyed catching up with Erik, Katie and the rest of the Postal by Sendoso team at their annual Oktoberfest-themed shindig. And I had a fantastic stroll down email memory lane with the Beefree and Really Good Emails team. Thanks for having me Justine, Matt, and Mike, even though I showed up super late! 4️⃣ Our G2 Data Solutions Dinner. Did you know G2 sells a data product to the world's leading investors and consultants? If you ask me, not enough people do. But I thoroughly enjoyed breaking bread with this group, in particular catching up with my many times emailed, but never met in real life fellow software data nerd, Matt Harney. 5️⃣ Watching Godard Abel in action. 25+ meeting in two days. I think that qualifies as founder mode? With that many Cloud/AI/SaaS entrepreneurs in one room, he's truly in his element, and it shows. Always an inspiration, amping it up even if I get tired just thinking about it. 🙌 Thanks to the SaaStr Ai team for bringing it all to life: Jason, Amelia, Taylor, Bryan, and everyone else on the team there...and last but not at all least: a very special shoutout to Sunnie Niklaus for keeping all our trains running on time and looking good, too.

author: Godard Abel
content: Sharing my key takeaways from an exhilarating couple of days at SaaStr last week! 𝟭). 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝗮𝗮𝗦. Both disruptive startups and incumbent market leaders are shipping new AI-first products & features AND speeding up their own innovations and processes. Our G2 CMO Sydney Sloan shared how Grammarly leads in a category with 488 (and growing!) AI Writing Assistants on G2! 𝟮). 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗮𝗮𝗦 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁, per Jason M. Lemkin and our G2 buyer research. Buyers have leverage as they consolidate SaaS stacks and spend. And they want it all: “hyperfunctional” compound apps, AI innovation, and more flexible usage-based pricing models. As a result, sales cycles are lengthening and retention rates are increasingly difficult to maintain. 𝟯). 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗩𝗖 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 with ~50% fewer VCs attending. Only the highest quality teams and/or growth metrics are gaining new funding. At the same time, the IPO market bar has become incredibly high at ~$500M ARR with Rule of 40%+ and positive cash flow. Thus, many more founders are bootstrapping and well-funded companies are increasing capital efficiency and productivity substantially. 𝟰). 𝗦𝗮𝗮𝗦 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗴𝗼-𝘁𝗼-𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜 to meet higher buyer expectations for ROI in addition to investor-raised efficiency standards. This includes differentiating your value messages beyond just saying "it's AI" and engaging economic buyers in the C-suite to win deals and then deliver ROI quickly post-sale. 𝟱). ‘𝗚𝟮 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲’ 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗮𝗮𝗦𝘁𝗿 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺. I thoroughly enjoyed meeting so many SaaS founders and leaders with stellar customer reviews. I also loved seeing the well-earned G2 Badges appearing in the booths of so many amazing SaaS providers! Thanks to Jason & the SaaStr Ai team for hosting us at another great event! 👏 SaaStrAnnual hashtag #SaaS hashtag #AI

author: Agostina Albamonte
content: What a fantastic Day 1 at SaaStr Ai 2024! 🎉 I had the chance to connect with some incredible founders of SaaS companies and agencies, which made the experience even more enriching. I attended 2 impactful sessions that sparked my thinking about the SaaS industry: 👉 Enterprise Customer Demands Jonathan Rosenberg shared some eye-opening insights about what enterprise customers are looking for—think innovation, real-time data, and ethical AI. It's clear that the expectations are high, and transparency is a must! 👉 Product-Led Growth Decoded Maria Thomas emphasized that PLG isn't just about your product; it's about empowering users to drive growth. Consumer-grade UX is key! Making products more accessible, intuitive, flexible, and visually appealing will lead to great results. Other important strategies included maintaining consistent content, creating organic channels for growth, and focusing on pre-signups. The day wrapped up with a lively Happy Hour hosted by Gynger, where I connected with so many amazing people .Can’t wait for Day 2! If you’re around, let’s connect! 🌟 hashtag #SaaStr2024 hashtag #SaaStr

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: When I look across my investment portfolio for past 11 years, the #1 issue I think isn’t pricing, or TAM, or making a terrible mishire, or competition. Those all matter, but … The #1 issue ends up being waiting too long to truly go multi-product. No matter what you do, if you are too slow here, growth stalls. Parker Conrad has done a great job including at SaaStr Europa talking about building compound startups. In an ideal world, many of us would do just that. But he’s also been clear and honest how expensive his approach is. We can’t all be Rippling. But what I think all of us probably have to do is make a Clear and Big Second Product Bet earlier than planned. An experiment or two helps, but it’s not enough. What I mean is going all-in on a Big Second Product that doubles your market or more. Not in Year 1 :). But almost always earlier than planned. And for most of us, that Second Big Product has to be even bigger than the First. This makes it even harder. Because if it isn’t, the first one just keeps growing even bigger. Look at HubSpot. CRM is probably bigger than Marketing now (HubSpot doesn’t break it out anymore). If not, it will be soon. They started making that bet in 2013 or so, maybe earlier.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Are any sales reps truly, 100% honest? Ok I know this sounds triggering, and it is triggering, and it's not fair. But it's literally what one of the most ethical CEOs I've ever invested in asked me the other day. It's a question that comes up more and more these days. Is the pricing I'm getting ... really fair? Is it really the same deal a similar company just got? Do I really, truly need the enterprise edition? Do I actually have to buy all the seats upfront? Is that deal really going to close? Will you really sue me if I don't honor that auto-renew clause? Is it OK for sales to be say 80% honest? 95%? It's an interesting question. As founders, we want everyone to be 100% honest. Or at least 98%. But ... there are conflicts there with some sales processes. Especially at the IC level. What do you think?

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: You're At Fault, Too. In 2024, this might be the single best piece of advice I can give to folks. It took me a while to see it, too. That VP of Sales that came in and sales -- went down? Yeah, but you hired him. How could he really know what he was getting himself into? That's on you. Those VCs that took all the money via "liquidation preferences"? Slow it down. The company raised too much money is what happened. And no one really made any money as a result. Raising too much money? That's on you. The prospect you spent months on that in the end, didn't close? They didn't spend all that time for fun. It's never fun shopping for business apps. You didn't provide enough value. Or maybe the competition provided more. That's on you. As passionate people we often think we're right on our mission, and others failed us, or did the wrong thing, or should have done things differently. There's probably a ton of truth there. I fall into that trap of thinking all the time myself. But it's your job as leader, as a founder, as an exec to go further. To make sure that VP knows what they are getting themselves into. To make sure it really makes sense to be a unicorn. To think of things from the customers' perspective. Too few in sales do the latter these days, in tougher times. When I look back on tough situations, where I was in the right. When I think about them calmly, over time. I often see I was a little bit more at fault than I thought, too.

content: When times get tougher, some folks will start to check out. You have to step up and show them the way back. Show them the path forward, to getting back to growth. Then thank them, and show them kindly ... a gentle way out.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: What's #1 on the path to becoming a great VP of Sales? Each story is different, but there is one clear penultimate step, one rite of passage to VP of Sales you just have to pass first: recruiting and managing a small sales team yourself. From scratch. What 95 times out of 100 is a recipe for failure is jumping straight from successful individual rep to VP of sales: ⚡ If you are the #1 rep at a hot startup, you will get VP of Sales offers from other up-and-coming startups. A CEO or two will want to take that risk, to hire the #1 rep at Hot Startup to be their VP of Sales. My advice is don’t take that job. Wait untl you've built a small team first. 🚫 And CEOs, my strong, strong, strong advice is never hire a VP of Sales that hasn't hired at least 2-3 reps themselves that truly hit quota. Find out. Ask. Go talk to them. To be even a stretch VP of Sales, you have to learn to recruit. 50% of the job of a VP of Sales is recruiting a great team. Not just managing one. A related mistake is a director of sales who inherited a team but didn’t recruit one, jumps straight to VP of Sales. That almost always = failure as well. Take your time, get promoted at least to manager or director level and recruit 2–3 reps yourself that hit quota. Then you're ready for a stretch VP of Sales role at an early but fast-growing startup. If you can find a way to recruit 2–3 reps that can hit quota … which is hard, and a very different skill than hitting your own quota … you can recruit 20–30, or more. You then can be a very successful VP of Sales.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: You need new DNA at your start-up. Because, and I know this will be triggering to some, but the past 18-24 months ... many folks didn't step up to the challenge. It doesn't matter why. I never totally got the expression, "When the Going Gets Tough, The Tough Get Going." Personally, I'm always going :) But it's been clear the past 24 months, at least at startups, scale-ups and public companies where things got harder, many folks didn't work even harder. Was it fair to expect them to? Probably not. But only your true Pirates and Romantics will work even harder when ... it gets harder. You can't push people that don't want to be pushed. You can't tell them to do more calls, to go meet more customers, to push code faster -- if they aren't feeling it. No, you need new DNA. You need fresh blood. You need a few high-energy leaders that can come in and see the Good today. What's working, and what's still special. And want to run with that, and build on it. Go find them.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: If you're unhappy at work, should you threaten to quit? I think you can do it once. Once. If you are truly a top performer, top 10%, folks will react. First, you may get a raise. In fact, this is one of the easiest ways to get a raise in a BigCo. HR always saves some budget for a top performer that is leaving. If you aren't a top performer, well, at least you'll find out when you threaten to quit. They'll say Good Luck! We Understand! Time to Spread Your Wings! Just don't do it twice. Don't say it twice. Don't even half-say it twice. Too many folks say it too many times. I know if you're frustrated, it can feel a bit cathartic to allude to quitting several times. But if you do, you'll be put off the critical path, at least in a startup. No one can really count on anyone that says twice they may leave.

The "Supply Chain Risk" Weaponization The Department of Defense’s designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk is a massive escalation. While the immediate loss is a $200 million contract, the real "blast radius" is the potential to freeze the company out of the broader B2B economy. 2. Ambiguity is a B2B Deal Killer In enterprise sales, risk doesn't have to be certain to be fatal: it only has to be ambiguous. Anthropic’s already seeing deals cut in half or stalling because prospects fear government exposure. Competitors like OpenAI are reportedly capitalizing on this by positioning themselves as the "no-problem" alternative. 3. The Death of the Junior Employee We are entering a "world of the middle of the bell curve" regarding experience. Companies no longer want to spend 3–6 months training juniors when AI tools can provide instant, senior-level productivity. This isn't just a theory; Computer Science and Math graduates from solid state schools are already seeing "zero jobs" as companies stop hiring entry level jobs. 4. 24/7 Persistent AI is the Real Compute Driver Most people are currently using AI for episodic tasks (chatting, coding for an hour). But the next frontier is 24/7 persistent AI agents that watch, listen, and run in the background of your entire life. Moving from one agent to 50 agents running in parallel 24 hours a day will require orders of magnitude more compute than we have today. 5. The End of "Gentle Deceleration" In the public markets, the era of managing a polite, high-margin slowdown is dead. Investors are now brutally punishing any company that isn't actively re-accelerating. If you aren't showing CloudFlare-level acceleration or better, the public markets have effectively abandoned you. 6. Built-in Distribution vs. Product Velocity Wix is a fascinating lab experiment for the AI age. They have 6.1 million customers to cross-sell to, which helped their new AI product, Base 44, hit $100 million ARR. However, if that $100M doesn’t exponentially compound to $600M+ quickly, it won't be enough to offset the 1-2% decline in their core legacy business. 7. "Agent-Led Growth" is the New PLG The startups seeing "lines out the door" right now are the ones offering wholesale human replacement.. Founders should be building agents that are 90% better than humans in specific categories like GTM or support. author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: What’s stressful for many SaaS and B2B founders today is they can feel the window closing. It hasn’t always shown up in the numbers yet. With say 110%+ NRR, it takes a while to see it in the numbers. You can say you’ve added AI to the product. But that's not enough. If adoption isn’t through the roof, if customers aren't happy to pay 50%-200% as much for your AI agent as your core product ... then it’s not real. And every founder knows it. At least they should. There is still time. But the window is closing. It won't be open in 2027.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We went from zero to 20+ AI agents in 9 months. But how to really manage them is the one thing nobody really tells you about. The numbers sound great: → $2.75M+ booked by AI SDRs → 5-7% outbound response rates (2x industry average) → 150,000+ "Digital Jason" and Amelia AI chats handled → Eight-figure revenue with single-digit headcount But every single agent requires weeks of training and daily management. There’s no magic button. Every agent has hallucinated at some point. Quality requires constant calibration, not perfection. Managing 20+ agents now consumes 30% of our Chief AI Officer’s time. The 5 biggest mistakes executives make with AI agents: 1. Running 8-10 vendor bakeoffs instead of picking one and going deep 2. Expecting automation and getting a 30%-of-your-time management job 3. Scaling too fast — you can only absorb ~1.5 agents per month effectively 4. Ignoring soft costs — “quiet can be lonely” when AI replaces most of your team 5. Judging vendors by demos instead of talking to the person who actually deploys your agent The agents that “don’t work” are the ones nobody trained. The first agent is YOUR job — not an agency’s, not a consultant’s. 30 days of hands-on work. No shortcuts. But if you’re willing to invest the effort, the competitive advantage is massive. We’re their #1 performing customer at both Artisan and Qualified. That didn’t happen by accident.

content: We’ve closed over $100,000,000+ in sponsorships at SaaStr over the years and I am still learning about real marketing ROI from them. I used to think marketers were all doing it wrong. When growth explodes, everyone would want to sponsor. When growth slowed, sponsors would churn as budgets tightened. Marketing budgets were often the first to be cut. For years I thought this was backwards. The ones hitting headwinds are the ones that should be marketing more. Not the ones that are exploding. But as time has gone by and we have the numbers and experience I see this is probably right. Marketing a product folks just don’t want to buy can work, but it’s very hard. What’s easier? Reminding folks that already might want to buy your product … to buy it now. It’s easier to meet folks that are already somewhere in your funnel and use that meeting to close them. It’s easier to meet folks already excited to buy from some vendor in your space, and decide after meeting you IRL, to pick you. So I was wrong. Folks that are crushing it should market more, not less. And folks seeing huge growth declines should probably put that money into … product. See also, SuperBowl ads.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We now run SaaStr with 3 humans, 1 dog, and 20+ AI agents. We've vibe-coded 8+ apps into production. Bought dozens of third-party tools. And last week, we replaced a paid SaaS tool we'd been using for years — with a vibe-coded app built in a day and a half. Here's what we've learned after 9 months of this: 🫤 The 90/10 Rule still holds. Buy 90%. Build 10%. We're not trying to vibe-code our own CRM. We're not rebuilding Salesforce. If a good tool exists off the shelf, we buy it. But we added a new exception: 🏗️ If a tool you're paying for has zero AI features in 2026, and you need those features --0 that's when you build. Our sponsor portal tool had no AI. None. Not even basic company enrichment. The SSO wasn't persistent. Adding a new user required a human to manually invite them. So Amelia Lerutte — who is not an engineer — gave herself one day to get true SSO working in a vibe-coded replacement. If it worked, she'd build the rest. If not, back to the old tool. It worked. She used Claude Co-work to write the spec, process 150+ sponsor contracts, and auto-generate registration codes in Bizzabo. What used to take a human a full day took Claude a couple hours. SaaStrSponsors.com is now live. External-facing. Managing millions in sponsor revenue. That vendor lost us forever. They don't even know yet. Here's the honest part though: Every app you build is an app you have to maintain. We're at our max. There's no economic justification based on software cost — you can buy these tools for $5K-$10K. You only build when the off-the-shelf options are so far behind they're hurting your business. The real question for B2B founders: 👉 Does your product still make your customers' jaws drop? At some point it did. That's how you got your first customers. They didn't buy you because you were 1% better. Is that still true in the age of AI? If not, that's why you're decaying. And there is no middle ground anymore. You're either at the cutting edge of AI, or you're getting displaced. The only question is speed.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 10 months ago, we were barely using Salesforce. Even though I've been a customer since 2005 (!) Why? Our sales team had dwindled to 3 people. And two of them wouldn't log in at all. When we added Momentum.io to auto-log sales calls to Salesforce, one rep quit. Not because the job got harder. Because they didn't want their activity tracked. Our CRM had become a ghost town. 🤖 Then ... we deployed 20 AI agents. And Salesforce became the most important piece of software we run. Here's what nobody warns you about when you go AI-first: All your agents need somewhere to live. Somewhere to share data. Somewhere to avoid stepping on each other. Without a hub, you get chaos. Your AI SDR reaches out to someone who just had a bad support interaction. Your inbound agent re-qualifies someone already deep in a sales sequence. Your agents conflict. Your data fragments. We now run 4 AI SDRs — Artisan, Monaco, Qualified, and Salesforce Agentforce — all syncing back to Salesforce CRM: → Artisan: 15,000 messages in 100 days, 5-7% response rates across 3 outbound campaigns → Monaco: booked meetings with some of the biggest names in AI. From Day 1 after go-live. → Qualified (just acquired by Salesforce): powers our inbound "digital Amelia." 700K+ sessions. $3M+ closed. 71% of our closed-won sponsorship deals in one month came from AI-qualified leads. Historic average? 29-34%. → Agentforce win-backs: this one I'm almost embarrassed about. After SaaStr AI 2025, we audited Salesforce and found ~1,000 people who filled out our sponsorship interest form and got ZERO human follow-up. Ever. We put Agentforce on it. 72% open rate. (Not a typo.) 10%+ response rate on "dead" contacts. Already closing deals from leads ghosted 6+ months ago. Why such insane open rates? Because in this use case, Agentforce isn't doing cold outreach. It knows their full Salesforce history — past events attended, prior sponsorship levels, every interaction we've ever had. The emails feel like a relationship continuing, not a recovery sequence. Cold email: 2-4% open rates. Artisan outbound: 5-7% response rates. Excellent. Agentforce on warm CRM contacts: 72% open rates. Different categories entirely. (And notice the pattern: Salesforce acquired Momentum. Salesforce acquired Qualified. They're not building from scratch — they're buying the best agents and pulling them into the platform.) 🚀 The CRM that becomes the hub for AI agents wins. The one that doesn't becomes a database you're overpaying for. Going AI-first didn't make CRM less important. It made us finally use it the way it was always meant to be used. If you're deploying AI agents: don't skip the hub. Your agents need somewhere to live. .......... And want to see how all these AI Agents >truly< work? And deploy them yourself -- for real? They'll all be there at SaaStr AI 2026, May 12-14 in SF Bay!!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: How Long It Really Takes to "One-Shot" an App? The vibe coding movement, from Claude Code to prosumer apps, still has a narrative problem. Every week someone posts "I built a SaaS in 2 hours! I one shot a marketing app!" And then I ask if it's >really< done. It never is. I just spent 16 days building http://Founderscape.ai. It's a pretty cool game that simulates taking a start-up from Day 0, to YC, to IPO, and beyond! Here's what it actually took: - Development Period: Dec 20 - Jan 5 - Calendar Days: 16 - Total Commits: 3,158 (a lot was design) - Lines of Code: ~47,000 - Main Game File: 6,122 lines - Estimated Hours: 40-55 That's not "prompt and forget." Constant iteration. What actually happened: - Days 1-3: Honeymoon. Everything works. You're a genius. - Days 4-7: The reckoning. Edge cases. You rebuild core systems. - Days 8-12: The grind. You're not building new features. You're fixing what broke when you built the last one. - Days 13-16: Polish. The game works. Now it needs to feel good. This phase never ends — you just decide to ship. The one-shot math today: Simple landing page: 1-4 hours Information web app: 10-20 hours Complex interactive product: 40-100+ hours Production-ready at scale: Add 30-60 min/day, forever And here's the kicker: we're not done. 16 days and 47,000 lines just got us into production. To make it great? So, so much more. Production is not the finish line. Production is the starting line. The 40-55 hours got Founderscape into players' hands. The next 400 hours will make it something they can't stop playing. Would I do it again? Absolutely. 40-55 hours to build a game with 47,000 lines of code is still insanely fast. A game studio would scope this as 6 months with a team. I did it solo over winter break. The leverage is real. The speed is real. But "one-shot" is a lie we tell ourselves to feel like wizards. How long to one-shot an app? Prototype: hours Something people use: weeks Something you're proud of: longer than you think Something truly great: you're never done Try it free → http://Founderscape.ai Go from startup to YC to IPO. Raise from Sequoia, Benchmark, FF. Beat your AI rivals. Hit a trillion-dollar valuation before you run out of runway. MMORPG version coming soon.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: I know ‘memory’ is a big deal in AI — what I don’t know is how >much< of it you really need to have a great AI experience. The more I learn about how our own AI Agents work, the more I learn it’s less important our own SaaStr AI Agents are trained on 20,000,000+ words of SaaStr content (and 2,000+ videos and pods) … and more important that it is well trained on the last 50-100 most important pieces of content. And that that training gets updated constantly with the top fresh learnings. I’m not an expert. Memory is critical. What I don’t know is exactly how much of it our AIs need. Quality and recency seem to trump quantity, at least right now. A little memory done well may go a long way for 95% of use cases. Not all. But perhaps most.

A T3D2 deal was amazing, and still could be amazing. But if you don't get credit at the firm ... the price is 2x what is was a few years ago .. and you own less ... It can be tough to do that deal. author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We all know how much AI has already changed customer support. But -- it's not cheap. Across all my investments in the space, the average price to resolve or deflect a ticket is about $1.00 For complex issues, around $5.00 in tokens etc. That's much cheaper than a human. And it never sleeps, complains, or quits. But it's not "cheap". Especially if the vendors want 80% gross margins ... To get software-like margins, you'd have to charge $5 - $10 per ticket / issue resolution. Right now the market won't pay that, and VCs are subsidizing it Yes, inference and token costs will fall ... but also, competition will force higher and higher quality ticket and issue resolution. AI can do much more than it can today. That will burn a lot more tokens. A lot more. Who will pay for top tier AI support? And how much? We don't know yet. It's all still subsidized.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: We had an app we’d been reference customers for — for years. Our case study was on their website, we got them several of their largest customers via our direct recommendations. Then last year they told us had to pay another $20,000 a year to brand the app. I.e., to add a JPEG. Which we’d done for 5+ years. It wasn’t even a new feature. “Why?” we asked the new CRO, who had implemented the new fee. “Because we need the revenue”, the CRO answered directly. “So I’m forcing you to pay it.” This is why SaaS is Dying in 2025. Some of it is AI. Some of it is vendor consolidation. But some is self-inflicted. As growth slows, the leaders in SaaS keep sticking it to their installed base as the only source of reliable growth: ➡️ Excessive and endless price increases ➡️ Threats on leaving ➡️ “Customer Success” calls that are only about forcing you to buy new products you don’t want. And in doing so, they may hit the quarter. But they are slowly destroying their customer base. And themselves. Yes, for many growth is harder than it was in 2021. Of course it is. But the only way out is new, happy customers. Not sticking it to your base, year after year after year.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: ICONIQ's latest State of Software 2025 report is out. Buried in 73 pages are some great data on just how AI is changing B2B software Here are my Top 10 Learnings: 🧵 #1. AI Companies Burn More Cash — But Also Have Better Capital Efficiency. It’s Not a Paradox But … It’s Complicated. This one breaks your brain at first: AI-native companies under $100M ARR have a median FCF margin of -126% (they’re burning cash at 126% of revenue). That’s more than double the -56% for non-AI companies. Yet their burn multiple—the key metric for capital efficiency—is actually better: 0.4x versus 1.8x for non-AI companies. #2. GTM for AI Products Is Flipped: 55% of High-Growth Teams Are in Post-Sales Traditional B2B companies put 55% of their GTM headcount in sales roles. For high-growth AI-native companies, that ratio is flipped: 47% in sales, but 31% in post-sales (versus just 23% for traditional SaaS). AI leaders have sales teams. They are just much smaller. And much more of that budget is going to FDEs, SEs, and post-sales. #3. Private AI Funding in First Half of 2025 Already Exceeds All of 2024. And Deal Sizes Doubled YoY. Private AI/ML companies raised $377 billion in the first half of 2025. That’s more than the $363 billion raised in all of 2024. The average deal size jumped from $17.2M in 2024 to $35.9M in 1H 2025—more than doubling. #4. AI-Native Companies Are Hitting $100M ARR with Teams of Less Than 100-150 People Traditional SaaS wisdom says you need 500+ employees to reach $100M in ARR. Probably 100+ sales reps alone. AI-native companies are throwing that playbook out the window. Perplexity got to 5,000 customers with 5 sales reps. Cursor reached $100M ARR in one year with less than 60 employees. Lovable hit the milestone in 8 months with 45 people. ElevenLabs got there in roughly 2 years with around 150 employees. #5. Forward-deployed engineer job postings increased 12x in one year, fastest growing in software—from ~30/month in early 2024 to 375/month by April 2025. The fastest-growing job title in software isn’t “AI engineer,” it’s customer-facing technical roles. It's really hard to roll out a B2B AI product that needs training without a strong FDE team. #6-#10 at link in comments!!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's a "weird", less discussed, and tough-to-predict start-up M&A strategy: Be #2. It happens all the time. A Mega Tech Leader wants to enter a space, but the #1 player is just ... too expensive. Or simply won't sell. Or has raised an insane amount at a huge valuation. Now if #2 has done the same -- raised a massive amount at a super high valuation -- they may be a tough spot. But if they've been very capital efficient, and have a simpler cap table, and a low burn ... That Mega Tech Company will often buy the #2 player. Because it's what's available. And sometimes, what they can afford. You can't count on this playbook. Even being #2 is hard. But it's a reason to push on, and if you are #2 ... to consider being as capital efficient as practical.

content: So many folks felt burnt out in 2022-2023 when things got harder after The Best of Cloud Times of 1H'20-2021. Now we're in the AI Age and most of us are working far, far harder than we ever did then. Far harder. And more intensely. Managing AI agents all day is so cool, but it's intense. The output rate, the productivity rate is so high, it takes so much concentration to manage it. Versus checking in with a teammate once a week for a coffee chat. So I think the >real< burn-out is still coming. The burn out people felt in 2022-2023 will be minor compared to what's coming. We're now orchestrating 10 AIs at SaaStr with a tiny team, and while I love it, I can already see hints on burn-out on our own tiny team here. It's an arms race in AI and a gold rush. But it will also leave many of us burnt like never before 18-24 months in. 996, 80+ hours a week intensely in office, keeping up with 100+ AI competitors doing daily releases ... it's exhilarating. It's necessary now in many cases to win and not fall behind. Necessary. But it can't really be sustainable ... Where that goes, I don't know.

The AI-native advantage is creating growth speeds that were literally impossible in traditional software.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The toughest job in SaaS and B2B might just be CMO. In the early days of a B2B start-up, marketing spend isn’t that complicated. Marketing itself might be a bit of a mystery in the early days, but the spend part typically isn’t. Because you make small bets. A few thousand on Adwords or Facebook, or Reddit ads. The smallest possible booth at just one event. Some limited joint marketing with partners. Maybe a few podcast ads in your industry. You try it with very small dollars, and if it actually works, you do more of it. And in the early days, most things don’t really work in marketing, so you often stop after an experiment. But as you scale, and as you acquire a mini-brand and then a real brand in your industry, it changes. Many things in marketing start to work. And you also see that some things do work that didn’t used to. ✅ Billboards? They seem dumb in the early days to most, but later you may find many of your top prospects saw them. ✅ A massive presence at a big industry event? Seems like a huge waste when you’re small. But later, you may see strong ROI from taking over the place. ✅ And other things like webinars, paid channels, etc. do work, but sometimes take 2x-10x longer to convert that a high-quality in-bound lead. So as you scale, and even hire a CMO, the marketing job becomes making a series of bets out of a fixed budget. Many B2B leaders spend 10%-30% of their new bookings on marketing, sometimes more if they are well funded. So if you want to add say +$30m in new bookings this year, you might spend $3m-$10m on marketing. That’s your head of marketing’s budget. ⏰ And the clock starts to tick. Because in the end, a head of marketing has a year or so to develop pipeline for sales. If they don’t generate enough, they are often … fired. Fair or not. Some of that pipeline has to come fast, but you’ll need to develop it over the course of the year. And you’ll need to reinforce that pipeline so more of it closes. So you make a series of bets, some short-term (digital), some more medium-term (enterprise leads, field marketing), and some to support momentum (branding, PR) across the year and beyond. But unless it’s a rocketship that truly exceeds expectations, the job quickly gets hard. If various marketing initiatives don’t achieve quick results, you can cut them all off. Then what if that leaves you with no new pipeline at all? If you say no to everything in marketing, you can lose your job by spending too little. And a new CMO with a proven playbook often wants to quickly deploy capital in marketing initiatives that worked in their last role. They can be tempted to overspend, they know the clock is ticking. I don’t have a magical answer here other that to understand the CMO’s job is complicated and a slow race against the clock. It’s why so many get fired around months 12-14. When it becomes clear their spend didn’t deliver the results intended -- or so often these days, when their lack of spend did the same.

content: If you hook up an AI SDR and go away and do nothing, you will get nothing. Zilch. Nada. Nothing. Will fail. If you hook up an AI SDR and * train it every day, * every single day, * and keep iterating on anything that works * and give yourself a month to nail it * and make sure you respond to every response it gets ASAP, not ghost prospects that actually respond * make sure the messaging is dynamic and A+, all of it * and audit and read the emails it sends every day * and watch what works and doesn’t every day * and QA the output yourself daily * and be honest is what it is outputting as good or better than a human Well then, it probably will work

They'll pretend a bit, send a few emails, but that's about it. 95% of sales reps that will do outbound ... will stop once they have enough inbound leads to hit their comp goals. 95% of sales reps don't really want to visit customers in person. Even many "enterprise" reps. And most will visit the fewest possible. Not all, but most. Most B2B sellers want to just work warm, qualified, in-bound leads and renewals. From home, ideally The full stack AE does exist, but in SaaS, it remains a rarity. If you want your sales team to do more, you have to hire exactly that.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: My biggest heartbreak ever as a founder: if my CTO and I could have gotten along better. Because we'd both be billionaires, running a great public company together. I tried. I know so much more today than I did then. I did everything I could, and we worked together from Day 1 through our exit and beyond. Even with not being able to work together well enough, we built a business with top 1% growth at its time. A business that scaled to hundreds of millions in revenue. But we could have gone so, so much further if we were both 100% there, together. 100% aligned. So this is why today I obsess about great CTOs and great CEO + CTO pairings when I invest. I'm out if there isn't a great CTO. And I'm out if they aren't as close as two founders can be. Because that team, a great CEO and an S-tier CTO ... it's so rare in SaaS and B2B. But when you have it, and you have any traction at all -- you can't be stopped. I'd be a billionaire if I could have gotten it to work better. I gave it all I could. I know better now. If you have an incredible partner here, as CTO, never let them go. Make it work. And to the S-tier CTOs out there? If your CEO is trying 110%, and they believe in you 110% ... maybe cut them a little slack ;). They are trying.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So many people are producing B2B content these days, let me just give my #1 bit of advice: 👍 If you truly think it's great, it may or may not perform that well. You'll see. 💣 But if you don't think it's great, it will bomb. Some of the best of our 1000s and 1000s of top speakers, blog posts, podcasts, etc. at SaaStr over the years haven't gotten the attention I would have hoped. Some more obscure start-ups and even public companies ... folks just don't engage with as much as they should. Sometimes I push hard to get folks to pay attention. When we did the first interview ever with Peter Gassner, CEO of Veeva, folks didn't totally get Vertical SaaS at the time. But it was an A++ discussion no one had done before. We pushed and pushed and over the years so many have learned from it. Pushing can help. But a dud? A dud just never performs, no matter how strong the brand even. At least I haven't seen it work. If you know it just not a great post, or interview, just put it away. Even today, Harry Stebbings still doesn't publish a number of interviews. In the early days, it was a pretty high percent. For SaaStr Annual, every year we let a few sessions in that I know are duds, but we do them as favors, or because the company is well known, but the content is terrible. They always bomb. I'm 100% right here. I've never seen a "Bomb" talk even from an A-tier CEO perform at SaaStr Annual. No one comes. A few years ago, 2 of my favorite, top-tier well-known CEOs came to SaaStr. The best of the best. But the topic was way too obscure and just not relevant to the audience. It was the worst attended of 300+ sessions. The #1 worst. One of the CEOs yelled at me. If you want to do more content, great. Do it. Just when you know it's not great. Take a pause and find a piece of content that you truly believe it. The odds are much higher it will have an impact.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's a wave of SaaS IPOs coming that are less discussed The ones that were >already< public, went private, & are waiting to IPO a second time. Zendesk, Squarespace, Smartsheet, Coupa, Anaplan, Avalara and dozens more are waiting to IPO. Again. First up: SailPoint. IPO'ing again at $820m ARR 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. SailPoint is accelerating. Cloud security remains very strong. * $820m in ARR * Growing 25%+ (financials are a bit complex) * 114% NRR, and going up * Very profitable (Rule of “44”) * With the founder still CEO after 20 years!! #2. $1m+ Customers Are The Focus Now If you do them right, big deals can be more efficient than smaller ones. And they are for SailPoint. It has 140 $1m+ customers. And that’s the biggest growth vector. #3. NRR Only Going Up, From 108% in 2023 to 113% Today. And a Stunning 95% GRR. SailPoint may be in efficiency mode as part of Private Equity, but that hasn’t led to a drop in NRR. In fact, it's gone up. And just as importantly, GRR is a stunning 97%. Folks just don’t leave SailPoint. Note: contracts are typically 3 years in length. That helps. #4. SaaS Business Growing 40% SailPoint has transitioned to SaaS, and it’s now 60% of its total ARR, up from 40% 3 years ago. These transitions can be confusing, but in any event, overall revenue is growing 25%-30%, and the SaaS-ification is going well. The SaaS business is growing 40%. #5. Founder Still CEO after 20 Years — Taking Company Public a Second Time! Private Equity firms sometimes bring in new CEOs, but often they keep the existing founder CEO if they want to stay. When Vista bought Gainsight, for example, Nick Mehta is still running it. But I don’t know of too many where the founder CEO is still CEO at the second IPO. This probably explains why NRR and retention are so high. I doubt an outside CEO would be able to keep an older player in the space current enough to keep so many customers after a PE buy-out. Mark McLain founded the company in 2005, took it public in 2017, got bought out in 2022 for $6.9 Billion — and is getting to go public again in 2025! I’m kind of jealous :)

content: The larger a check a VC writes, the lower the returns it needs from that check. This sounds wrong, but on balance, it’s correct. E.g., ⏩ Invest $1B in OpenAI, it 3x’s to $3B, VCs take home $400m+ of it themselves (20% of gains) ➡️ Invest $1m in a start-up and it 10x’s to $10m, VCs take home $1.8m of it themselves (20% of gains) Both investments honestly are about the same amount of work. But the first investment “only” needs to triple, and the VCs make 200x more. 200x more. This is a vast oversimplification many will poke holes in. There are a number of great examples of VCs making tons from owning a huge stake in a decacorn early. 👉But also, it explains why many top VC funds raise as many billions as humanly possible

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A top regret for many (even myself perhaps) is leaving anywhere on less than good terms. But why? Who really cares in 2025? No one does reference checks. No one will care if you quit with zero notice in 2022. No one will really check that you moved on and left your customers in the lurch. No one will care. Not many, at least. 🙋 Here's the simple reason it matters: the simplest way to get a new client, a new job, a new role, a new opportunity is a strong referral. If you leave on great terms, you can almost always email the CEO, the CTO, the CRO, whomever you worked with even years down the road and ask for help. For help with another client, another job, another part-time role, another opportunity. I'm literally still helping find new opportunities for many folks on our old team at Adobe Sign / EchoSign -- even a decade down the road. And look at the amazing places they've gone into leadership roles, from Rippling to Gong to Talkdesk to Brex to Cloudinary to MaestroQA and more. That's worth leaving on good terms for. You don't know when you'll need that referral. But I've found you almost always want it down the road, in some fashion. Myself included here. When the time comes to move on -- move on. Just slow it down. Talk about it. Be appreciative. Give 30 days notice, not 3 hours. Maybe even source your replacement. Leave how ... you'd want someone on your team to leave you. It pays off. Rarely this year or even next. But IMHE, so often down the road.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Something counterintuitive: it may be easier to sell your second product to 𝗻𝗲𝘄 customers than your 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 ones. It's a point I find many founders, CROs, CMOs and more get wrong. I got it wrong for a while too, until I started investing in and working with more vertical SaaS companies. And that is something somewhat counterintuitive: We've all learned we need to generally bring second products to market earlier than before, often as early as $10m ARR, to keep the engine going. And what we think we're often doing is building another product to sell to our existing customers. Which 9 times out of 10, you should. It's easier to sell an existing product to the same buyer than find a brand new buyer (although even that has nuances, as you max exhaust the budget your existing buyer has). But what many of us miss is the attach rate for second products is often higher on 𝗻𝗲𝘄 prospects. And it's for one simple reason: you often aren't asking them to switch. Let me give you an example from MangoMint, where I'm an investor. They are SaaS for spas and salons. They were the first in their category to add payroll, and it's gone well. But the attach rate for new customers is 50% higher than existing ones. Why? New SMB customers often don't already have a next-gen payroll platform in place. But the ones that have already been a customer for a year or two or more have already found a payroll vendor. I've now seen this to be the case many times: the attach rate for a second product is higher from new customers than existing ones. Just be aware of it. Most SaaS companies do a big push to cross-sell a new product into the base. But maybe save 20%-30% of that energy for marketing the combined product to new customers. That may be an easier sell. Somewhat counterintuitively.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: If you want to potentially get acquired — start now. It often really, quietly takes years. What do I mean? Well for sure, acquisitions themselves technically often happen very quickly. The acquiring CEO reaches out, they meet up and shake hands over the weekend, a term sheet is signed on Monday. It does happen that way all the time. From handshake to term sheet. But before that happens, there are often years of watching, learning, getting to know each other. Either directly or from a distance. My first start-up was acquired for $50m after 12.5 months. And the deal happened over a weekend. But we’d known each other, and competed, even longer than the start-up existed. For years. The second time, when Adobe acquired us, the deal again happened over a week or two. But we’ll known our deal lead for 5 years. Kept them updated. Went and met in person several times a year. And by email more often. The other day on the SaaStr podcast HubSpot chair and co-founder Brian Halligan said he kept potential acquirers updated by email consistently. Nurtured them. They never took an offer, or got one they really wanted, but he maintained that optionality. A BigCo buying a start-up is risky. It’s measured risk, but risky. The more you know the company you are buying, and its leaders, the less risky it is. If you want to even just keep options open to be acquired … nurture those leads. Over years, in fact.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Looking to be a VP of Sales in 2025 for the first time? Here are my Top 5+ Tips to make sure you succeed. #1. Don’t lower the bar on hiring. Almost every first-time VP of Sales does this, across almost every portfolio company and every startup I’ve worked with. The pressure is on the day you start as a new VP of Sales. The clock may be ticking to get some AEs and SDRs in the door, but you are still better off making sure whomever you hire is truly strong enough. Way too many first-time VPs of Sales I see make check-the-box hires — often because they aren’t sure they are senior enough to attract top talent. But then those hires often perform worse than the handful of existing reps. This is especially risky for any first-time VP of Sales who has never built a strong team under them before. #2. As you scale, you’ll have to hire managers better than you. And often more experienced. If you want to scale past 18-24 months as a VP of Sales, you are probably going to have to hire a few managers under you that know more than you, and are arguably “better”. But if you don’t, you won’t be able to scale. Yes, that’s hard. But it’s the job. You’re the boss. Your job isn’t to know everything and have every single skill. That’s why you’ll have to hire a few managers under you that do. #3. Be positive but honest with the CEO Way too many VPs of Sales, first time and 10th time, overpromise to the CEO. And / or hide misses. It only makes things worse. Be positive but transparent. If the CEO doesn’t have your back — then at least you know. Too many first-timers especially try to hide things when they fall behind. Or make crazy promises they’ll make up the gap in Q4. This just leads ultimately to an exit — for the VP of Sales. Don’t Hide Stuff. #4. Do a Real 30-60-90 Plan. And get the CEO to Agree To It. Many founders skip this and don’t push anymore. That doesn’t help you. You’ll start off disaligned without realizing it. 5. Know the Product Cold Before You Start There just isn’t time to wing it once you start. Don’t start until you can truly sell it yourself. Push off your start date, if need be. It’s better. 6. Get the CEO To Give You a Prospect Meetings-Per-Month Commit Say 10 meetings a month, 2.5 a week, they'll join. Too many founder CEOs exit sales once they hire a VP of Sales. That’s bad for both of you. So get a commit. To attend 10 customer meetings a month on Zoom, and say 6-10 a quarter IRL. You pick the meetings, they come if they can. This is magical. It really, really works.

content: Have we lost interest in investing in human sales? It sort of seems like it. AI has hardly disrupted the sales professional. Salesforce itself is hiring 2,000 sales execs this year to … sell its AI platform, AgentForce. At most B2B companies, 35%+ of the headcount is in sales and it’s often the largest functional area. And yet, there’s one thing that’s clearly changed the past 18 months. For the most part, folks seem done investing in more productivity for their humans. Unless it leverages AI. In 2021, everyone bought 100 new sales and revenue apps to keep the sales engine humming. Today, SaaS and growth are back, but it’s a new SaaS. We want our sales team to just work with the tools and platforms they already have. And our energy to invest in sales is very AI and automation focused. 2021 was peak Gong-Calendly-Zoominfo-Outreach-etc. At least of those versions of those apps and use cases. 2025 won’t be the death of the AI or even the SDR. But it may be the peak of looking for AI to supplement them, rather than adding tools to just make sales execs work better. We may be building Mech AEs. Surrounded and powered by AI, making them much more powerful than before. ZoomInfo already is off to $100m of its AI Copilot.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Now that time has gone by, I'm 100% sure that the worst mis-hire is CTO / VP Engineering. Because it becomes the death of innovation. I've seen this fact pattern or some variant thereof so many times: * Founder CEO + CTO * CTO gets start-up to $5m, $10m, $20m but just "can't scale" * VP of Engineering or CTO from Big Tech Company hired * Everyone chooses the Nice Candidate * The Nice Candidate never codes, never learns the code base, never gets the magic * The Nice Candidate hires a bunch of engineers under them that aren't great and never know the customers or the why At first, things seem better. Things are more organized under The Nice VP of Engineering. There are a lot more discussions. Fewer erratic changes. Releases are smoother. And ... innovation just ends. This VP of Eng / CTO never knows the magic, the why, or the how. And the competition pulls ahead. And even worse, the founding CTO often either leaves or disengages. And the magic is lost. Even at Adobe Sign / EchoSign, my last start-up, my co-founder and CTO is still at Adobe. Why? Because they know even at $200m+ ARR they still need him. He wrote all the original code base, and the original magic. They don't need him for everything. But when they need him -- they really need him. Even today. 👔 I have a rule: never hire a CTO that wears a suit (or tie). It's always a sign they are selling up, rather than being a hacker. You need a hacker at the head of engineering. Maybe forever. 🔟 / 🔟 And whatever you do, when the time comes to hire an outside VP Eng / CTO, try to make sure you and your co-founder both are 100% aligned they are a 10/10. An epic hacker and engineer, not just a manager. Managers are a dime a dozen today. And they can't win in engineering in a world that is more competitive than ever. When I see this happening, I fight. I fight to help the founders see it. I go down with the fight. Because when you hire a VP Eng / CTO that isn't a 10, it's the day your start-up starts to die. The other VPs, if you make a mis-hire, you can recover. But 2 years of no more innovation? I don't know if most of us can fight our way back from that.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So Figma stock has had a wild ride since its IPO. But the business itself? Man, it's delivered. It's now crossed $1B in ARR growing a stunning 41% (!). And it's generating massive free cash flow. 5 Interesting Learnings: 1️⃣ Enterprise Customers Continue to Accelerate at Scale, Now Top Segment 1,119 customers paying $100K+ ARR, up from 963 last quarter (that's +16% QoQ growth!). This segment now represents the fastest-growing customer cohort. Why This Matters: At $1B+ ARR run rate, growth increasingly comes from land-and-expand with large enterprises rather than new logo acquisition. The $100K+ cohort represents less than 10% of total paid customers but likely drives 40-60% of revenue. 2️⃣ NDR Consistency at Billion-Dollar Scale. 129% = A Strong Future to Come. 129% NDR (for customers with $10K+ ARR), holding steady between 125-134% for six consecutive quarters. Why This Matters: Many B2B companies see NDR compression as they scale due to law of large numbers. Maintaining 129% NDR at $1B+ run rate means existing customers are growing 29% annually from expansion alone, before any new customer acquisition. Figma has an epic run of 30%+ growth ahead of it, just as long as it keeps NRR up at this rate. 3️⃣ 41% Growth Rate at Billion-Dollar Run Rate -- That's About As Good At It Gets in SaaS $250M quarterly revenue (41% YoY growth), guiding to $1.021-1.025B for full year. Most of the top tier $1B+ ARR B2B companies see growth rates of 25-30%. Figma’s 41% growth at this scale puts them with companies like Snowflake and MongoDB during peak growth phases. 4️⃣ $100k+ Customers Are The Growth Engine, But $10k-$100K Are The Fuel Figma has 11,906 customers paying $10K+ ARR vs 1,119 paying $100K+ ARR. This means 10,787 customers are in the $10K-$100K range. This $10K-$100K segment represents Figma’s expansion opportunity. These customers have demonstrated significant commitment but haven’t reached full enterprise scale yet. 5️⃣ Insane Growth AND Insane Free Cash Flow 24% free cash flow margins! 5% non-GAAP operating margins in Q2, down from 18% in Q1, but full-year guide suggests 9-10% operating margins by year-end. Rule of 40: 41% growth + 5% operating margins = 46% Rule of 40 performance while investing in future growth drivers. Rule of 64 if use Free Cash Flow. 🔮 The big question is does AI benefit Figma in the end? A net neutral? Or create new big competitors? We shall see. But it looks like a tailwind for Figma, not a headwind.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: 100% of the start-ups I’ve worked with where the Founder CEO quit are struggling hard right now. When times change quickly (like now with AI), few can make that change as deeply and radically as a founder can. I don’t think any of them will really make it without the founder CEO running the place. When times are easy, demand is strong, and change is limited, any professional CEO can run the place. It’s knobs and dials. Not an easy job per se, but one mainly of tweaking what already mostly worked. Today there’s no chance. So I know it’s tough. But before you quit, before you leave the keys on the table … make sure you are 100% OK with your start-up / company failing if you leave as founder CEO. Because it probably will IMHE in any highly dynamic environment. Not overnight. Recurring revenue does recur. But fail nevertheless over time.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So before we had AI, we had automation 😉 Of course, we still have plenty of automation. So much of business software in the end is about automation. But AI has begun to change everything here. And before AI, RPA was revolutionary. Robotic Process Automation. Call it fancy scripts if you want, but UiPath is the clear leader here and after struggling for 10 years to get to the first $1m in ARR, then exploding to $1B (!) in ARR in less than 8 years after. Wow. If you needed to automate data entry, data extraction, and so much more from older software especially, UiPath was the answer. And it was and is magical. But it’s also right in the crosshairs of AI. And so that hypergrowth … has slowed. Dramatically. At $1.5B ARR, it was still growing 31%. At $1.7B ARR? Just … 5%. Today, UiPath is at: ➡️ $1.7B ARR ➡️ Growing 5% ➡️ 32% non-GAAP margins, so very profitable But will UiPath have an answer to the AI Age? We’ll see. It’s been so much change, so quickly. For all of us. But especially — for UiPath. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. NRR Holding at 110%. And a Stunning 98% GRR. A reminder that enterprise software is very sticky. Even with so much change, NRR remains 110%. And no one leaves, not really. GRR is a stunning 98%. But that NRR is down from 145% at $600m ARR and 123% at $1.2B in ARR. #2. Still Growing Its $1m and $100k+ Customers Materially I can’t quite get this math to tie to the 110% NRR (which isn’t a GAAP metric), but in any event, UiPath is still growing its customer count. It’s grown its $100k+ customers +10% to 2,292 over the past 12 months, and now had 317 $1m+ customers, also up +10%. Pretty impressive. #3. Dramatically Cut Sales & Marketing — But Investing Much More in Engineering and Product If growth slows, one option is to invest even more in sales — what Salesforce is doing. Another is to cut sales & marketing to focus on existing customers and select logos, and potentially, to put that money into product. UiPath is doing the latter path, materially cutting sales & marketing expense, but boosting engineering and product materially. Going long here. It’s probably not a coincidence this is happening after founder Daniel Dines returned as CEO. #4. 2%-3% Dilution Target Per Year UiPath is still investing in engineering and with that, equity. This is a relatively standard amount of dilution for a public tech company, but perhaps more than one might expect for one growing 5% that could buy back stock to offset it. UiPath is still investing in the future, not just the present. #5. Leaning Deep Into Agents As they should be. But will UiPath be where more enterprises want to get them from? We will see!

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So there’s a lot of angst on LinkedIn about CROs and VPs of Sales getting fired. But let me tell you a tip: maybe go SMB. What do I mean? I see so many of the top sales leaders that started SMB stay 6, 7, 8+ years at leading tech companies in VP and CRO level roles. Again and again and again. Why? You just get more at bats, more chances. If you sell $3k deals, to hit a $600k quota, that’s 200 deals. Per rep. If you manage even a tiny team, that still can be 1000s of deals a year. You get better — fast — if you care. 1000s deals is a lot. Compare that to coming in as a CRO at a solely enterprise play that’s still early. You might work on just a few deals really at a time, with long sales cycles. You might never get a chance to truly learn. And if even a few push, sales might even go down under your watch at first. SMB sales really can lead to longevity if you keep at it. You just get so, so many at bats. So quickly.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: So last year just before SaaStr Annual a top CRO speaker cancelled at the very last minute. From a top B2B company we all know. It happens. This used to stress us out in the early days but now we have so much redundancy across the schedule that it doesn’t matter when someone drops. But it was weird. Literally the day before, a CRO that lived a few minutes away in the SF Bay cancelled with zero reason or notice. That doesn’t happen too often. Then the other day the CEO reached out to me. He wanted to speak at SaaStr Annual this year. Great. It would be a great AI-centric session. He had just one question: “What happened last year with my CRO? Is there some sort of bad blood with SaaStr?” My ears certainly pricked up. That’s not us. We thought … he’d canceled on us! Well eventually someone on their team forwarded an email the CRO was sent by an extended part of our team. And my heart just sank. 🤷‍♀️ Literally it was an email no one should have ever sent. It was rude, condescending, and didn’t value their time at all. It turned out, we’d canceled the CRO at the last minute! It wasn’t send by our core team, but it was send by someone in our brand. Using a saastr email. So from any third party’s perspective, it was still … from us. So what’s my point here? I guess it’s around trust and macro-managing. I trust everyone 100% on the team. All I ask for is a weekly status update and coming to the team meetings. Other than that, I trust you. Go forth and conquer! But someone on our core team should have read these emails. Should have monitored them. Should have seen they weren’t representing our values or brand. It was a reminder. You gotta read the emails, listen to the Gongs, and watch the Zooms. For your top performers, it gives you a chance to maybe backfill a bit. For the non top performers, well, it gives you a chance to spot issues. And issues there always are.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There's lot of debate about how big you have to be to IPO today. The last 4 SaaS IPOs were all at $500m+ ARR: Rubrik, OneStream, Klaviyo and Sailpoint. But that's hasn't always been true. One that IPO'd at < $200m ARR is Similarweb Today they're at ➡️ $260m ARR ➡️ Growing 16% ➡️ 112% NRR ➡️ 11% FCF ➡️ And Trading at $841m or ~3.2x ARR 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Growth is Modest, But is Re-Accelerating Similarweb’s growth isn’t the 25%+ that Wall Street likes to see at this size, but it is re-accelerating, from a low of 11% in Q4’23 to 16% today. #2. Growing Net New Customer Count as Fast as Revenue (17%) Similarweb is keeping net new customer growth at almost 20%. That's impressive at $200m+ ARR and positions it well for a good run of growth in the future. Too many mature SaaS companies these days that are at lower growth rates get almost all their growth from the base. From price hikes and more. Similarweb is still earning its new customers. #3. Deal Sizes Coming Down, Which Pressures ARR Growth While customer count growth is strong, and NRR is good (101% for smaller customers, 112% for $100k+ deals), the overall deal size is down. This is in part due to more smaller customers, but likely also in part due to contractions. $100k+ deals are still growing in number and ACV (next point). But the smaller customers are smaller and smaller, leading to 16% net growth in revenue. #4. $100k+ Deals a Big Push This is true almost across the board, from Monday to HubSpot to Asana to Procore to Pagerduty and more. #5. CAC Elevated, Acquisition Costs Up From Historical Norms Similarweb has gotten a lot more efficient, but not by driving down CACs. Right now CACs are at 21-22 months, up from 15-16 months historically. And a bonus learning: #6. Like Many, Radically More Efficient Than Just 2 Years Ago In 2022, Similarweb had -33% non-GAAP operating margins. Today? +6%. That’s a huge swing toward efficiency. And it came by cutting costs in every department. Still, its market cap >hasn't< benefitted. It's still half of what it was at IPO. The markets still value growth and scale over efficiency. You need efficiency today too post-IPO. But alone, it's not enough.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: It used to be in SaaS and B2B, when you went to hire your first VPs … there just weren’t enough of them. It felt like there was no way you could get to, let alone convince, execs at leading SaaS and B2B companies to join you. It seemed almost impossible to even get the attention of senior folks at the top players. Fast forward to day, the market is flooded with seasoned candidates. The question you have to ask now that they are out there is — do they still really want it? Do they have the fire? Building, competing, winning, crafting an A+ team … it’s really hard. Not everyone is honestly up for doing it again. Many aren’t. There are a few days a quarter I'm not even up for it anymore myself. I get it. It's just, you can't hire them. The world is too fast and too competitive today. You have to hire VPs that still truly have the fire. That truly, really want it. That are already building their teams -- now -- because they're ready to go. That are overflowing with ideas -- before they start. The ones that aren't sure they want to do it again, many do have incredible experience. Ask them about it, learn from it. But you can't hire them as your VPs and CXOs at your start-up. They need to be somewhere more mature.
