Spotify 👉 https://lnkd.in/eDd_6w5g Youtube 👉 https://lnkd.in/e62CEP_c Apple Podcasts 👉 https://lnkd.in/eqAudSGm My 8 takeaways with Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll 👇 1. How a16z Do 3x On Their New Fund Size? - a16z raised $15B, about 20% of total venture capital raised. - Exits hit roughly $300B this year, making 3x returns mathematically possible. - With IPOs coming, the market may absorb big funds without breaking. 2. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. Why The Wealth Tax In California Being Proposed Is Much Worse Than It Seems - This wealth tax is a Trojan horse, not a one-time hit. - The real plan is an annual tax on $25–$50M of paper wealth. - It risks pushing founders to leave long before liquidity. 8. To Do ElevenLabs At $11 Billion, You Have To Believe... - An $11B deal assumes a large, distributed customer base. - Not a few power users, but many real adopters paying. - The bet is that this proven trend keeps scaling for years. hashtag #founder hashtag #funding hashtag #business hashtag #investing hashtag #vc hashtag #entrepreneur hashtag #startup hashtag #investment hashtag #20VC Captions are auto generated Play Loaded: 24.44% Remaining time 1:20 1x Playback speed Turn closed captions off Unmute Turn fullscreen on In the early stage, you're taking uncorrelated business 25 4 comments Like Comment Repost Send

How a16z Do 3x On Their New Fund Size? - a16z raised $15B, about 20% of total venture capital raised. - Exits hit roughly $300B this year, making 3x returns mathematically possible. - With IPOs coming, the market may absorb big funds without breaking. 2. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. There Are Only Two Types of Companies - Private companies: either hypergrowth or effectively unfundable in today’s market. - Public companies: only accelerating businesses matter, not ones that are slowing. - If you’re not clearly improving fast, it’s not worth the time. 2. The Shift From Being Valued on Revenue Multiples to Free Cash Flow - When investors are comparing you to steady industries, it’s a huge valuation reset. - It will take years of flat stock price and reasonable growth before you can be worth 10-15x FCF. - You don’t see a bottom until these stocks trade at free cash flow multiples net of dilution. 3. NVIDIA Would Have to Bail Out OpenAI - If NVIDIA can afford it, they have to bail out OpenAI if they stumble. - Other competitors like Anthropic are already diversifying to TPUs and AWS. - OpenAI is too big to fail. 4. The Dispersion Between Old and Low Growth and New and High Growth in Terms of Valuation Has Never Been More - We are seeing a heightened dispersion: low-growth companies are at 3x, and high-growth companies are at 50-100x. - New & exciting companies are getting insane multiples, while old & boring companies are going down. - A lot of software companies are moving to old & boring. 5. Why the $100BN Paid for Waymo Is Actually Cheap - Tesla’s market cap is ~$1.2TN. Assume the $100BN car business is valued at 2x revenue = $200BN. - That leaves ~$1TN for non-car assets. - Assuming a 50/50 split between Optimus & self-driving = ~$500BN each. - Waymo’s $100BN looks cheap compared to Tesla’s $500BN. 6. Is the Elon Premium on SpaceX Justified? - SpaceX had ~$15BN revenue in ‘24 and ~$18BN in ‘25, growing ~30%. - The market is valuing it at ~50x run-rate revenue. - It feels like 80% of the value is the Elon premium, and 20% of the value is the actual business. hashtag #founder hashtag #funding hashtag #business hashtag #investing hashtag #vc hashtag #entrepreneur hashtag #startup hashtag #investment hashtag #20VC Captions are auto generated Play Loaded: 30.25% Remaining time 1:04 1x Playback speed Turn closed captions off Unmute Turn fullscreen on Would you prefer to be a SpaceX investor taking 20% 19 1 comment 2 reposts Like Comment Repost Send

Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. There Are Only Two Types of Companies - Private companies: either hypergrowth or effectively unfundable in today’s market. - Public companies: only accelerating businesses matter, not ones that are slowing. - If you’re not clearly improving fast, it’s not worth the time. 2. The Dispersion Between Old and Low Growth and New and High Growth in Terms of Valuation Has Never Been More - We are seeing a heightened dispersion: low-growth companies are at 3x, and high-growth companies are at 50-100x. - New & exciting companies are getting insane multiples, while old & boring companies are going down. - A lot of software companies are moving to old & boring. 5. Why the $100BN Paid for Waymo Is Actually Cheap - Tesla’s market cap is ~$1.2TN. Assume the $100BN car business is valued at 2x revenue = $200BN. - That leaves ~$1TN for non-car assets. - Assuming a 50/50 split between Optimus & self-driving = ~$500BN each. - Waymo’s $100BN looks cheap compared to Tesla’s $500BN. 6. Why Did Nvidia Spend 20BN on Groq - NVIDIA has the world’s largest market cap, making a complex technical product, and charging a small number of customers 75% gross margins. - The last thing they need is someone who can make a vaguely comparable product – and that is Groq. - Buying up a competitor & eliminating that potential margin pressure for less than 1% of market cap & 20% annual free cash flow is worth it. 3. Can the World Support Ten New AGI Labs or Not? - We don’t know if we have enough new territory in AI that won’t be annexed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and other big labs. - New labs will need to meaningfully differentiate themselves to justify multi-billion dollar valuations. - It will be interesting to see if the world can support 10 research labs with 10 different variants of AI. 4. Why OpenAI Has the Largest Stock Based Comp of Any Company Ever? - If you are the CEO with zero shares, you do not worry about dilution. - Sam wants to build the greatest AI company. - If he needs to use equity for hiring & retention, it does not impact him as a shareholder. 5. You Can Identify a Top 0.1% Founder Without Ever Speaking to Them - I have had multiple billion-dollar exits from cold inbound deals. - I analyze the inbound & measure the quality of the founder. - It is not a leap of faith to imagine an AI could do a better job. 6. The "Supply Chain Risk" Weaponization The Department of Defense’s designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk is a massive escalation. While the immediate loss is a $200 million contract, the real "blast radius" is the potential to freeze the company out of the broader B2B economy. 2. Ambiguity is a B2B Deal Killer In enterprise sales, risk doesn't have to be certain to be fatal: it only has to be ambiguous. Anthropic’s already seeing deals cut in half or stalling because prospects fear government exposure. Competitors like OpenAI are reportedly capitalizing on this by positioning themselves as the "no-problem" alternative. 3. The Death of the Junior Employee We are entering a "world of the middle of the bell curve" regarding experience. Companies no longer want to spend 3–6 months training juniors when AI tools can provide instant, senior-level productivity. This isn't just a theory; Computer Science and Math graduates from solid state schools are already seeing "zero jobs" as companies stop hiring entry level jobs. 4. 24/7 Persistent AI is the Real Compute Driver Most people are currently using AI for episodic tasks (chatting, coding for an hour). But the next frontier is 24/7 persistent AI agents that watch, listen, and run in the background of your entire life. Moving from one agent to 50 agents running in parallel 24 hours a day will require orders of magnitude more compute than we have today. 5. The End of "Gentle Deceleration" In the public markets, the era of managing a polite, high-margin slowdown is dead. Investors are now brutally punishing any company that isn't actively re-accelerating. If you aren't showing CloudFlare-level acceleration or better, the public markets have effectively abandoned you. 6. Built-in Distribution vs. Product Velocity Wix is a fascinating lab experiment for the AI age. They have 6.1 million customers to cross-sell to, which helped their new AI product, Base 44, hit $100 million ARR. However, if that $100M doesn’t exponentially compound to $600M+ quickly, it won't be enough to offset the 1-2% decline in their core legacy business. 7. "Agent-Led Growth" is the New PLG The startups seeing "lines out the door" right now are the ones offering wholesale human replacement.. Founders should be building agents that are 90% better than humans in specific categories like GTM or support. When they can deliver that, the "budget magically comes out of nowhere". "Priced for Perfection" is a Dangerous Game When cybersecurity stocks dropped $20BN following an Anthropic feature release, it wasn't just about the tech; it was about the math. Rory notes that when companies trade at 16x–22x revenues, markets assume "perfection". In this environment, any "increase in tail risk" or a narrative shift leads to a brutal correction. 2. The "Fortnite" Circle is Shrinking for Software Jason uses a powerful analogy: Claude is like the game Fortnite: the safe territory for standalone software is shrinking as AI consumes more features. If your product can be "vibe coded" or exists purely as a feature within a browser or desktop, your surface area is under direct threat from foundation models. 3. Agents > "AI Dust" Incumbents struggle because they merely "sprinkle AI dust" on old analytics. To win, you must own the agent layer for your category. Real agents require custom training and data cleansing—complex work most firms aren't equipped to handle yet. 4. Great Productivity, Brutal Transition Productivity gains are "fricking awesome" long-term , but "Ghost GDP" warns of a "macroeconomic shock". If millions are displaced in months rather than decades, the pace of AI adoption may outstrip society's ability to adjust. 5. The "Toby Playbook" vs. Draconian Cuts Shopify has grown revenue by 50% to $12B without adding a single net headcount in three years. This is the "new normal." While healthy firms can hold headcount flat, Rory warns that highly levered, PE-backed SaaS companies may soon face "traumatic surgery": drastic 50% layoffs just to service their debt. 6. The Era of "Frankenstein" B2B Consolidation What happens to the $50M ARR unicorns with no acquirers? Jason predicts a "capitulation" where 5–20 startups are mashed together at "nominal prices" (1x–2x revenue) to create profitable, professionalized entities. It’s a "miserable way to consolidate debt," but it may be the only play left for many. 7. Momentum is the Only Play (For Now) In a state of total flux, value investing is out; momentum is in. The "Supply Chain Risk" Weaponization The Department of Defense’s designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk is a massive escalation. While the immediate loss is a $200 million contract, the real "blast radius" is the potential to freeze the company out of the broader B2B economy. 2. Ambiguity is a B2B Deal Killer In enterprise sales, risk doesn't have to be certain to be fatal: it only has to be ambiguous. Anthropic’s already seeing deals cut in half or stalling because prospects fear government exposure. Competitors like OpenAI are reportedly capitalizing on this by positioning themselves as the "no-problem" alternative. 3. The Death of the Junior Employee We are entering a "world of the middle of the bell curve" regarding experience. Companies no longer want to spend 3–6 months training juniors when AI tools can provide instant, senior-level productivity. This isn't just a theory; Computer Science and Math graduates from solid state schools are already seeing "zero jobs" as companies stop hiring entry level jobs. 4. 24/7 Persistent AI is the Real Compute Driver Most people are currently using AI for episodic tasks (chatting, coding for an hour). But the next frontier is 24/7 persistent AI agents that watch, listen, and run in the background of your entire life. Moving from one agent to 50 agents running in parallel 24 hours a day will require orders of magnitude more compute than we have today. 5. The End of "Gentle Deceleration" In the public markets, the era of managing a polite, high-margin slowdown is dead. Investors are now brutally punishing any company that isn't actively re-accelerating. If you aren't showing CloudFlare-level acceleration or better, the public markets have effectively abandoned you. 6. Built-in Distribution vs. Product Velocity Wix is a fascinating lab experiment for the AI age. They have 6.1 million customers to cross-sell to, which helped their new AI product, Base 44, hit $100 million ARR. However, if that $100M doesn’t exponentially compound to $600M+ quickly, it won't be enough to offset the 1-2% decline in their core legacy business. 7. "Agent-Led Growth" is the New PLG The startups seeing "lines out the door" right now are the ones offering wholesale human replacement.. Founders should be building agents that are 90% better than humans in specific categories like GTM or support. When they can deliver that, the "budget magically comes out of nowhere". "Priced for Perfection" is a Dangerous Game When cybersecurity stocks dropped $20BN following an Anthropic feature release, it wasn't just about the tech; it was about the math. Rory notes that when companies trade at 16x–22x revenues, markets assume "perfection". In this environment, any "increase in tail risk" or a narrative shift leads to a brutal correction. 2. The "Fortnite" Circle is Shrinking for Software Jason uses a powerful analogy: Claude is like the game Fortnite: the safe territory for standalone software is shrinking as AI consumes more features. If your product can be "vibe coded" or exists purely as a feature within a browser or desktop, your surface area is under direct threat from foundation models. 3. Agents > "AI Dust" Incumbents struggle because they merely "sprinkle AI dust" on old analytics. To win, you must own the agent layer for your category. Real agents require custom training and data cleansing—complex work most firms aren't equipped to handle yet. 4. Great Productivity, Brutal Transition Productivity gains are "fricking awesome" long-term , but "Ghost GDP" warns of a "macroeconomic shock". If millions are displaced in months rather than decades, the pace of AI adoption may outstrip society's ability to adjust. 5. The "Toby Playbook" vs. Draconian Cuts Shopify has grown revenue by 50% to $12B without adding a single net headcount in three years. This is the "new normal." While healthy firms can hold headcount flat, Rory warns that highly levered, PE-backed SaaS companies may soon face "traumatic surgery": drastic 50% layoffs just to service their debt. 6. The Era of "Frankenstein" B2B Consolidation What happens to the $50M ARR unicorns with no acquirers? Jason predicts a "capitulation" where 5–20 startups are mashed together at "nominal prices" (1x–2x revenue) to create profitable, professionalized entities. It’s a "miserable way to consolidate debt," but it may be the only play left for many. 7. Momentum is the Only Play (For Now) In a state of total flux, value investing is out; momentum is in. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. Why The Wealth Tax In California Being Proposed Is Much Worse Than It Seems - This wealth tax is a Trojan horse, not a one-time hit. - The real plan is an annual tax on $25–$50M of paper wealth. - It risks pushing founders to leave long before liquidity. 8. How a16z Do 3x On Their New Fund Size? - a16z raised $15B, about 20% of total venture capital raised. - Exits hit roughly $300B this year, making 3x returns mathematically possible. - With IPOs coming, the market may absorb big funds without breaking. 2. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. Why The Wealth Tax In California Being Proposed Is Much Worse Than It Seems - This wealth tax is a Trojan horse, not a one-time hit. - The real plan is an annual tax on $25–$50M of paper wealth. - It risks pushing founders to leave long before liquidity. 8. Everyone Is Coming for Nvidia Now - Whether it’s buying from AMD, partnering with Broadcom, building your own chips… - NVIDIA’s numbers will still crush this year. - But we will likely see the competitive pressure start to build. 2. Why Did Nvidia Spend 20BN on Groq - NVIDIA has the world’s largest market cap, making a complex technical product, and charging a small number of customers 75% gross margins. - The last thing they need is someone who can make a vaguely comparable product – and that is Groq. - Buying up a competitor & eliminating that potential margin pressure for less than 1% of market cap & 20% annual free cash flow is worth it. 3. Can the World Support Ten New AGI Labs or Not? - We don’t know if we have enough new territory in AI that won’t be annexed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and other big labs. - New labs will need to meaningfully differentiate themselves to justify multi-billion dollar valuations. - It will be interesting to see if the world can support 10 research labs with 10 different variants of AI. 4. Why OpenAI Has the Largest Stock Based Comp of Any Company Ever? - If you are the CEO with zero shares, you do not worry about dilution. - Sam wants to build the greatest AI company. - If he needs to use equity for hiring & retention, it does not impact him as a shareholder. 5. You Can Identify a Top 0.1% Founder Without Ever Speaking to Them - I have had multiple billion-dollar exits from cold inbound deals. - I analyze the inbound & measure the quality of the founder. - It is not a leap of faith to imagine an AI could do a better job. 6. No politics. Just tech. - SpaceX Completes $1.25TRN XAI Acquisition - The 2026 SaaS Massacre: Public Market Collapse - Microsoft's $360 Billion Market Cap Loss - NVIDIA's $100BN Investment Dispute with OpenAI - Waymo Raises $16 Billion at a $110 Billion Valuation Spotify 👉 https://lnkd.in/e-ZqhrF7 Youtube 👉 https://lnkd.in/eT28C6vp Apple Podcasts 👉 https://lnkd.in/e2DAq5pa My 6 takeaways with Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll 👇 1. There Are Only Two Types of Companies - Private companies: either hypergrowth or effectively unfundable in today’s market. - Public companies: only accelerating businesses matter, not ones that are slowing. - If you’re not clearly improving fast, it’s not worth the time. 2. The Shift From Being Valued on Revenue Multiples to Free Cash Flow - When investors are comparing you to steady industries, it’s a huge valuation reset. - It will take years of flat stock price and reasonable growth before you can be worth 10-15x FCF. - You don’t see a bottom until these stocks trade at free cash flow multiples net of dilution. 3. NVIDIA Would Have to Bail Out OpenAI - If NVIDIA can afford it, they have to bail out OpenAI if they stumble. - Other competitors like Anthropic are already diversifying to TPUs and AWS. - OpenAI is too big to fail. 4. The Dispersion Between Old and Low Growth and New and High Growth in Terms of Valuation Has Never Been More - We are seeing a heightened dispersion: low-growth companies are at 3x, and high-growth companies are at 50-100x. - New & exciting companies are getting insane multiples, while old & boring companies are going down. - A lot of software companies are moving to old & boring. 5. Why the $100BN Paid for Waymo Is Actually Cheap - Tesla’s market cap is ~$1.2TN. Assume the $100BN car business is valued at 2x revenue = $200BN. - That leaves ~$1TN for non-car assets. - Assuming a 50/50 split between Optimus & self-driving = ~$500BN each. - Waymo’s $100BN looks cheap compared to Tesla’s $500BN. 6. Is the Elon Premium on SpaceX Justified? - SpaceX had ~$15BN revenue in ‘24 and ~$18BN in ‘25, growing ~30%. - The market is valuing it at ~50x run-rate revenue. - It feels like 80% of the value is the Elon premium, and 20% of the value is the actual business. hashtag #founder hashtag #funding hashtag #business hashtag #investing hashtag #vc hashtag #entrepreneur hashtag #startup hashtag #investment hashtag #20VC Captions are auto generated Play Loaded: 5.97% Remaining time 1:06 1x Playback speed Turn closed captions off Unmute Turn fullscreen on 19 1 comment 2 reposts

Why Anthropic Will Go Out at $500BN for the IPO - Databricks is currently trading at 20x multiple. - Assuming Anthropic hit $25BN ARR next year. $25BN x 20 = $500BN - Even if they’ve just raised at $350BN, it’s still a good IRR for investors. 2. This Is Why Harvey Deal Is Simple; Just Do the Deal - They have 178% NRR and 98% logo retention. - Their revenue tripled from $50M to $150M in one year. - It’s a no-brainer. 3. Will the Models Come After the App Layer, the Simple Test? - If you are investing in an AI app, try and recreate it using the core model. - Build a functional version of the app as simply as you can. - If you are anywhere close to it, you need to pause. 4. Why Are Model Companies Not Fated to Be the Same Business as Airlines - Airlines have high fixed costs, and they are easy to switch. - But it is not an awful business. - If antitrust allows, we could see model companies consolidate. 5. Open Source Chinese Models Are a Real Threat and Are Used by the Best Silicon Valley Startups - Many startups claiming their own LLM actually rely on cheap Chinese open source models. - They are a fraction of the cost & good enough. - It is a real threat. 6. How Do You Value Companies When They Re-Accelerate - When companies start re-accelerating at scale, the valuation model breaks. - When Anthropic re-accelerated this year, everyone realized the model was wrong. - That’s why we saw a step-function increase in valuation. 2. Analysis of Eventbrite Acquisition by Bending Spoons - Two points: - 1. The public-company reality: Slow-growth public companies with low valuations become vulnerable to these acquisitions. - 2. Investors with smart money thinks these businesses are still worth buying. - It’s very likely PE firms would buy these companies, pair them with a sharp AI startup, and bring back 20% growth. 3. The TAM Trap and What It Means for Startups and Public Companies - B2B SaaS founders used to have 4-5 years to figure it out & grow out of their small TAMs. - Now, the average public SaaS company is growing at 16% YoY. - We’ve never grown more slowly. 4. Why SaaS Is Like Japan - It’s a great economy, but the population is shrinking. - There are only so many seats to go around. 5. What It Takes to Get to $100M ARR Faster Than Ever - Startups are reaching $100M ARR faster than ever & we don’t care how they get there. - You cannot hire 1,000 people & brute force your way to $100M ARR in 10 months any more. - You need massive inbound demand and AI leverage to hit that pace. 6. The Future of Labour Markets Is Fucked - Big companies aren’t hiring because they need to be efficient. - Model companies are only hiring a small number of geniuses. - Small AI app startups are growing so quickly that they can’t hire fast enough. hashtag #founder hashtag #funding hashtag #business hashtag #investing hashtag #vc hashtag #entrepreneur hashtag #startup hashtag #investment hashtag #20VC …more Captions are auto generated Play 19 3 comments 1 repost

Just tech. - Anthropic vs The Pentagon: Who Wins - The Data Centre Arms Race: Is the Capex War Stalling - The Era of Public Company Deceleration is Dead - The Ultimate Stock Picks: What to Buy Spotify 👉 https://lnkd.in/eGNN_Mxa Youtube 👉 https://lnkd.in/eue9dsPp Apple Podcasts 👉 https://shorturl.at/p7ETJ My 7 takeaways with Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll 👇 1. The "Supply Chain Risk" Weaponization The Department of Defense’s designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk is a massive escalation. While the immediate loss is a $200 million contract, the real "blast radius" is the potential to freeze the company out of the broader B2B economy. 2. Ambiguity is a B2B Deal Killer In enterprise sales, risk doesn't have to be certain to be fatal: it only has to be ambiguous. Anthropic’s already seeing deals cut in half or stalling because prospects fear government exposure. Competitors like OpenAI are reportedly capitalizing on this by positioning themselves as the "no-problem" alternative. 3. The Death of the Junior Employee We are entering a "world of the middle of the bell curve" regarding experience. Companies no longer want to spend 3–6 months training juniors when AI tools can provide instant, senior-level productivity. This isn't just a theory; Computer Science and Math graduates from solid state schools are already seeing "zero jobs" as companies stop hiring entry level jobs. 4. 24/7 Persistent AI is the Real Compute Driver Most people are currently using AI for episodic tasks (chatting, coding for an hour). But the next frontier is 24/7 persistent AI agents that watch, listen, and run in the background of your entire life. Moving from one agent to 50 agents running in parallel 24 hours a day will require orders of magnitude more compute than we have today. 5. The End of "Gentle Deceleration" In the public markets, the era of managing a polite, high-margin slowdown is dead. Investors are now brutally punishing any company that isn't actively re-accelerating. If you aren't showing CloudFlare-level acceleration or better, the public markets have effectively abandoned you. 6. Built-in Distribution vs. Product Velocity Wix is a fascinating lab experiment for the AI age. They have 6.1 million customers to cross-sell to, which helped their new AI product, Base 44, hit $100 million ARR. However, if that $100M doesn’t exponentially compound to $600M+ quickly, it won't be enough to offset the 1-2% decline in their core legacy business. 7. "Agent-Led Growth" is the New PLG The startups seeing "lines out the door" right now are the ones offering wholesale human replacement.. Founders should be building agents that are 90% better than humans in specific categories like GTM or support. When they can deliver that, the "budget magically comes out of nowhere". "Priced for Perfection" is a Dangerous Game When cybersecurity stocks dropped $20BN following an Anthropic feature release, it wasn't just about the tech; it was about the math. Rory notes that when companies trade at 16x–22x revenues, markets assume "perfection". In this environment, any "increase in tail risk" or a narrative shift leads to a brutal correction. 2. The "Fortnite" Circle is Shrinking for Software Jason uses a powerful analogy: Claude is like the game Fortnite: the safe territory for standalone software is shrinking as AI consumes more features. If your product can be "vibe coded" or exists purely as a feature within a browser or desktop, your surface area is under direct threat from foundation models. 3. Agents > "AI Dust" Incumbents struggle because they merely "sprinkle AI dust" on old analytics. To win, you must own the agent layer for your category. Real agents require custom training and data cleansing—complex work most firms aren't equipped to handle yet. 4. Great Productivity, Brutal Transition Productivity gains are "fricking awesome" long-term , but "Ghost GDP" warns of a "macroeconomic shock". If millions are displaced in months rather than decades, the pace of AI adoption may outstrip society's ability to adjust. 5. The "Toby Playbook" vs. Draconian Cuts Shopify has grown revenue by 50% to $12B without adding a single net headcount in three years. This is the "new normal." While healthy firms can hold headcount flat, Rory warns that highly levered, PE-backed SaaS companies may soon face "traumatic surgery": drastic 50% layoffs just to service their debt. 6. The Era of "Frankenstein" B2B Consolidation What happens to the $50M ARR unicorns with no acquirers? Jason predicts a "capitulation" where 5–20 startups are mashed together at "nominal prices" (1x–2x revenue) to create profitable, professionalized entities. It’s a "miserable way to consolidate debt," but it may be the only play left for many. 7. Momentum is the Only Play (For Now) In a state of total flux, value investing is out; momentum is in. There Are Only Two Types of Companies - Private companies: either hypergrowth or effectively unfundable in today’s market. - Public companies: only accelerating businesses matter, not ones that are slowing. - If you’re not clearly improving fast, it’s not worth the time. 2. The Shift From Being Valued on Revenue Multiples to Free Cash Flow - When investors are comparing you to steady industries, it’s a huge valuation reset. - It will take years of flat stock price and reasonable growth before you can be worth 10-15x FCF. - You don’t see a bottom until these stocks trade at free cash flow multiples net of dilution. 3. NVIDIA Would Have to Bail Out OpenAI - If NVIDIA can afford it, they have to bail out OpenAI if they stumble. - Other competitors like Anthropic are already diversifying to TPUs and AWS. - OpenAI is too big to fail. 4. The Dispersion Between Old and Low Growth and New and High Growth in Terms of Valuation Has Never Been More - We are seeing a heightened dispersion: low-growth companies are at 3x, and high-growth companies are at 50-100x. - New & exciting companies are getting insane multiples, while old & boring companies are going down. - A lot of software companies are moving to old & boring. 5. Why the $100BN Paid for Waymo Is Actually Cheap - Tesla’s market cap is ~$1.2TN. How a16z Do 3x On Their New Fund Size? - a16z raised $15B, about 20% of total venture capital raised. - Exits hit roughly $300B this year, making 3x returns mathematically possible. - With IPOs coming, the market may absorb big funds without breaking. 2. Founders Do Not Care If A Firm Can Invest More At Every Stage - Founders don’t really care if a VC can fund every stage. - They care about help, capital, and terms right now. - Winning great early deals matters more than future promises. 3. Adding A Growth Fund Is A Very Strategic Addition To Small Funds. - Adding a late-stage fund can raise a firm’s profile with founders. - It meaningfully boosts partner economics if executed well. - The risk is misplaying growth and damaging the core franchise. 4. How a16z’s Strategy is Genius & What it Means For The Rest Of Us - a16z split into $BN boutique funds to avoid quality decay. - The real edge is brand power and late-stage cleanup capital. - Smaller funds can win by being earlier and non-consensus. 5. Is The Market So Efficient That Every Great Company Has To Go Through Yc Or Andreessen? - Can $10B companies still be found outside YC and Andreessen? - If not, venture becomes access, signaling, and small checks. - Real alpha depends on true discovery still existing. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. Why The Wealth Tax In California Being Proposed Is Much Worse Than It Seems - This wealth tax is a Trojan horse, not a one-time hit. - The real plan is an annual tax on $25–$50M of paper wealth. - It risks pushing founders to leave long before liquidity. 8. Can the World Support Ten New AGI Labs or Not? - We don’t know if we have enough new territory in AI that won’t be annexed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and other big labs. - New labs will need to meaningfully differentiate themselves to justify multi-billion dollar valuations. - It will be interesting to see if the world can support 10 research labs with 10 different variants of AI. 4. Why OpenAI Has the Largest Stock Based Comp of Any Company Ever? - If you are the CEO with zero shares, you do not worry about dilution. - Sam wants to build the greatest AI company. - If he needs to use equity for hiring & retention, it does not impact him as a shareholder. 5. You Can Identify a Top 0.1% Founder Without Ever Speaking to Them - I have had multiple billion-dollar exits from cold inbound deals. - I analyze the inbound & measure the quality of the founder. - It is not a leap of faith to imagine an AI could do a better job. 6. Business Risk vs Valuation Risk - Early-stage takes uncorrelated business risk. - Late-stage takes highly correlated valuation risk. - When markets dislocate, late-stage pain hits everyone together. 7. author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: There are two things I see SaaS entrepreneurs who are post-Traction and post-Scale say again and again: 1) We’re So Sticky. Once we’re in, it’s so hard to rip us out. 2) Our Churn is Basically Zero in the Enterprise. We’re doing great because No One Leaves. If you’re coming from a Freemium background, or B2C, that will sound amazing! Compare Freemium churn rates of 2-3% a month, to Enterprise SaaS net churn (including upsell / upgrades) that is often less than zero … man it sounds like those Enterprise customers don’t go anywhere. And in truth, Enterprise customers usually don’t go anywhere for 1 or 2 or even 3 years. If you close a Starbucks, and they invest 3 months getting up to speed on your product, and you see real usage — they’re not going anywhere. For now. But here’s the thing. That’s not enough. For two key reasons.

content: If VCs are willing to hand a founder $100m to buy some of their shares, what’s wrong with that? Look, I’m all about Founder Power and I firmly believe, and have for many, many years, that founder secondary done right is a great thing. If founders have been at it for 5+ years, and the business is truly at scale, and past the risk stage, then helping them sell some shares can be just the right thing to help them go long. I believed it then, I believe it now, And as a SaaS founder, I wish I’d taken some of the founder secondary offered to me. It would have pushed me not to sell. But … but … here’s the thing. Traditionally, founders came last. Even in secondaries.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The best way to get from $1m to $10m ARR? More of what you are already doing. Just better. Not new stuff.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: A top piece of advice I can give you as you round $3-$4m in ARR is … expect your sales efficiency to decline after $8-$10m in ARR or so, almost no matter how great your sales team is. Usually, it falls by about half. Why would this be? Let’s examine several factors:

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Because I waited until $4m in ARR, with hindsight, I wasted a lot of time from $1.5m to $4m in ARR. Because we should have just hired every single employee that was Great, no matter if it seemed expensive on paper. But There are two caveats here.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: You don’t have to figure out how to fund a World-Class Revenue Team on Day 1, or even Day 365, probably. But you need to start figuring it out as you pass about $1-$1.25m in ARR.

author: Jason M. Lemkin

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Start-ups are so, so hard. So hard. If you haven’t been a founder before, you really just can’t know how hard it is to create something from dirt and drag it to the first $1m in ARR. And then drag it right up that hill to $10m ARR. And then realize there — it’s just begun. You really can’t know how hard it is, even if you were a VP at a great start-up, even if you were the first employee, even.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: To keep you honest, and help the entire company and team keep track of how you are really doing … build a simple, rolling, “L4M” (Last Four Months) model. It will take just a few minutes. Then use it every month to track against your goal for year-end ARR.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Get to $10m ARR, growing at a decent clip, with positive revenue retention. And then you can get to $300m ARR. It's just math.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Valuations have always come down in each round, but it’s even more accentuated these days. Why? A combination of the fact that so much seed capital in the market is keeping multiples close to all-time highs there (at least for the hottest seed and pre-seed startup.) But also by the fact that public valuations are back to the lows of many years past. Far lower by most counts than any of the past 5+ years. So, what you see is the steepest decline in ARR multiples by stage that I’ve ever seen in my career investing or as a founder. Multiples start off high, and then plummet in each round.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: Almost all of us go through a rough patch right now, and often, one really rough patch. > You can’t fix everything overnight < And maybe sometimes, you can’t even grow your ARR. Some of you won’t be able to grow revenue at all for a stretch or so. But that doesn’t mean you can’t still grow. Grow something that matters, so that when you get back to product-market fit, you’ll grow revenue again, and maybe even faster than before.

author: Jason M. Lemkin
content: The best startups burn less each month than they bring in from new bookings and revenue. A Burn Multiple of 1x or less is relatively efficient, but it’s still a burn. And especially these days, having a Burn Multiple of 1x or less will certainly make you more attractive to VCs — if the growth is also there. If. However, I’ve seen this metric now misused by many venture-backed startups as a magical health meter for a “good enough” burn rate. Why? Well, at a practical level, it assumes the next round is coming.

I can’t tell you how many emails a week a month that go something like this: “It’s been a challenging year with 30%-50% growth, but with some funding, we can grow much faster next year!” or “Our customers love us. While growth has slowed the past few months, with just a bit more capital …” or “We’d be growing faster, but we don’t have the capital” or … Well, you get the point.
